articles.title: Zelenskyy says Russia isn't honoring Trump's energy ceasefire
articles.body:
Ukraine's Zelenskyy says it's "increasingly evident that Russia is unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire"
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that so far, "there is no indication that Russia is complying" with an energy ceasefire announced by President Trump the day before.
Just hours after Mr. Trump's announcement, Zelenskyy said Russia struck a power plant in eastern Ukraine. By Monday afternoon, Russia had attacked six additional energy facilities across Ukraine.
"Ukraine is ready to guarantee the energy ceasefire, as announced by the American President, and Russia must take corresponding steps," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "As of now, there is no indication that Russia is complying with the conditions outlined by the American President."
Asked Monday about reports that Russia had violated the energy ceasefire, Mr. Trump said: "I'm not sure about that, and we'll take a look. But all I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war." He also said "there's been violations on both sides."
The U.S. president later told reporters that he believes Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to make a deal more than Zelenskyy."
Over the last year, Mr. Trump has made several attempts at brokering deals to halt strikes on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine that failed to materialize or were quickly violated.
In January, Mr. Trump claimed that Putin agreed not to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure for a week, but Russia attacked Kyiv's power and heating plants four days later. In September, Mr. Trump said both Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to refrain from striking one another's energy infrastructure, but neither side halted attacks.
Zelenskyy told CBS News in an interview after the September proposal that Ukraine would be willing to agree to such a moratorium but doubted Russia would ever reciprocate.
One reason for the Kremlin's intransigence is that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have a relatively greater impact than Ukraine's. Ukrainian strikes primarily target Russian oil and gas infrastructure, attempting to cut into the energy revenues Russia uses to fund its war effort.
The attacks have brought Russian oil refining to a 20-year low and reduced diesel production by 30% in 2026, according to the International Energy Agency, but Russia's economy has shown little sign of collapse.
"For Russia, Ukraine's attacks are an inconvenience and an inflationary pressure," Alexander Kolyandr, director for Europe at Eurasia Group, told CBS News. "It is definitely damaging Russia's economy, but it isn't putting it on the verge of collapse."
Russia — with more drones and missiles and an economy 10 times the size of Ukraine's — is able to inflict more relative pain on both the country's economy and its civilians. Ukraine has already begun to experience power outages this fall as Russia hammers its power grid heading into winter.
"Because the Ukrainian economy is so much smaller than the Russian one, the relative effect is much higher," Kolyandr said. "And the Russians by and large do not distinguish between civilian and military infrastructure. Their theory is that any kind of infrastructure is used or can be used for military purposes."
Last winter, as Ukrainians faced frequent power and heating outages through one of the coldest winters in recent memory, Mr. Trump requested Putin stop striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. This week, though, he has directed pressure toward Ukraine.
The pressure comes as Mr. Trump grapples with high global energy prices — a situation he has argued has more to do with the Russia-Ukraine war than the Iran war. Last week, Mr. Trump announced a deal to allow Russia to sell some diesel to the U.S. and global markets, a change of course after years of U.S. efforts to block Russia from financing its war effort by selling petroleum products abroad.
A European official and a Ukrainian official told CBS News that the Trump administration has threatened to stop sharing intelligence and to halt the purchase of U.S.-made weapons by European allies for Ukraine via the PURL procurement system if Ukraine does not stop deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian official said that Ukraine's government is taking the threats very seriously as intelligence sharing allows Ukraine to know where and when Russia launches its ballistic missiles from, and the PURL program is the only way Ukraine can purchase its Patriot air defense missiles, already in short supply.
The Financial Times was first to report the American threats to pause intelligence and weapons shipments to Ukraine.
CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.
Zelenskyy said progress toward an energy ceasefire hinges on the White House's willingness to impose more pressure on Russia.
"A lot depends on America's position for de-escalation to actually succeed," he wrote on X. "Pressure on Russia is needed."

articles.title: US Marines to deploy missile systems on Japan island near Taiwan for first time
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US Marine Corps plans to deploy anti-ship and air-defense systems to Japan’s Yonaguni Island, about 110 kilometers from Taiwan, for the first time during a military exercise later this month.
In an article published Saturday by The National Interest, defense analyst Harrison Kass described the planned deployment as part of a “significant transformation in Marine Corps strategy.” The shift emphasizes small, mobile missile units across the Pacific rather than traditional amphibious assault operations.
The deployment is planned for the biennial Keen Sword exercise, scheduled for Oct. 19–29, involving Japan’s Self-Defense Forces and the US military. The Marine Corps plans to bring its Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) and Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS) to Yonaguni.
Yonaguni is Japan’s westernmost inhabited island, near maritime routes connecting the East China Sea and the Pacific. In a Taiwan Strait conflict, “the waters near Yonaguni would become one of the most crucial operating areas in the world,” Kass said, adding that anti-ship missiles could “complicate” Chinese naval movements.
Japan established radar and surveillance facilities on Yonaguni in 2016 as regional security concerns grew, per Defense News. During Chinese military exercises around Taiwan in August 2022, a Chinese ballistic missile landed in waters about 80 kilometers from the island.
NMESIS combines an unmanned ground vehicle with a launcher capable of carrying two Naval Strike Missiles, Kass said. The sea-skimming cruise missiles have a publicly reported range of about 185 kilometers, potentially putting waters off northeastern Taiwan within reach from Yonaguni.
MADIS provides short-range air defense using vehicle-mounted sensors and weapons to counter drones, helicopters, and low-flying aircraft. While NMESIS provides anti-ship firepower, MADIS is designed to protect deployed Marines and missile units from aerial threats.
The systems are part of the Marine Corps’ Force Design modernization initiative, which shifts away from some traditional heavy equipment, such as tanks, toward mobile expeditionary units, precision missiles, drones, and reconnaissance capabilities in contested coastal areas.
Japan is also expanding its missile defenses in the southwestern island chain. Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro said in February that Japan plans to deploy a Type 03 surface-to-air missile unit on Yonaguni by 2030.
The Type 03 system has a reported range of about 50 kilometers and can track up to 100 targets simultaneously while engaging as many as 12, per UDN. Koizumi described the planned deployment as a measure to strengthen Japan’s southwestern island defenses.
During this year’s Keen Sword exercise, Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force is expected to train with its Type 25 anti-ship missile system, which has a reported range of 1,000 kilometers, UDN reported. It will also use the Type 88 anti-ship missile system, which has a range of about 180 kilometers.

articles.title: Iraq targets lingering ISIS pockets with airstrikes, operations in security vacuum after US pullout
articles.body:
In the wake of the US withdrawal from Iraq on September 30, the Iraqi government has increased airstrikes and operations against the Islamic State to avoid ISIS seizing the opportunity to try to mount a comeback. ISIS, though, has been considerably weakened and generally only consists of scattered cells in very rural areas. Iraq appears to be trying to send a message that it will not allow ISIS to exploit the situation.
ISIS rose in Iraq in 2014 during a time of sectarian tension and chaos. The United States had left Iraq in 2011. Under Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, it was not a strong state. Maliki, who was very pro-Iran, was seen as an abusive prime minister by Iraqi Sunnis. The large Arab cities resented his rule. When ISIS appeared as an alternative, sweeping into Iraq from Syria, many backed it in places such as Mosul, Ramadi, and Fallujah.
ISIS was able to defeat two Iraqi army divisions and take most of the equipment from the depots of the units. That move gave it a lot of strength.
Today, ISIS no longer has such strength or any of the influence that gave it power in the past. It consists of aging fighters or a few young recruits and it is scattered in various areas.
However, it has pockets that have never been defeated. One is in the Hamrin Mountains and areas near the Hawija district. Some of these cells have connections further north in the area of Mount Qarachogh, where ISIS has exploited the vacuum in power between the Kurdistan Regional Government and the Iraqi federal forces.
F-16 Airstrikes destroy ISIS elements in Iraqi territory
On Sunday, Iraq’s Security Media Cell, which posts official statements on the Iraqi security forces, said that it had carried out strikes against ISIS.
It said that “based on intensive field monitoring to track terrorist elements, and relying on precise and confirmed intelligence provided by the Military Intelligence Directorate, and in joint coordination with the Aerial Reconnaissance and Surveillance Center in the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, F-16 aircraft carried out two airstrikes targeting a hideout belonging to remnants of ISIS elements in the Nareen area within the Diyala Operations Command sector, resulting in its complete destruction.” The statement didn’t name Islamic State, but it was clear it was the target.
Iraq is worried about ISIS activity west of Kirkuk. It sent Brig.- Gen. Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, to chair a meeting with the Deputy Chief of Staff of the Army for Operations and the Commander of Kirkuk Operations.
“The director of the office listened to a detailed briefing from the commanders regarding the plans for the deployment of units and their openness within the sector of responsibility of the Kirkuk Operations Command,” Iraq’s Security Media Cell said.
“The meeting witnessed in-depth discussions regarding the enhancement of security measures and the securing of borders and villages within the sector, and the attendees concluded with a number of important recommendations that emphasized the importance of intensifying intelligence efforts and coordinating efforts among the various security units to ensure security stability and protect citizens in the province.”
Further reports discussed the threat of ISIS in Iraq.
Shafaq News noted that “ISIS militants struck the same village in Kirkuk’s Hawija district twice in less than 24 hours, and both times they went after the cameras. The attacks disabled thermal imaging equipment that Iraqi forces use to watch open farmland and valleys at night. They have also renewed attention on stretches of northern Iraq that local commanders concede are not fully covered.”
Iraqi, Kurdish forces fighting ISIS for decades
It also noted how Hawija, west of Kirkuk, has been an ISIS hotbed for years.
During the war on ISIS, there was a line of hills overlooking the valley near Hawija. The Kurdish Peshmerga held this line at the time. During most of the war the Peshmerga looked down on the ISIS-held areas in the desert around Hawija. It remained an Islamic State holdout until October 2017, when the Iraqi federal government finally conquered it.
Shafaq said that “on the evening of October 5, militants attacked a position held by the 3rd Battalion of the Federal Police’s 9th Brigade in al-Bargliya, in Hawija’s al-Danadish sector. One officer was killed, four were wounded, and several thermal cameras at the site were destroyed.”
Meanwhile, Arab Weekly noted that “Iraqi security forces carried out an airborne assault on six suspected Islamic State hideouts in Kirkuk province on Monday, highlighting Baghdad’s continuing campaign to eliminate the group’s remaining cells nearly nine years after declaring victory over the militants.”
Iraq’s Joint Operations Command said they had sent forces by helicopter into Zghaitun.
Rudaw, a Kurdish media outlet, wrote that “Iraqi F-16 fighter jets carried out two airstrikes targeting an alleged Islamic State (ISIS) hideout in Diyala province late Sunday, destroying the site as concerns grow over the group’s movements in areas where security gaps persist between Iraqi forces and Kurdish Peshmerga.”
Meanwhile, in nearby Kirkuk, there is a meeting taking place as candidates seek out the office of governor. According to Shafaq, several Turkmen candidates are running.
In another development, Shafaq noted, “Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair is heading to Saudi Arabia to prepare for Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s upcoming visit, with discussions expected to focus on reviving a long-idle oil pipeline linking Iraq to the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu, a government source told Shafaq News on Monday.”
The pipeline stretches from the Zubair oilfield in Iraq’s southern Basra province to Yanbu and was built in the 1980s.
“Operations ceased in 1990, following Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait, while Saudi Arabia repurposed sections on its territory in 2001 to connect with its East-West pipeline, which provides an alternative export route bypassing the Strait of Hormuz,” Shafaq noted.

articles.title: Imagined threat: How Europe learned to manufacture enemies from Israel
articles.body:
The rhetoric of “existential threat” has become the dominant currency of political legitimacy in both Israel and Europe. In Israel, this rhetoric is deeply entrenched—a well-documented doctrine of “permanent war” that frames every adversary as an existential danger requiring eradication rather than negotiation or a possible settlement. In recent years, Europe appeared to have adopted the same Israeli playbook, with leaders warning of an imminent Russian attack on NATO territory despite their own intelligence agencies admitting they see no evidence of such a threat. This is not paranoia; it is a calculated rhetoric, deliberately cultivated by warmongering politicians who benefit from sustaining a permanent threat – real or imagined – whether in Israel, Europe, or anywhere else.
The most striking recent exposure of this manufactured threat came not from Moscow, but from a NATO member state on the front line. On 30th September 2026, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius stated plainly after meeting NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels: “Is there any proof, real proof intelligence services are providing, something on the table, that Russia is getting ready for something? And there is actually none.” If any country had reason to sound the alarm, it would be Lithuania due to its bordering of the Russian territory. Yet its prime minister explicitly warned against exaggeration, stating: “You can’t exaggerate and say, Oh, something is happening in the upcoming months or weeks.” When a leader of a frontline state with Russia is publicly dismissing the narrative of an imminent Russian attack, the question becomes unavoidable: who benefits from insisting otherwise?
Israel’s playbook: The doctrine of permanent war and victimhood
Israel’s use of the existential threat narrative is not a reaction to genuine peril but a deliberate strategy. To justify its open-ended military occupation, aggressive and expansionist agenda, Israeli leaders for decades played the victimhood card that it is being under constant existential threats, invoking the Holocaust and the spectre of annihilation.
Imagine how this playbook is blatantly applied, Israeli leaders, after committing a genocide and almost totally destroying Gaza, still say about dangers and threats coming from Gaza.
In both southern Syria and Lebanon, Israel occupies vast areas of both countries while still pretending to be under the threat and danger.
Israeli Army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has framed the current confrontation as a “decisive battle” against existential threats that emerged after 7th October, opening the door to continuous fighting that will not stop until the “imagined threat” to the security establishment disappears. David Barnea, while in power as Mossad chief, similarly re-proposed the goal of “overthrowing the Iranian regime” as an existential imperative.
This doctrine serves multiple functions. Domestically, it suppresses any discussion of political alternatives or peaceful settlements, and allows to move ahead with its expansionist agenda in the region, making war the only option on the table.
Externally, it exploits Europe’s guilt over the Holocaust to extract unconditional support for such policies, with Netanyahu claiming Israel is defending “Western civilisation” against “evil regimes.”
The result is a permanent rhetoric that legitimises aggression as self-defence and portrays Israel as a victim.
Europe follows: The Russian threat that isn’t
Over the past years, it became clearer that Europe adopted this same tactic toward Russia. In mid-September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament that intelligence assessments suggest Russia may be preparing a drone or missile attack on NATO territory in the near future. However, he did not identify the intelligence services behind his assessment, according news reports. French President Emmanuel Macron backed Tusk’s assessment, calling the warnings “sound and well documented,” and convened an emergency meeting in Paris to discuss “the threat.”
Yet the evidence for this imminent threat is strikingly thin. A senior EU official, speaking anonymously, stated in August 2026 that “European intelligence services generally do not currently see the risk of a Russian attack on European countries, and this assessment has not changed.” The official added that regarding potential threats to NATO members, “we see nothing indicating that anything is currently being prepared.” Estonian Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov went further, criticizing what he called “panic on social media.” These official denials are not isolated remarks; they reveal a systematic effort by certain European circles to cultivate a state of enmity with Russia and to keep the narrative of an imagined threat alive on the table—not because the threat is real, but because it serves their political agenda.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly denied any intention to attack Europe. “I want to emphasise once again: we are not preparing any military action against Europe, we have no such plans. Most importantly, there is no reason to do so.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also dismissed the warnings as “alarmist stories” that “of course have nothing to do with reality.”
The function of manufactured threats
Why would European leaders manufacture a threat that their own intelligence services say does not exist? The answer lies in the same functions the tactic serves in Israel, which is to advance a political agenda over any other one, domestic control, military budgets, and justification of aggressive policies.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico warned in September 2026 that some Western politicians are trying to provoke a direct NATO-Russia conflict after their strategy of defeating Moscow via Ukraine failed, calling it a “deadly danger.” The logic is clear: when military and political strategies fail, a new threat must be invented to justify continued militarisation and the suppression of any opposition.
Europe’s adoption of Israel’s playbook is not merely an imitation; it is a shared strategy of governance through permanent emergency. Both Israel and Europe have found that an imagined enemy is more useful than a real one. A real enemy can be negotiated with, contained, or defeated. An imagined enemy is eternal, requiring eternal vigilance, eternal militarisation, and eternal obedience.
The danger of this approach is not just that it manufactures war. It also manufactures the conditions for the erosion of democracy. When every critic becomes a potential traitor and every question becomes a security threat, the space for genuine political debate collapses. The playbook that Israel perfected in its treatment of Palestinians — dehumanisation, permanent emergency, and the criminalisation of dissent — is now being applied to Europe’s relationship with Russia. A stark example on this imitation was documented in early October when Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken publicly claimed that Russian drones had been detected over Belgian military barracks, presenting it as proof of Russia’s hostile intentions. However, the Belgian public broadcaster VRT investigated and found that the drones never existed. The report revealed that Francken had invented the threats to obtain additional budget funds for his ministry.
While a genuine conflict and dispute do exist between Europe and Russia, Moscow has consistently called for dialogue to resolve their differences. It did so in the context of the war in Ukraine, only to find that Zelensky was provoked – or perhaps even ordered – to reject a negotiated settlement and to continue his endless war with Russia. This serves the interests of some European circles and leaders who persist in portraying an imagined Russian threat, revealing themselves as warmongers as their Israeli counterparts; more committed to prolonging the conflict than to seeking its settlement.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: Europe still divided on buying locally for defence, MBDA CEO says
articles.body:
Europe still divided on buying locally for defence, MBDA CEO says
Oct 12 - The head of European missile maker MBDA said on Monday that efforts to steer more defence spending towards European suppliers faced political hurdles, with EU governments still divided over how much to rely on US security guarantees.
Washington has been pressing European NATO allies to increase defence spending, while France has led calls to buy more European-made weapons amid questions over the US commitment to Europe's security.
"Do we want as Europeans to really take our own fate in our hands and then bring our European capabilities to the NATO alliance, or are we simply increasing our capabilities by buying outside?" MBDA CEO Eric Beranger asked the Warsaw Security Forum.
"There are some different attitudes between the various governments. I think the jury is still out," Beranger said, adding: "There is still some way to go".
DETERRENCE
Beranger, who steps down next month, was among several speakers debating European strategic autonomy at the forum, which is taking place amid heightened tensions over the war in Ukraine.
Several European countries, including conference host Poland, Germany and the Netherlands, have turned to US suppliers for equipment such as F-35 fighter jets.
"Limiting American defense industry in European procurement programs threatens that partnership and weakens our mutual security", the US mission to the European Union said in February.
Nuclear deterrence was also a focus of the discussion, with Russia recently renewing warnings that it could use nuclear weapons to defend itself.
"Of all the events at this conference that the Russians will be most interested in hearing ... it will be this one", former British defence minister Ben Wallace said, referring to Europe's ability to strengthen its nuclear and conventional deterrence.
"Deterrence is not only capabilities; deterrence is also perceptions. Do we believe our American allies will come? Does Russia believe our American allies will come?" said Claudia Major, senior vice president for transatlantic security at the German Marshall Fund.
"I don't say give up on the US. I just say don't blind ourselves", Major added, citing recent friction with the US over Greenland, Russia and Ukraine.
NATO members, including the US, reaffirmed their commitment to collective defence in the Ankara Summit Declaration in July, repeating that "an attack on one is an attack on all".
Stressing that credibility is central to deterrence, Beranger said Europe already had the industrial base it needed to strengthen its defences. REUTERS

articles.title: Iran’s two-front war on Israel: From October 7 to election interference - opinion
articles.body:
Iran’s hand in the Hamas-led October 7 massacre went beyond rockets and training camps. Reports say Persian was heard among the terrorists during the attack. A parallel campaign of Iranian hackers and fake accounts opened a second front, now reopening ahead of the election.
The internal front
Three years after the massacre
On the morning of October 7, 2023, on Simchat Torah, thousands of terrorists broke through the Gaza border fence, overrunning IDF posts, kibbutzim, the Nova music festival, and Sderot. Some 1,200 people were murdered, most of them civilians, and 251 were dragged into Gaza as hostages. It was the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust.
‘They were speaking Farsi’
Survivors are still piecing together that day themselves.
Eyal Eshel, whose daughter Roni was killed at the Nahal Oz base, told Channel 2 that survivors heard terrorists inside the compound speaking to each other in Farsi.
“I understand from this detail that they collected information about us before October 7,” he said, adding that bereaved families were gathering such facts “ourselves.” The IDF has not confirmed the account, which remains survivor testimony. But it raises the question Israel has asked since that morning: How deep was Iran’s hand in the attack?
Why Persian? Tehran’s fingerprints
Evidence of Iranian sponsorship is heavy: training, planning, money, and weapons.
The Wall Street Journal reported that some 500 Hamas and Islamic Jihad operatives received combat training in Iran in September 2023, led by the IRGC, with Quds Force commander Esmail Qaani attending.
Hamas minutes seized by the IDF show Yahya Sinwar spent over two years planning the attack and worked to persuade Iran and Hezbollah to join a wider war.
The IDF has accused Iran of supplying Hamas with weapons, money, and technological know-how for years.
Washington was more cautious: the secretary of state at the time, Antony Blinken, said the US had no direct evidence Iran planned the attack, “but that could change.”
The pattern is clear: Hamas pulled the trigger, but the gun, the training, and the strategy of a multi-front war came from Iran.
The external front
Cyber warfare: hacking for headlines
Since October 7, Iran has sharply escalated cyber operations against Israel, according to the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), through fronts such as Handala Hack, CyberAv3ngers, and IDFLeaks.
Handala, tied to Iran’s Intelligence Ministry, has leaked the phone of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s aide Tzachi Braverman, breached Naftali Bennett’s Telegram account, doxxed Unit 8200 members, and claimed 197 gigabytes from the Nahal Sorek nuclear center.
“Most of its mission is to damage public trust, create a sense of penetration, and amplify media resonance,” said Rafael Franco, former deputy head of the National Cyber Directorate.
Offline, counter-espionage arrests rose 400% in 2024 as Iran recruited Israelis on Telegram for surveillance and sabotage.
The bot army that was waiting
The Israeli firm Cyabra scanned over 162,000 accounts discussing the attack and found one in four was fake.
In the first 48 hours, it found ~40,695 fake profiles and 312,000+ pro-Hamas comments and posts, with 531 million+ views.
Many accounts were created over a year earlier and lay dormant until October 7 – preparation, not spontaneous outrage.
Iran hosts, its partners amplify
Iran did not fight alone – its partners shared interests, not a command.
Iran played the role of the host, sponsoring Hamas and contributing hacking units, fake outlets, and bots to their mission.
Qatar was the megaphone. It contributed to Hamas’s Doha leadership and Al Jazeera’s reach. Nearly a third of profiles engaging with AJ+ on X/Twitter were fake.
Turkey was a safe haven. It hosted Hamas officials and contributed by pushing the same narratives through state media and troll networks.
The result: an echo chamber, where a Hamas Telegram claim could be picked up by Al Jazeera, repeated by Turkish outlets and multiplied by fake accounts within hours.
What the bots did
According to Cyabra and FDD, the networks hijacked hashtags like #IStandWithIsrael, recycled old war footage as fresh evidence from Gaza, rewrote the massacre as justified (seeds of today’s denial), and targeted Israelis directly through Hebrew fake outlets like “Dofek TV” and AI deepfakes.
They left a distorted global picture, pressure on hostage families and soldiers, eroded trust at home, and an infrastructure that can be switched back on at any moment.
The next battle: October 27
The bots are back
Security officials warn Iranian influence operations are already underway to deepen Israeli divisions ahead of the vote.
An investigation by the OSINT platform Golden Owl, reported by The Jerusalem Post, mapped 119,717 accounts and confirmed 57 as part of an Iran-linked campaign posing as Israelis.
Fifty-seven may sound small. But October 7 showed what a small, patient network can do: plant a narrative and let real users spread it for free.
Israel cannot be caught off guard twice
Before October 7, the warning signs were there. Israel saw pieces of the picture and didn’t act on the whole. Three weeks before the vote, we cannot make that mistake again.
Israel should treat October 27 as a likely target and prepare now. That means protecting the vote. Election systems, party databases, and the Central Elections Committee’s infrastructure should be hardened and tested, with backup plans ready.
It also means we must expect a strike timed to the vote. Handala hits at the moment of maximum impact; a fake “leak,” false results, or a deepfake on election morning should be planned for, not hoped away.
Platforms must be held accountable. X, Meta, TikTok, and Telegram must act fast against networks researchers have already exposed.
We must also stay alert beyond the screen. Iran has opened multiple fronts before. Security services should be on heightened alert for any attempt to exploit election day, online or off.
The front line is every phone
The government can’t do this alone. Before you share a shocking clip, an anonymous “leak,” or a post designed to make you hate your neighbor, ask who benefits. Too often, the answer is Tehran.
Three years ago, Iran helped bring a massacre to Israel’s border. Since then, it has waged a quieter war on what rockets can’t destroy: Israelis’ trust in each other. The answer is not panic but preparedness.
If Israel goes into October 27 alert, protected, and united enough to vote on its own terms, it will have won a battle Iran spent years preparing for.

articles.title: US claims do not match what we see on the ground: Baqaei
articles.body:
US claims do not match what we see on the ground: Baqaei
TEHRAN— Iran has dismissed US assertions that maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to normal, saying Washington’s continued naval blockade and economic sanctions are incompatible with restoring security to the strategic waterway.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei made the remarks at his weekly press conference in Tehran on Monday, addressing the situation in the strait, the latest exchanges between Tehran and Washington through mediators, US sanctions, regional tensions and remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio invoking ancient Greek and Persian history.
Baqaei said the situation in the Strait of Hormuz was a direct consequence of the US-Israeli war against Iran, which began on February 28, and rejected assertions that Iran had lost its strategic leverage.
“The Americans’ claims do not match what we see on the ground,” he said. “They can continue to claim that the Strait of Hormuz no longer matters and that Iran has lost its leverage, but we will continue to do our job.”
He added that developments in international markets and efforts by countries to secure fuel supplies demonstrated the continuing importance of the waterway.
Hormuz security linked to an end to US pressure
Baqaei stressed that Iran had not introduced maritime controls to gain leverage over other countries, arguing that the measures taken in the strait were a response to the security circumstances created by the US-Israeli attacks.
“What we have been witnessing in this waterway since February 28 is the direct result of actions by the US and the Zionist regime in attacking Iran,” he said. The waterway, he added, had been used to launch attacks against Iran, prompting Tehran to adopt measures that it considers consistent with international law.
The spokesperson said security would not be restored while Washington continued its naval blockade and economic pressure against Iran. He described these measures as acts of aggression that had consequences extending beyond Iran to the wider region and international markets.
“We are not pleased with this situation, as the security of the Strait of Hormuz is necessary for us more than anything else,” Baqaei said. “However, the United States’ aggressive actions have caused trouble for itself, the region, and the world.”
The remarks also addressed Washington’s claims that the waterway was under US control. Baqaei said such assertions bore little resemblance to the situation on the ground and questioned why the United States would seek assistance from Russia to address its oil supply needs if, as Washington maintained, the situation in Hormuz had been resolved.
Responding to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s stated readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to international markets, including the United States, Baqaei said each country was entitled to make decisions according to its national interests. He nevertheless described Washington’s reported interest in Russian supplies as significant in light of its assertions about the strait.
Iran reviewing US response to seven-point proposal
Baqaei said Iran was still examining Washington’s response to Tehran’s seven-point proposal, with communications between the two sides continuing through intermediaries.
He said the proposal, discussed on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, addressed Iran’s demands, including the lifting of the naval blockade, an end to the war on all fronts and the release of Iranian assets. According to the spokesperson, these issues were also covered by a memorandum of understanding previously agreed upon.
Iran would convey its position to the mediators once the review was complete, he said, adding that the new US sanctions imposed during the process must also be lifted.
Pakistan and Qatar, he said, remained the principal mediators between Tehran and Washington. Iran also welcomed the good offices of friendly countries, including Russia.
Addressing remarks that the US response had fallen short of Iran’s expectations, Baqaei indicated that Tehran was still assessing the points raised by Washington before communicating its position through the intermediaries.
Baqaei also addressed the nuclear issue, questioning Washington’s continued emphasis on Iran’s nuclear program after US officials had repeatedly asserted that it had been destroyed. He argued that attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities and the lack of an effective international response had prompted debate inside Iran about the benefits of continued membership in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).
He said the international non-proliferation framework faced challenges in all three of its principal areas: nuclear disarmament, preventing the spread of nuclear weapons and ensuring countries’ access to peaceful nuclear technology.
Iran seeks dialogue to ease regional tensions
Turning to regional developments, Baqaei said Iran remained deeply concerned about escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and was ready to use its good offices to facilitate dialogue.
He said Tehran opposed continued conflict between two Muslim countries, arguing that further escalation would undermine regional stability and create opportunities for Israel to exploit divisions.
Iran had repeatedly supported the implementation of understandings previously reached between the parties, he said, urging them to return to dialogue and prevent further deterioration.
Baqaei also welcomed the prospect of stronger relations between Iraq and Saudi Arabia, reiterating Iran’s support for greater cooperation among regional countries. Tehran had previously proposed meetings involving Persian Gulf littoral states, including Iran and Iraq, and continued to support initiatives aimed at strengthening regional trust.
“Strengthening relations and trust among regional countries is the foundation and prerequisite for creating a secure region, free from the destructive interference of foreign actors,” he said.
On reports alleging that the United Arab Emirates was providing intelligence, financial or logistical support to terrorist groups operating in eastern Iran, Baqaei said Iranian security, military and law-enforcement agencies were monitoring such activities.
He described efforts to destabilize Iran’s borders as part of a US-Israeli plan, while emphasizing that Tehran was in continuous consultation with its land and maritime neighbors to prevent terrorist groups from exploiting the regional situation. He did not identify a specific neighboring country as responsible for supporting the groups.

articles.title: When pilgrims became targets, billions could not save them
articles.body:
The white ihram garments of Umrah pilgrims, stained crimson on the departure concourse of King Khalid International Airport. That image, seared into the global consciousness across the first weeks of October 2026, will define this moment for generations. It marks far more than a military operation; it is a definitive rupture in how the world understands power, vulnerability, and the fragile architecture of modern security.
What unfolded across 6–11 October was not merely a barrage of missiles and drones. A non-state militia emerging from one of the most impoverished regions on earth achieved what no conventional military force had accomplished in decades, piercing the multi-billion-dollar defensive shield of a G20 capital and bringing its flagship aviation hub to a standstill.
The multi-day bombardment killed at least 13 people and injured over 320, including pilgrims, international workers, and families with no connection to any political or military decision. Among the dead were Mohammed Yousuf, a 46-year-old Indian IT professional travelling with his family for Umrah, and Mufti Md Nasrullah Badrpur, a respected Bangladeshi Islamic scholar. These were not combatants. They were the guests of God.
This tragedy forces an urgent reckoning with a foundational doctrine of the modern state: that capital and technology can purchase absolute security. Riyadh constructed a defensive architecture of extraordinary sophistication: Patriot batteries, layered radar networks, advanced early-warning systems. The Houthis defeated it not through superior technology but through superior arithmetic.
Their layered assault combined low-altitude radar-evading cruise missiles, swarms of cheap suicide drones, and heavy ballistic missiles timed to exploit the window when defensive batteries were overwhelmed or reloading.
This is the buffer overflow doctrine: every defensive system possesses finite computational bandwidth, and when incoming threats exceed that capacity, the system collapses into paralysis.
The cost-exchange ratio is devastating. A single Patriot interceptor costs between three and four million dollars, with some estimates placing the PAC-2 GEM-T variant as high as four to six million dollars. A Houthi drone costs as little as $20,000 to $50,000, while a modified R-27 air-to-air missile repurposed for ground attack carries a conversion cost of roughly $20,000. This creates an exchange ratio sometimes estimated at eighty-five to one, according to analyses; the attacker needs to succeed only once to shatter the illusion of stability; the defender must be perfect one hundred per cent of the time.
As reported, Saudi Arabia is now running low on air-defence interceptors, shifting batteries around the country to protect palaces and energy infrastructure while seeking emergency assistance from Pakistan and other allies. This asymmetry represents the most significant strategic development since the advent of precision-guided munitions.
The ideological architecture behind Saudi statecraft, known as the ‘myth of impermeability’, was based on the notion that superior riches and Western defence technologies could create an inviolable island of hyper-modernity amid a chaotic area. The strikes exposed this as a dangerous delusion.
But something far more profound was also revealed: the targeting of pilgrims in ihram, individuals in a state of sacred purity entirely separated from worldly conflicts, represents a transgression that has unified the global Muslim community in unprecedented condemnation.
Al-Azhar Al-Sharif, the premier seat of Sunni Islamic learning, issued a binding fatwa classifying the attack as Hirabah, a crime of waging war against society and divine order, effectively stripping the perpetrators of any religious legitimacy.
The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation has condemned the targeting of Makkah-bound pilgrims as an affront to Islamic values, emphasising that the safety of pilgrims is a sacred red line that must transcend any geopolitical conflict. As coalition spokesman Turki Al-Maliki declared, the security of the Two Holy Mosques and the safety of pilgrims remains a red line.
The economic implications for Saudi Vision 2030 are equally severe. National carrier Saudia was forced to cancel seventy per cent of scheduled departures from Riyadh. Flights at the airport were reduced by approximately eighty-five per cent as of 11 October. The nascent flagship carrier Riyadh Air paused its operations entirely. Global carriers including Emirates, Etihad, and Qatar Airways suspended hub connections.
The strikes occurred on the eve of the World Petroleum Council Energy Congress and weeks before the Future Investment Initiative events where billions in foreign direct investment were to be secured for the kingdom’s transformative agenda.
BP CEO Meg O’Neill and Shell CEO Wael Sawan both notified organisers they could not attend due to flight disruptions. The Clingendael Institute has assessed that Vision 2030’s core assumptions attracting foreign investment, competing with the UAE, and prioritising sectors like AI and tourism are threatened by wartime physical, economic, and political damage. The lesson for global investors is stark: no amount of sovereign wealth can guarantee the physical security upon which economic continuity depends.
The international response has been remarkable. The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, representing pilgrim-sending nations including Indonesia, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Egypt, and Turkey, has moved rapidly to establish a Sacred Corridors framework, a diplomatic initiative to designate all transit routes for religious pilgrimage as permanently demilitarised zones under international protection.
This represents an extraordinary innovation in international humanitarian law, expanding the concept of protected spaces from fixed properties to dynamic transit vectors. The proposal would move through a UN General Assembly resolution to establish broad consensus, followed by a Chapter VII Security Council mandate to make the protection binding and enforceable.
For the United States, the strikes present a strategic dilemma of profound consequence. President Trump has confirmed that Washington is evaluating direct military action against Houthi infrastructure following the death of an American citizen. Yet Washington has so far resisted Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s requests for military help to roll back Houthi advances in Yemen, though it has sent military advisers.
The argument for diplomatic enforcement rather than kinetic escalation grows more compelling by the day. The security of the Two Holy Mosques, revered by over a billion Muslims worldwide, cannot be guaranteed through military means alone. The sanctity of Makkah and Madinah demands a political settlement that addresses the underlying regional conflicts driving this escalation.
The Houthis themselves are no longer second- or third-tier members of Iran’s Axis of Resistance, as RAND analysts have observed. While they benefit from Iranian weapons, training, and know-how, they also have their own interests at heart and behave accordingly. They are in a position to shape the next phase of the conflict between the United States and Iran, and they control a choke point at the Bab al-Mandeb through which twelve to fifteen per cent of maritime trade travels. This is not a proxy that can be controlled; it is an autonomous actor with strategic reach.
The Riyadh strikes have definitively ended the era of localised warfare. Geographic distance no longer guarantees safety. A militia operating from one of the world’s poorest nations can now directly disrupt the economic continuity of a global superpower.
The hub-and-spoke model that underpins modern globalisation the concentration of value in single nodes of maximum efficiency has revealed itself as a single point of failure. As researchers have demonstrated, critical infrastructure networks exhibit complex interdependencies that can lead to cascading failures with catastrophic consequences, where single-node disruptions propagate rapidly due to structural dependencies and high-impact linkages.
The implication for the global community is unmistakable. Security in the twenty-first century cannot be purchased through technology alone. It requires political stabilisation, diplomatic engagement, and the construction of new legal architectures capable of protecting the innocent from the cruel arithmetic of asymmetric conflict.
The blood on those white garments demands nothing less. The question is not whether the world will learn these lessons, but whether it will act before the next illusion of security is shattered.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.
