articles.title: Trump's energy truce claim baffles Kyiv as Russian strikes continue
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Russia continues to strike Ukraine's energy facilities, despite President Donald Trump's claim a day earlier that both nations had agreed to an energy cease-fire.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had learned through media reports that Trump had secured an energy cease-fire deal with Russia which would involve a mutual pause in strikes on energy sites. Zelenskyy said he would be willing to honor such an agreement, if Moscow did the same.
"We support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side," Zelenskyy said.
Trump's brief social media post Sunday claiming the purported agreement offered few details but said that the energy cease-fire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!"
Yet Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been "horribly surprised" that following Trump's "sudden but very important post," Russia had struck numerous energy facilities including a power plant in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, as well as a gas production facility and a civilian gas station.
"It was clear that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform.
Trump previously announced a similar agreement on ceasing energy strikes that did not come to fruition. In a social media post on Sept. 14, he said both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure, but offered no details on that proposal either.
Russia has used attacks on energy facilities in order to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter," and fear Russia could ramp up such attacks as cold weather approaches.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has leveled strikes against Russian energy sites like oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory, prompting Trump to blame Zelenskyy for high diesel prices on world markets.
On Friday, Trump struck a deal with Putin to import Russian diesel in an attempt to address high fuel prices just weeks ahead of U.S. midterm elections.
On Monday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to comply with Trump's requests to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree. He added that if Moscow does not agree to an energy cease-fire this winter, "we will respond."
"We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take," he said. "This energy cease-fire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war."
The European Union's top diplomat Monday welcomed the prospect of a pause in energy strikes in Ukraine, particularly as winter approaches, but said she sees no sign that Russia would be willing to respect it.
"We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
"Personally, I would also welcome that the cease-fire would include people not being killed, not only energy," she added.
Ukrainian and European officials reacted with dismay to Trump's diesel deal with Putin, saying it will help fund Russia's war effort.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told reporters in Luxembourg Monday that he doesn't believe the deal "is actually going to change anything" in terms of fuel prices and that it is "much more connected to the domestic situation in the U.S."
Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief, also pushed back on Trump's comments on Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and that Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war. She said that now is not the time to hold elections in Ukraine, at least not without a cease-fire.
On Monday, Zelenskyy said holding elections in Ukraine was impossible during war time, especially with new Russian tactics involving attacks during both the day and night.
"Under such circumstances, it's impossible to hold elections," he said, but added that he would be ready to work toward doing so if Ukraine secured a full cease-fire lasting at least 60 days.
A Russian drone attack on the village of Pisochyn in the Kharkiv district on Sunday evening killed three people and injured nine others, including children, according to the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office.
Investigators said the attack occurred at approximately 7:25 p.m., striking a densely populated area near apartment buildings and grocery stores and sparking a fire.
Ukrainian air defense forces shot down or suppressed 89 of 121 Russian drones overnight Monday, Ukraine's Air Force said in a Telegram post.
The attack involved one Kh-59 guided air-to-surface missile and 121 drones, including 76 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, the statement said.
Strikes were recorded at 15 locations in Ukraine, while debris from downed drones fell at four locations.
The Russian Defense Ministry Monday said its air defenses overnight intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions as well as the illegally annexed Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.
In a separate statement, the ministry said its forces overnight carried out drone strikes on Ukraine's unspecified port infrastructure and a bulk carrier heading to Ukraine's port city of Odesa with military cargo on board.

articles.title: Iran offers to mediate between its Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Iran offers to mediate between its Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia
Erika Solomon
- Iran offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia, saying there is no military solution to conflicts in the Middle East.
- A Houthi strike on Riyadh airport killed at least 12 people and injured hundreds, followed by reported strikes on Sanaa and more drone and missile threats.
- The conflict has widened across Yemen and the Gulf, raising fears of fresh regional fighting as Iran warns it could target digital infrastructure if war resumes.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen, after a string of deadly attacks on the kingdom, warning that overlapping conflicts in the region have no military solution.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made the offer to his Saudi counterpart, Faisal bin Farhan, during a telephone call on Oct 11, according to a statement posted on social media by the Iranian minister’s office.
“Insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution will further complicate the current situation,” the statement, posted on Araghchi’s Telegram channel, said.
Araghchi said Iran stood “ready to provide any assistance to help initiate a dialogue” between the two sides.
The Saudi government said the two ministers spoke, though it made no reference to any mediation offer from Iran. The call was a day after the deadliest attack on a Persian Gulf country since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran.
On Oct 10, a Houthi strike on an airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, killed at least 12 people, with hundreds injured.
That sparked an exchange of strikes with Saudi-led forces targeting the airport in Sanaa, Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, according to reports on Oct 11 in local news media affiliated with the group.
The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was also killed in a strike on a residential building in Sanaa.
Saudi authorities have not commented on those assertions, but reported another deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s airport on Oct 11.
On Oct 12, a state-owned Saudi television channel, Al Ekhbariya, warned that the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen was fending off drones and cruise missiles headed toward Saudi Arabia. The Saudi authorities have not commented publicly.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis rapidly escalated in September when Houthi forces seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking territory that sits alongside a strategic waterway for global trade and a key export route for Saudi oil.
The militia has been fighting the internationally recognised government of Yemen, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, since 2014. A fragile truce agreed in 2022 has unravelled in recent months.
The conflict has stoked further upheaval in the oil-rich Persian Gulf region, which was already reeling from the economic fallout of the US-Iran war.
US and Iranian officials appear braced for the possibility that their stalemated regional conflict could spill back into the open, with the Pentagon drawing up new plans for strikes.
Iran’s national security adviser, Mohsen Rezaei, threatened on Oct 11 that if fighting were to resume, Iranian forces would target digital infrastructure in the Gulf, including data centres, cables, and artificial intelligence facilities.
The Houthis are one of several militant groups that Iran is allied with across the region, and part of what the Islamic republic calls its “Axis of Resistance”.
Though the Houthis have benefited from years of military and financial support from Iran, regional experts have long described them as among the most independent of these allied forces, with ambitions distinct from Iran’s. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

articles.title: Report: Trump administration threatens Ukraine arms cutoff over Russian oil strikes
articles.body:
Russia struck power plants in Ukraine on Sunday night despite U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement of an "energy ceasefire" between the two countries. Meanwhile, Britain's Financial Times reported that the Trump administration had threatened to suspend arms supplies to Ukraine unless Kyiv halted its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
The report, citing senior European officials, said Washington was pressuring European governments and Kyiv to stop attacks on oil refineries deep inside Russia. The American message reportedly included threats to cut off intelligence sharing and suspend the mechanism through which Ukraine obtains U.S. weapons.
Among those contacted by U.S. officials was Zelensky's military adviser Pavlo Palisa, a former Ukrainian army general. One European official who spoke to the Financial Times said he had personally received a call from a U.S. defense official. "They're calling Kyiv, they're calling everyone in Europe," he said.
On Sunday, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had both agreed to an energy ceasefire under which neither side would attack the other's energy facilities. Neither country confirmed his announcement, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky responded shortly afterward: "That's news to me."
Despite Trump's announcement, Russia struck power plants in Kharkiv and Kyiv on Sunday night, shortly after the purported ceasefire was supposed to take effect. "Our repair crews are only now restoring electricity and water supplies to Kyiv. Nobody has heard of a ceasefire," a senior Ukrainian official close to Zelensky told the Financial Times.
Zelensky's pointed response came after he had already reacted to Trump's call for him to be replaced, saying he would be prepared to hold elections if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. "With all due respect to President Trump, our society, our people, are the ones who should decide who will be president of Ukraine," Zelensky told ABC News.
‘Find a new leader who can make a deal’
Trump called on Ukraine on Saturday to find a "new president" after Zelensky criticized a diesel agreement the American president had reached with Putin's Russia. The agreement would ease sanctions on Moscow and allow it to export diesel to countries around the world in an effort to ease shortages and curb rising prices. The deal drew sharp criticism from Ukraine and European governments, which warned that it would generate substantial revenue for Putin's government and help finance Russia's continued war against Ukraine.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump was asked about Russian attacks on Ukraine, which have intensified recently and killed dozens more civilians in two particularly deadly strikes in recent days. But rather than offer even indirect criticism of the Kremlin, he turned his anger on Zelensky. "I suggest they find a new leader who can make a deal. Because he could have made a lot of deals, and for some reason he never does. This is a war that should never have started, and I think it's time for Ukraine to find a new president," Trump said.
For the past two years, Zelensky and his aides have repeatedly rejected the idea of holding elections while large numbers of Ukrainian refugees remain outside the country and Russia continues its attacks. His statement on Sunday that he would be willing to organize elections if Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire appears to signal an initial willingness to hold a vote even before the war ends. However, Zelensky likely knows that the Russian president is unlikely to accept such a condition.
Earlier, Zelensky also responded to Trump's demand that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv has targeted in recent months. Those strikes caused a severe fuel crisis in Russia over the summer and forced Moscow, normally a major fuel exporter, to temporarily suspend diesel exports to preserve supplies for its own population. The disruption contributed to rising diesel prices, alongside increases driven by the war with Iran. For weeks, Trump has blamed Zelensky for rising global diesel prices, seeking to portray Ukraine, rather than the war with Iran, as the main cause of higher fuel costs burdening Americans ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections.
In a response posted on X, Zelensky wrote: "Ukraine will be ready to stop striking oil refineries in Russia if Russia stops attacking our energy infrastructure. Strikes on energy infrastructure could stop today, but Putin is not interested." He added that any step toward de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by concrete guarantees. A few hours later, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire, but neither side has formally confirmed such an agreement. Zelensky said the announcement was "news to me," adding that Ukraine would agree to such a ceasefire if Russia did.

articles.title: NATO says will do ‘anything and everything’ if alliance is attacked
articles.body:
NATO says will do ‘anything and everything’ if alliance is attacked
NATO commander issues warning as European officials suggest potential Russian attacks.
NATO’s top commander has warned that his forces would destroy “anything and everything” if someone was “foolish enough” to attack the alliance, as European concerns have mounted over a potential Russian attack on its territory amid the war in Ukraine.
“We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us,” US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich told the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, without mentioning Russia by name.
Grynkewich stressed that NATO is a defensive alliance and that he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable. The most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to “resolve misunderstandings”, he added.
European governments have accused Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks against them, while Russia warned last month it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Baltic Kaliningrad exclave where it has a major military outpost.
NATO’s 10-year strategy, created in 2022, described Russia as the alliance’s most significant security threat.
“We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile,” Grynkewich said.
Attacking anything that ‘supports, sustains and controls that force’
Grynkewich added that NATO’s response would not be limited to forces involved in an initial attack.
“Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us,” he said.
“This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls that force.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin said this month that Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully. Such declarations have not reassured European leaders, who cite similar statements by Russia before its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Moscow has also repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage and other hybrid operations.
‘We’ve got this’
Grynkewich said he had decided to talk publicly about NATO’s plans because recent acts of sabotage and arson had made people around the alliance nervous.
“What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it,” he said.
Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington’s commitment to the alliance, citing President Donald Trump’s reception at a NATO summit in Ankara in July.
“I was in the room and I felt the love,” he said.

articles.title: The weapon shifting Yemen’s frontlines
articles.body:
The weapon shifting Yemen’s frontlines
By Ali Minabi
TEHRAN – While Yemeni missile attacks on Riyadh airport capture global headlines, another tactical weapon has shifted the frontlines near Bab al-Mandab.
Recent military developments on Yemen’s southwestern fronts have introduced a new and significant tactical shift in the course of the confrontation between Sanaa and Riyadh. This came after the Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF) announced that the Shawaz drone had entered operational service for the first time.
The drone was used to target Saudi-backed forces advancing from the direction of Lahij governorate toward the areas of Al-Wazi’iyah district (Taiz governorate) and Kahbub (strategic high ground), both adjacent to the international shipping lane at Bab al-Mandab.
Over the past week, the YAF’s War Media division has released footage documenting operations to repel and pursue Saudi-backed forces and their vehicles using this type of drone. The footage shows substantial losses among those fighters at their field positions, creating an obstacle to attempts to break through in this strategically vital sector.
The YAF has succeeded tactically in turning attempted breakthroughs into mobile killing zones that consume Saudi manpower and equipment. This type of weapon, the Shawaz drone, along with preemptive operations, may have played a decisive role in that success. As a tactical weapon, the Shawaz drone has transformed both the battlefield equation and the battle of competing narratives.
Characteristics and capabilities
Shawaz drones represent a model of low-cost, highly maneuverable tactical weaponry. They are remotely operated and provide live video feeds of the battlefield. Their significance extends beyond carrying out offensive strikes; they also provide real-time reconnaissance and intelligence on enemy deployments and the scale of their movements. This gives field commanders the ability to manage engagements according to the principle of proportionality while minimizing human losses along the front lines.
The footage released by the War Media division shows that Shawaz operations should not be dismissed as another set of battlefield images. By analyzing the footage, several functions of this tactical weapon can be identified.
Direct pursuit and attack
The Shawaz drone’s role is not limited to pursuing and targeting military vehicles, armored vehicles, fortified positions, and barricades. The footage has also demonstrated its ability to pursue individual personnel on the battlefield, as seen in the recent operations in Kahbub and Al-Wazi’iyah.
Dual offensive and intelligence-gathering
The Shawaz performs two military functions: offensive operations and intelligence-oriented reconnaissance. It enables the YAF to monitor enemy mobilizations, deployments, numbers, weapons, and other relevant details. This allows the Sanaa government to apply the principle of proportionality in accordance with the demands of the battlefield.
Remote observation and engagement
The drone provides the ability to observe and engage targets remotely, thereby reducing the potential human losses among YAF personnel in direct confrontations.
Psychological impact and the changing battlefield equation
Psychologically and perceptually, the documented footage has created an atmosphere of fear and deterrence among the YAF’s foes on the ground. Its effects have extended beyond the immediate battlefield, influencing the wider environment surrounding Saudi-backed forces.
These drones have established a new battlefield reality, forcing Riyadh’s forces to abandon their customary displays of strength through large military convoys and adopt dispersed positions and defensive concealment out of fear of this weapon.
Yet these measures have neither protected them nor prevented them from being targeted. This is evident in the footage of the Kahbub and Al-Wazi’iyah operations, in which Shawaz drones pursued individual personnel and military vehicles in multiple directions, while those targeted were gripped by fear and panic.
The recent footage of Shawaz drones and their operations also brings to mind the attack drones used by Hezbollah against the Israeli Occupation Forces (IOF) in southern Lebanon. Those drones became a source of terror and an enduring nightmare for the regime’s occupying troops. Their impact was not confined to those on the battlefield; their psychological effects extended to political and military decision-making circles, as well as field commanders.
There is little doubt that Yemeni drones exert a similar psychological impact on Saudi-backed forces operating on the Yemeni battlefield.
Battlefield implications and the battle of competing narratives
An examination of recent developments suggests that the latest offensive operations have inflicted substantial attrition on Saudi-backed forces between Lahij governorate and Bab al-Mandab. These operations have come alongside earlier missile and aerial strikes that inflicted extensive losses on Saudi forces, their vehicles, and their modern armored equipment, whether American-made or Saudi-made.
The footage recorded by Shawaz drones, together with material documented by Yemen’s War Media division, has made a significant difference in the media battle over competing narratives. The visual evidence, captured by both the Shawaz drones and War Media cameras, has refuted claims promoted by Saudi news outlets and some Arab television channels that Saudi-backed forces had “established full control over Bab al-Mandab” or were “advancing toward Al-Mokha.”
The Shawaz footage, by contrast, showed that these forces are suffering military attrition, including casualties and equipment losses, while operating under severe psychological pressure. It also showed these forces retreating rather than occupying positions from which they could launch an offensive and establish control.
In the battle of narratives and competing accounts, the YAF’s documented operations, filmed both from the air and on the ground, have demonstrated a consistency between the battlefield situation and the account presented to the public. When the YAF or military sources announce an operation or achievement and substantiate their claims with footage, their account becomes more convincing.
This visual documentation has played a central role in dismantling opposing media narratives and has reinforced the YAF’s claimed operational and psychological advantage in managing the battlefield.
The opposing side, by contrast, has gone beyond propaganda. It now lies more often on the falsification of facts and the construction of reality through crude, repetitive, and theatrical claims unsupported by any visual evidence.
This was evident last week when Saudi outlets claimed to have “secured control over Bab al-Mandab and advanced toward Al-Mokha.” Within hours, however, those claims, and those promoting them, had been discredited because they lacked elements of credibility, as well as tangible evidence from the battlefield.

articles.title: EU Blacklists Nearly 1,600 in Russian Defense Firms and Executives
articles.body:
The European Union adopted its largest-ever single set of sanctions against Russia to date on Monday, blacklisting 1,569 individuals and companies within the country's military-industrial complex.
The measures blacklist 826 Russian companies and 743 chief executives, bringing the total number of listings under the EU sanctions regime protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity to nearly 4,600. The designated entities face immediate asset freezes and funding blocks, while the targeted individuals are now barred from entering the bloc.
The package specifically targets mid-level suppliers that form the "core" of Russia's defense sector, which together generate an annual turnover of at least 20 billion euros ($22.32 billion) and employ more than 250,000 people.
According to the European Council, the designated companies supply critical components for advanced weapons systems, including semiconductors, radars, satellite systems, explosives, and optics. Notably, more than half of the new listings address the production chain for the ballistic missiles Russia uses in its daily strikes against Ukrainian infrastructure.
"Bombing Kyiv’s bridges, ships transporting grain, and the National Academy of Sciences are not the actions of a country seeking peace," said Kaja Kallas, the EU's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.
The sweeping European measures come just three days after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an agreement on Truth Social with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to American and global markets in an effort to lower domestic fuel costs.
Further commenting on the latest EU sanctions, Kallas, however, stressed: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Moscow but to increase it."
The new listings follow the European Council's June 2026 directive to intensify pressure on Moscow in response to an escalating military campaign that has deliberately targeted civilian infrastructure and, according to the Council, aims to undermineUkraine's resilience.

articles.title: Republicans Denounce Trump’s Diesel Deal With Russia’s Putin Amid Mounting Backlash
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Monday defended his plan to import diesel from Russia amid mounting calls from within his own party to reverse course on the controversial deal. "I made the right choice for the American People—always America first," Trusmp said of the move.
Lawmakers across party aisles, however, argue that the deal goes against a 2022 law which banned Russian oil imports and is not in the best interests of the American public.
“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: The U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO allies,” read a joint bipartisan statement released Sunday by four Republican Senators and three Democrats.
The lawmakers argued that Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. “runs directly counter to that law” and criticized the lack of congressional overview, insisting that the Administration had failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation over its decision. “The United States should not provide [Russian President Vladimir] Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they urged.
The statement was co-signed by GOP Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Susan Collins of Maine, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah, alongside Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Ron Wyden of Oregon, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
Trump said Friday he had reached an agreement with Putin for Moscow to "immediately" supply 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets. The move comes amid a renewed push by the Administration to lower energy prices for Americans, which have skyrocketed since the Iran war began in February. The increased diesel fuel prices have shaken the loyalties of some of Trump’s most ardent support groups, with farmers telling TIME their day-to-day operations are being severely impacted.
In the wake of the diesel supply deal, Trump on Sunday claimed Russia and Ukraine had “agreed” to an energy cease-fire “effective immediately.” However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday said Russian strikes overnight and into the morning had included attacks on energy facilities, with 33 people wounded across the country.
“So there were Russian violations of the energy cease-fire announced by President Trump,” said Zelensky. “For now, this is Putin’s answer to Trump—Russian attacks. But we are waiting. We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians. We are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take.” Trump over the weekend responded to Zelensky's initial criticism of the diesel deal by telling reporters "it's time for Ukraine to get a new President."
U.S. lawmakers pushing back against Trump’s Russia diesel plan had sternly warned against putting trust in Putin.
Sen. Tillis, during an appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, expressed concern that the diesel deal could place American lives at risk. “These are bad people hanging out with bad people, putting American lives at risk—particularly our Special Operators and forward-deployed personnel,” Tillis said, insisting that Putin “cannot be trusted.”
He also doubled down on his argument that the President’s deal may violate the law passed by Congress four years ago, as it outright banned Russian oil imports unless specific criteria were met, including a full Russian withdrawal from Ukraine.
“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law,” Tillis said. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of [the] territory they occupied.”
Just three weeks ago, Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill, intended to target the country's financial institutions and the energy industry, which has largely financed the assault on Ukraine. The bill was named after Sen. Lindsey O. Graham, the late Republican Senator who spent the final year of his life building support for the measure.
Some Republican lawmakers mentioned this legislation as they criticized the diesel plan. “The President should be using those authorities instead of allowing Russia to export diesel, rake in revenues, and continue its catastrophic war in Ukraine,” said Murkowski.
“I oppose President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on the purchase of diesel from Russia,” said Collins. “I was a co-sponsor of the Russian sanctions law, which the President recently signed, but is now not following.”
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania announced Saturday he plans to introduce a bipartisan bill intended to stop Trump from lifting sanctions on Russian oil.
“We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. It will be called the ‘Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,’” said Fitzpatrick.
Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, a Republican who has clashed with Trump on other high-profile issues, said he has already agreed to be a co-sponsor of the bill, insisting that “Congress must make a stand.”
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has defended the move, insisting the agreement with Russia will work through existing legal channels the U.S. has to help bring prices down.
“We’re doing it with all the legal authorities we have, so anyone in Congress who says that—whether it’s an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill—prohibits us from doing it, is wrong,” he told Fox News.
Republican Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming has also defended the diesel deal, telling CBS' Face the Nation that the President “has to make tough decisions.”
European leaders warn Trump's diesel deal could bolster Russia's war
Kaja Kallas, the E.U.'s foreign policy chief, announced Monday that during a Foreign Affairs Council Meeting in Luxembourg, European Foreign Ministers had adopted nearly 1,600 new sanctions targeting Russia's military-industrial complex, underscoring the contrast between Washington's decision and Europe's continued push to economically isolate Moscow.
Ahead of the sit-down, Lithuania's Kęstutis Budrys led the criticism of Trump's deal with Putin, saying it "doesn't help neither the price of oil products nor the unity of the transatlantic community" and insisting “it is not the European way.” Latvia's Baiba Braže said the bloc’s position has “not changed” and that there “is no other way, just pressure on Russia, [and] support to Ukraine.”
Ireland's Helen McEntee called Trump’s deal “concerning” and agreed that European countries need to "redouble [their] efforts" in keeping the pressure on Russia.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson led the initial response from Europe last week, expressing his “regret” over Trump's deal with Putin and warning that “energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest.” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal similarly said the agreement was a “big miscalculation,” arguing that it “is opposite to the long-term activities of the western world to limit the flow of energy carriers to Putin.” Both Sweden and Estonia were among the top 10 countries providing aid to Ukraine as a share of their GDP between January 2022 and February 2026.
The U.K. has also opposed Trump's agreement. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Sunday that Britain did not support the deal with Putin and would instead look to "strengthen sanctions” against Russia. Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged that “the last 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine and reiterated his complete solidarity” during a phone call with Zelensky.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also spoke with Zelensky on Sunday and expressed his view that the “agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe.”

articles.title: Houthi missile attack targets Saudi capital Riyadh for third day in a row
articles.body:
Houthi missile attack targets Saudi capital Riyadh for third day in a row
Saudi Arabia says it intercepted a ballistic missile fired towards Riyadh, as Houthis say they targeted the King Khalid airport.
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting in Yemen has said its forces intercepted another ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as the city reels from attacks that have killed at least 14 people in recent days.
In a statement on X, Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the coalition, said the Houthis fired one ballistic missile at Riyadh and two towards Khamis Mushait, a city in the southwest.
All three were “intercepted and destroyed”, he said.
Residents of Riyadh reported several powerful explosions on Monday night, moments after a text message to their phones warned of an aerial threat.
The Houthis, who control Yemen’s most populous areas, including the capital, Sanaa, said their target in Riyadh had been King Khalid International airport.
Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the group had also sent a drone towards a military airbase at Khamis Mushait, near the Yemeni border. He again warned international airlines and travellers “against operating flights to airports” in Saudi Arabia, except in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, saying the facilities were “unsafe”.
The renewed attacks came as King Khalid International airport in Riyadh remains closed after a Houthi attack on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others. Another strike on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11.
Saudi authorities said the airport would remain closed until this Saturday, and airlines have canceled flights. The Houthis have also struck Saudi oil facilities.
The attacks come as the Houthis fight forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government for control of the country. The Saudi-led coalition has carried out an air campaign against the Houthis and backed the government’s ground forces. The fighting erupted amid regional tensions set off by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
Speaking at an energy conference in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud said the attacks on airports over the last week have tested the kingdom’s resilience.
“The events of recent weeks are serious,” the minister said. “Our response must be equally serious.” He added that Vision 2030, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plan to diversify the Saudi economy, “must continue. Investment must continue”.
Saudi authorities have meanwhile opened an investigation into why the country’s air defences failed to stop the barrage, according to two regional officials who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity. An initial inquiry found that the Houthis first launched several drones to clear a path for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles, which then reached the airport, the officials said.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles with warheads that can change direction in flight, posing a challenge to the Patriot interceptors and other systems the Saudis rely on.
One official told AP that investigators also wanted to know why the defences had not given earlier warning of an attack in which missiles and drones flew more than 1,000km, or 620 miles, to reach Riyadh.
US President Donald Trump separately criticised the Houthis but gave no indication that Washington would intervene. “Well, the Houthis are misbehaving very badly. No good,” he told reporters when asked what he planned to do about the group.
A Houthi official warned that US involvement would bring retaliation.
“If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told the AFP news agency.
Al-Bukhaiti also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”.
The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.
The United Arab Emirates’s national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Monday that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week. It also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah.
Bahrain’s national carrier Gulf Air said it, too, was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Saturday.
US operator Delta announced it would delay the launch of direct flights from Atlanta to Riyadh, scheduled for October 23.

articles.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles toward Sea of Japan
articles.body:
North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan on Monday, said South Korea's military, a little over a week after Pyongyang tested a suspected hypersonic missile.
The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected the launches around 9.20 am local time (0020GMT) from the Pyongyang area, with the missiles traveling more than 900 kilometres (559 miles), according to Yonhap News Agency.
South Korea's military said it had intensified surveillance for additional launches and was sharing intelligence with the United States and Japan while maintaining heightened readiness.
The launches followed North Korea's October 3 missile test from Wonsan, which Pyongyang described as training for troops operating its hypersonic strategic weapons system.
Tensions rise
South Korea conducted its own first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle on Thursday, in an apparent demonstration of its advanced missile capabilities.
Japan also detected two suspected ballistic missiles, which fell outside its exclusive economic zone.
The latest launches come amid tensions following a September 21 land mine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone that injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.
Seoul accused North Korean troops of deliberately planting the mines following a joint investigation with the UN Command.
Pyongyang denied responsibility, accused Seoul of fabricating the findings and warned of retaliation against any military counteraction.
North Korea has not issued any public statement on Monday's launches.

articles.title: Lockheed unveils longer-range Patriot missile, PAC-3 Edge
articles.body:
- Lockheed Martin unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a longer-range, higher-altitude Patriot interceptor, as its entry in the U.S. Army’s Future Interceptor competition.
- Lockheed says the U.S. Army advanced it to the next stage and it is working toward an early operational capability by 2031.
Lockheed Martin has unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a new Patriot interceptor designed to reach higher, fly farther and maneuver harder than the PAC-3 MSE now in service. It is the company’s entry in the U.S. Army’s Future Interceptor competition.
The company debuted the missile on Oct. 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. Lockheed says the U.S. Army has moved it into the next stage of the competition and that it is working toward what the service calls a residual operational capability by 2031, meaning a small number of missiles ready for emergency use before full fielding. The company did not release range, altitude, speed or cost figures, and did not name the other competitors.
PAC-3 Edge builds on the PAC-3 MSE, the hit-to-kill missile that destroys targets by striking them directly and has been used heavily against Russian missiles in Ukraine and Iranian missiles in the Middle East. Lockheed says the new version adds a new seeker, an upgraded propulsion system and improved flight controls. The seeker was designed by the company’s Strigo Product Center, which Lockheed says it funded with $250 million of its own money.
The company says the missile is meant to counter a wide range of aircraft, missiles and hypersonic weapons at higher altitudes and longer ranges than current Patriot interceptors. In the U.S. Army’s layered missile defense, it would sit between the PAC-3 MSE and the THAAD system, which intercepts ballistic missiles at much higher altitudes.
The U.S. Army has tried before to field a next-generation Patriot interceptor. It ran a Lower-Tier Future Interceptor competition between Lockheed and Raytheon, then announced in 2024 that it would cancel the effort before reviving the idea as the Future Interceptor program. The U.S. Army has not published the program’s budget, the number of missiles it plans to buy or when it will pick a winner.
PAC-3 Edge becomes the fourth missile in Lockheed’s Patriot family, alongside the older PAC-3 CRI, the PAC-3 MSE and the lower-cost PAC-3 ACE the company announced in July for European customers.

articles.title: Almost 20 wounded as explosion hits north Israel school
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia issued an early warning alert for a potential "hostile threat" in Riyadh on Monday, according to a message seen by Reuters.
Three booms were heard in the Saudi capital, a Reuters witness said.
A senior Houthi official warned the United States on Monday that it would receive a "swift and painful response" if it entered the war in Yemen, where Saudi Arabia has reportedly requested its help in dealing with the group.
"If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond, rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region," Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told AFP in an interview.
He also warned "all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets".
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they struck a vessel on Monday that was attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway that is crucial to global energy flows.
The Guards' navy said in a statement published on the force's news platform, Sepah News, that "a supertanker, was hit in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire".
The ship targeted on Monday had tried to sail through the area "by disabling its transponders" and "by ignoring warnings from the Guards' Navy", the statement said.
Delta Air Lines announced Monday that it will delay the launch of direct US flights to Saudi Arabia as US air safety regulators warned of continued safety risks.
Delta had planned to launch direct service from Atlanta to Riyadh on October 23, but postponed the plan following weekend Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport.
"Delta will delay the planned launch of its nonstop service between Atlanta and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, amid evolving developments in the region," the US carrier said.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said Monday that its forces intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-backed group at the capital Riyadh.
"Interception and destruction of a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," Major General Turki al-Malki, a spokesman for the coalition, wrote on X.
Iran on Monday denied any involvement in an incident at Britain's RAF Fairford airbase, which has been used by the United States in its war with the Islamic Republic.
"The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any".
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Monday that Palestinian legislative elections should be held "as soon as possible" after they were delayed to 2027.
Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas postponed the polls, set for 28 November, to September next year, official media said, confirming widespread speculation that they would be deferred.
"Ministers regretted the postponement of Palestinian elections. Palestinian legislative and presidential elections should take place as soon as possible," Kallas said, after a meeting of EU foreign ministers.
The international community has strongly advocated for legislative elections, which have not been held since 2006.
Now the elections will be held alongside the presidential vote on 11 September 2027, Abbas said in a decree, blaming "obstacles" imposed by Israel, according to the Palestinian official news agency Wafa.
Holding elections is part of the reforms the international community, including the European Union, the biggest international financial supporter of the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority, has demanded.
The UN rights chief on Monday urged all sides to "avert further catastrophe" following the Riyadh airport attack, saying continued fighting would only unleash more misery.
Saudi Arabia has said it will mount a "serious" response after a string of attacks on Riyadh's international airport by Yemen's Houthis that left 18 people dead.
Lethal airport strikes since last week have rocked the world's top oil exporter.
"I am appalled by the repeated attacks over the past few days by the Houthis on airports in Saudi Arabia, which have killed and injured dozens of Saudis and foreign nationals, notably yesterday's horrific attack on Riyadh's main airport," UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement.
A boy was killed in an explosion that injured around 19 others during a school trip in northern Israel near the Lebanese border on Monday, Defence Minister Israel Katz said.
"I share in the heavy grief of the family of the boy who was killed in the explosion during the trip near the northern border, and I wish a swift and full recovery to all the injured," Katz posted on X, adding that the incident was being investigated.
Airstrikes targeted two districts in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels reported Monday, blaming Saudi Arabia for the airstrikes that occurred around midnight. Saudi Arabia did not immediately respond to the claim.
A spokesman for Yemen's Houthi-run Health Ministry said Monday that airstrikes in the capital Sanaa killed one person and wounded 12 others.
Ministry spokesman Anees al-Asbahi said a strike on a salt factory in Sanaa's Hamadan district killed a man and wounded eight people. A separate strike on a house wounded a woman and three children, he said.
Houthi fighters have tightened their siege of the Yemeni city of Taiz, where fighting has killed more than 60 people in the past 24 hours, military sources from both sides told AFP on Monday.
The Houthis have blocked all exits and carried out several attacks overnight, said a military source loyal to the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government that holds the city.
The violence killed 22 members of the pro-government forces, the source said.

articles.title: US envoys present Russian diesel deal to Ukraine as bid to revive peace talks — report
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump's envoys have informed Ukrainian officials that a deal permitting Russian diesel exports is designed to draw Moscow back to the negotiating table following the collapse of earlier peace initiatives, according to Reuters.
During a closed-door meeting in Miami, Trump's Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner told Ukrainian delegates that Russian President Vladimir Putin was not currently prepared to negotiate an end to the four-and-a-half-year war but suggested the new fuel arrangement could help restart trilateral talks.
A third source noted that Washington framed the deal as a way to "soften" Moscow's position by signalling Trump's openness to reciprocal arrangements.
Under the agreement, Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to US and global markets.
The pact has drawn sharp criticism from US lawmakers.
Trump defended the measure on Monday as "the right choice for the American people", arguing it will lower domestic energy costs ahead of congressional midterm elections.
Refinery strikes
During the meeting, Kushner reiterated administration requests for Ukraine to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries, arguing they drive up global fuel prices.
"The idea was that the US could go back to Russia and say 'See, the Ukrainians stopped striking and we gave you this deal. Now it’s your turn to do something,'" a source familiar with the talks told Reuters.
US officials stressed past military and intelligence assistance, though they did not threaten to halt aid if strikes continued.
Ukrainian officials remained sceptical, viewing commercial concessions as appeasement that fails to shift Moscow's core demand for remaining territory in the Donbas.
Tensions escalated further after Trump said on Sunday that an energy ceasefire was in place—an announcement Kiev said it had not agreed to beforehand, whilst Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure continued.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denounced the diesel deal as a "gift to Putin", prompting Trump to respond that Ukraine should "get a new president".
Trump defends pact
Trump defended his diesel supply agreement with Russia, dismissing bipartisan backlash from Capitol Hill lawmakers who warn the pact breaches federal law prohibiting Russian energy imports during Moscow's ongoing invasion of Ukraine.
The White House insisted that lifting sanctions to permit Russian fuel exports would curb soaring domestic energy prices, which have surged more than 60 percent since the outbreak of hostilities involving Iran seven months ago.
Trump defended the temporary sanctions waiver as necessary to support domestic agriculture, writing on social media: "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" Departing for Ohio, Trump brushed aside criticism from his own party: "Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious.
We can do a restriction on oil, but the rest of the world would be greatly, greatly affected if we do that."

articles.title: North Korean missile launches may be response to South's hypersonic test, Seoul says
articles.body:
North Korea's launch of multiple ballistic missiles towards the East Sea appears to be an apparent response to South Korea's successful test of a hypersonic glide vehicle last week, the South Korean military has confirmed.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected the launches originating from the Pyongyang region.
At least one projectile flew more than 900 kilometres, Yonhap News Agency said.
JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the firing could also demonstrate technical advances under Pyongyang's five-year defence modernisation blueprint.
Jang declined to confirm whether the weapons tested were hypersonic systems or intermediate-range ballistic missiles, noting that further technical analysis is ongoing.
The launches followed South Korea’s inaugural test of a hypersonic glide vehicle on Thursday.
Regional reactions
Japan's defence authorities confirmed detecting two suspected ballistic missiles, reporting that the projectiles landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone.
The US Pacific Command issued a statement confirming close consultations with regional allies: "Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to US personnel or territory, or to our allies."
The command reiterated Washington's ironclad commitment to defending regional partners.
The missile tests unfold amid friction along the inter-Korean border following a September 21 landmine detonation inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that injured three South Korean soldiers, two critically.
Seoul accused North Korean forces of deliberately laying the explosives following a joint inquiry with the UN Command.
Pyongyang rejected the findings as fabricated and warned it would retaliate against any countermeasures.
Pyongyang has not issued an official public statement regarding Monday's launches.

articles.title: Anti-imperialist groups call for global action against US sanctions, military aggression
articles.body:
Anti-imperialist groups call for global action against US sanctions, military aggression
Three international anti-imperialist organizations have condemned US-Israeli military aggression against Iran and called for an end to economic sanctions, military intervention and foreign occupation as part of a global campaign scheduled for October 1-10.
In a joint statement titled “Stand With Palestine and All Besieged Nations,” the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS), Global Coalition for Resistance against US Imperialism (GCR), and Revolutionary Anti-Imperialist United Front (UPRA) urged trade unions, student organizations, peasant and women’s movements, Indigenous communities and anti-war activists worldwide to participate in a 10-day campaign from October 1 to 10 under the banner of People Against Siege and Sanctions (PASS).
The signatories described the United States as the principal driver of global military aggression and economic coercion, arguing that Washington increasingly relies on sanctions, assassination campaigns, direct military attacks and digital surveillance to maintain its international influence.
Regarding Iran, the declaration said the US-Israeli axis seeks to crush regional powers that refuse to submit through severe economic blockades, open warfare and assassination campaigns.
It stated that Iranian people have continuously mobilized in city squares across the country since the military attacks of February 28, describing these gatherings as a powerful demonstration of popular resistance. The organizations also accused major corporate media outlets of systematically ignoring these mobilizations while providing platforms to groups they characterize as counter-revolutionary.
The declaration invoked the anti-imperialist legacy of Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei, alongside Palestinian resistance leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh and Hezbollah Secretary-General Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah, in its condemnation of what it described as US-Israeli extrajudicial assassinations of political and revolutionary figures.
The organizations placed Iran alongside Cuba, Venezuela, Syria, Iraq and Yemen among countries affected by US sanctions and economic blockades, calling for the immediate removal of these restrictions in defense of national sovereignty.
They also demanded the withdrawal of US troops from West Asia and the dismantling of American military bases worldwide, with particular emphasis on West Asia, Latin America, the Sahel and the Asia-Pacific.
The declaration further criticized the US-led Pax Silica initiative, warning that efforts to control semiconductor supply chains, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and digital infrastructure threaten technological sovereignty. It accused major technology companies of supporting military operations through AI-based target selection and mass-surveillance systems.
As part of the campaign, the groups called for demonstrations on October 7, marking the third anniversary of the Al-Aqsa Flood operation, and coordinated international mobilization on October 8 in honor of Cuban revolutionary Ernesto “Che” Guevara.
The declaration concluded by calling for an end to US and Israeli military campaigns, the lifting of sanctions and international solidarity in defense of Palestinian liberation and national sovereignty.

articles.title: Trump says he may meet North Korean leader during Asia trip

Trump says he may meet North Korean leader during Asia trip
US President Donald Trump said Monday that he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his planned trip to Asia, Anadolu reported.
“I may, yeah. That'll be exciting, won't it? But I get along with him,” he said, speaking to reporters as he departed the White House for Ohio.
A meeting would mark a potential new chapter in Trump’s efforts to engage directly with Kim, with whom he held several historic meetings during his first term as president as the two leaders sought to address North Korea’s nuclear weapons program.
Trump will travel to the Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit on Nov. 16, then head to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit from Nov. 17-19.
Earlier, it was reported that North Korea launched multiple ballistic missiles toward the East Sea, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS).

articles.title: Saudi MBS 'shuttling between bunker palaces' amid Houthi attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi's MBS 'shuttling between bunker palaces' amid Houthi attacks
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is reportedly moving between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers in Riyadh as Yemen's Houthis intensify their missile and drone attacks on the Saudi capital.
The kingdom's de facto ruler has not been seen in public since last Tuesday and is travelling between fortified royal residences accompanied by a handpicked security team, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The reported movements come as the Houthis continue to bombard Riyadh with drones, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, forcing the closure of King Khalid International Airport until 17 October following repeated strikes.
On Saturday, a ballistic missile struck one of the airport's terminals, killing 13 people and injuring hundreds. Another missile hit the airport on Sunday, killing one person, while four others were killed in attacks on Wednesday and Thursday.
The strikes have raised concerns over Saudi Arabia's ability to defend its capital, amid reports that the kingdom is running low on interceptor missiles used to shoot down incoming ballistic and cruise missiles.
According to the Wall Street Journal, Saudi Arabia's air defence stockpiles have been depleted by repeated attacks, leaving the kingdom increasingly vulnerable to further strikes.
Saudi Arabia, like much of the region, has expended large quantities of interceptor missiles defending against Iranian ballistic and cruise missiles launched following the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Saudi air defences under strain
Dr Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab that Saudi Arabia faced significant challenges in countering Houthi attacks, particularly low-flying drones and cruise missiles that are harder to detect.
The kingdom's dwindling stockpile of interceptor missiles has further complicated its defensive efforts.
"It would be a mistake to say the Kingdom’s air defence systems are failing completely, they are under strain and stretched. But there are also reports of successful interceptions," Ozcelik said.
A report by the Associated Press in September revealed that Saudi officials had asked Britain, France, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence systems to the country amid concerns over dwindling interceptor stocks.
The US has also deployed additional Patriot missile defence systems to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to protect energy infrastructure, according to Axios.
Other countries, including Greece, Britain and France, have provided air defence support, while Turkey and Pakistan, both partners in the Mecca Defence Pact, are also assisting Riyadh.
Ozcelik said Saudi Arabia was facing an asymmetric threat similar to tactics previously employed by Iran and its regional allies during the wider conflict.
Iran launched thousands of ballistic missiles and drones across the region, including against Gulf states, striking energy facilities and US military bases.
"What we are seeing is the familiar playbook the IRGC used against the Gulf - even a small number of missile or drones that gets through sophisticated air defences can create disproportionate damage and disruption," Ozcelik said.
"That's the asymmetric warfare logic that is working to the Houthis advantage."
Saudi Arabia vows decisive response
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis has vowed to "respond decisively" to the attacks, having already resumed its air campaign against the group in support of Yemeni government offensives.
The renewed Saudi-led air campaign preceded the latest escalation in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, with the group initially concentrating its strikes on energy infrastructure.
The repeated attacks have heightened security concerns in the Saudi capital, with the reported movements of Mohammed bin Salman between fortified palaces highlighting the growing pressure on the kingdom's leadership as the conflict intensifies.

articles.title: Iran offers to mediate Saudi-Houthi talks as attacks mount
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran offers to mediate Saudi-Houthi talks amid mounting attacks
Iran has offered to help launch talks between Saudi Arabia and Houthi rebels as increasing attacks on the kingdom and renewed airstrikes on Yemen threaten to deepen the regional conflict.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made the offer during a phone call with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday evening, according to a statement from Iran's foreign ministry.
Araghchi expressed Tehran's readiness to provide all forms of assistance to facilitate dialogue between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthis and support efforts to reach a political settlement.
The two ministers also discussed the latest regional developments, with Araghchi expressing concern over rising tensions and warning that continued reliance on military action would further complicate the situation.
He stressed that the region's crises could not be resolved through military means and urged greater emphasis on political solutions.
Separately, Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry confirmed the call on Sunday, saying the two ministers had discussed the latest regional escalation and efforts to address it.
However, the Saudi statement provided no further details about the diplomatic initiatives discussed or whether any agreements had been reached.
The diplomatic contact came amid intensifying hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, including repeated missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi airports.
A recent Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed at least 12 people and injured 309 others, while Abha airport in southern Saudi Arabia has also been targeted.
On Sunday evening, the Saudi-led coalition reported another attack on King Khalid International Airport, saying an unidentified projectile struck Terminal 4 and sparked a fire.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said on X that emergency crews were working to contain the blaze. He subsequently announced that Saudi air defences had intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile near the airport.
Meanwhile, airstrikes targeted two districts of Yemen's capital, Sanaa, around midnight on Monday, according to the Houthis.
The group's media centre said the strikes hit the Hamdan and Thourah districts and blamed Saudi Arabia for the attacks, although it provided no further details.
The strikes come amid renewed military operations by the Saudi-led coalition and Yemeni government forces against Houthi positions in Sanaa, Taiz and areas surrounding the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The intensifying confrontation coincides with growing threats to maritime security elsewhere in the region.
India's foreign ministry said on Monday that two Indian sailors were missing after a drone struck the commercial tanker MT PETRO DOLPHIN near the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday.
The vessel was carrying 11 Indian crew members when it was attacked.
A second tanker, the Marshall Islands-flagged MT VALTHERA, was also struck by an unidentified projectile, causing a fire on board. All 11 Indian sailors aboard that vessel were reported safe.
India condemned the attacks on commercial shipping, warning that they risked further destabilising an already volatile region.
The latest developments have also prompted calls for greater security cooperation among Gulf states.
Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the United Arab Emirates leadership, called on Monday for joint Gulf action to counter attacks by Iran and its allied groups.
He warned that attacks on Saudi Arabia threatened the security of the UAE and other Gulf countries, stressing that their security was indivisible.

articles.title: Yemen Leaves Riyadh Grounded
articles.body:
Yemen Leaves Riyadh Grounded
Repeated strikes close Riyadh airport and shatter Saudi air defenses as Ansarallah enforces its 'blockade for blockade' doctrine
TEHRAN — Riyadh’s airport has been hit five times since Tuesday, October 6, by Saudi authorities’ own count, and the government cannot promise a sixth will not come. On Saturday, a missile struck King Khalid International Airport, killing at least 13 people and wounding more than 300, according to the kingdom. On Sunday, another projectile set Terminal 4 on fire. On Monday, the Saudi civil aviation authority extended the shutdown.
A wealthy kingdom that spent a decade selling itself as the Persian Gulf’s safe harbor cannot keep its capital’s runway open.
Cirium reported that 99.7 percent of scheduled flights at King Khalid were canceled on Sunday. Flightradar24 showed no aircraft over a city of roughly eight million. Lufthansa Group grounded its Riyadh service through October 16, Air France-KLM through the end of the month, and Etihad stretched its Saudi cancellations again.
The FAA warned American carriers about Saudi airspace, and Washington, London, Berlin, and Madrid told their citizens to stay away from the airport. Riyadh’s schools moved online. The metro stopped serving two airport stations.
The defenses are thin. Saudi officials have told the Wall Street Journal they are running low on interceptors.
The kingdom is shuffling air defense batteries between palaces and increasingly vulnerable energy sites and desperately searching the world for more.
Sanaa’s equation
Brigadier General Yahya Saree laid out the terms in his October 11 statement. Yemeni forces, he said, carried out four operations in 24 hours: three waves against King Khalid, a direct hit on King Fahd Airport in Dammam, and fires at Aramco’s Shedgum and Tanajib facilities in the Eastern Province.
He told airlines, airport staff, and travelers that Saudi airports and airspace are unsafe, exempting only Mecca and Medina, and put responsibility for any failed interception on Riyadh.
Sanaa’s rule is “airport for airport, blockade for blockade, and escalation for escalation.”
Ansarallah did not invent this logic out of a vacuum. There were documented Saudi strikes on Sanaa airport on July 13, with three munitions landing on its only working runway. That airport is the front door for aid to the area where most Yemenis live.
Saree said Saudi jets flew 124 raids in a single day, bringing the total of this escalation to 2,058. The World Food Programme says three-quarters of families in parts of Yemen are going hungry.
Eleven years of bombing and port restrictions taught Yemenis what a closed airport means. Riyadh is learning it now. Ansarallah’s warnings were repeated and ignored.
Washington stays out
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asked for urgent American help, according to multiple news reports in American media outlets.
He pledged around $1 trillion in U.S. “investment” this year and was embraced at the White House. What he has received in his war on Yemen so far is intelligence, targeting support, and military advisers.
Trump called the airport attack “very bad” and said of joining Saudi strikes: “We may. We’re going to look at it.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered “condolences.” Condolences do not intercept missiles.
The reasons for restraint are plain. The war on Iran has already consumed American munitions and attention, closed and disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, and pushed fuel prices high. Midterm elections arrive on November 3, and a Republican Party facing angry drivers has no appetite for another unwinnable quagmire.
Trump himself has said that the Yemenis contacted Washington to say they do not want to fight the United States. The American president certainly remembers the high costs of “Operation Rough Rider” from March to May 2025, when a massive multi-week air assault spectacularly failed to blunt Sanaa’s strategic capabilities.
Ansarallah announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July and has the range to successfully strike American ships in the Red Sea. It has not fired on one.
So far it has held back, as Riyadh realizes that Washington dreads the cost of a wider regional war far more than it dreads a weakened Saudi ally.
The bill for Vision 2030
The World Petroleum Council Energy Congress opened in Riyadh under security, but BP pulled out, and the chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell and Chevron vanished from the program.
The Finance Ministry expects the economy to shrink 3.6 percent this year. Foreign investment fell in each of the first two quarters.
Riyadh dropped the 2029 Asian Winter Games in January, and Neom and other showpieces sit stalled or under review. An effective attack on the East-West pipeline in September cut the kingdom’s route around Hormuz.
Vision 2030 asks visitors and investors to believe Riyadh is safe. A shuttered airport answers that question for them.
Expo 2030 and the 2034 World Cup now carry a plain logistical doubt, and so do the data centers meant to make Saudi Arabia an “AI hub.” Billions spent on golf, football, and festivals sought to buy an image, and Yemen's punishing strikes have thoroughly damaged it.
Furthermore, as the kingdom prepares to host the 2027 AFC Asian Cup across venues in Riyadh, Jeddah, and Khobar, the unfolding security crisis and shuttered transport infrastructure cast an immediate shadow over the tournament, turning what was intended as a grand showcase of soft power into a stark reminder of Saudi Arabia’s extreme vulnerability.
MBS’ war
Mohammed bin Salman launched the war on Yemen in 2015 expecting victory after mere weeks. He got a stalemate, a 2022 truce and, this summer, a resumed war he is losing.
When Ansarallah pushed down the Red Sea coast in August, Riyadh held back its air power, and Mokha fell. The coalition’s “Dawn of Yemen” counteroffensive, with 100 jets in its opening phase, has not stopped missiles reaching Riyadh, Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran. Sanaa has released footage of Saudi-backed fighters surrendering.
The crown prince now moves between bunkered palaces under a handpicked guard, the WSJ reports. His last public appearance was October 6, when he gave blood for a donation drive.
Saudi officials are quietly weighing a diplomatic exit. Sanaa has already named its price: stop the aggression and lift the siege.
