articles.title: Czech intelligence chief warns Russia may launch ‘significantly riskier’ operations
articles.body:
Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Russia could carry out “significantly riskier and more serious” operations in the Czech Republic or another democratic country in the coming months, Czech intelligence chief Michal Koudelka said Monday, according to Czech news agency Ceske Noviny.
“In recent weeks, we have been receiving very credible information indicating that Russia could move to a significantly riskier and more serious operation in a matter of months rather than years,” Koudelka said at an international security conference in the Chamber of Deputies.
He cited possible scenarios including sabotage targeting facilities supporting Ukraine, drone or missile attacks on weapons depots intended for Ukraine, and limited military action against a NATO member.
“The threat is not current now, but in the coming months, perhaps after some form of mobilization is announced, it cannot be ruled out,” Koudelka said.
He said there was no need for alarm, adding that the Czech Republic was capable of responding to such threats but needed to be prepared.
Koudelka described Russia as the Czech Republic’s biggest foreign security threat and said it would remain so for a long time.
He also warned about Russian disinformation efforts, saying Moscow sought to divide Western democratic countries because it could not defeat them militarily or economically.
“It is necessary to narrow the operational space of the Russian disinformation machine,” he said.
Koudelka also said the Czech Republic and other democratic countries should make clear to Moscow that they were aware of its actions and did not trust it.
He pointed to similarities between Russian statements about the rights of Russian-speaking populations in Ukraine and more recent statements concerning the Baltic states.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said in September that Moscow was not preparing for a conflict with Europe.
Western officials have warned of possible Russian actions against European countries supporting Ukraine.
Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title: Trump's Russia-Ukraine 'energy ceasefire' sparks confusion
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump's 'energy ceasefire' sparks confusion as Russia strikes Ukraine
US President Donald Trump sowed confusion on Sunday, announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia that sparked astonishment in Kyiv, silence from Moscow and support from Ukraine's Western allies.
But the ceasefire appeared shaky at best as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia struck multiple Ukrainian power plants on Sunday, including one in the capital and another in Kharkiv, leading to power outages and outrage.
Trump's announcement came two days after he declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage by European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said early Sunday on Truth Social. "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Zelensky appeared to express surprise at the announcement, saying he was seeking further details, but added that "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well."
Russia has yet to confirm its agreement.
Zelensky later said that multiple Ukrainian power stations had been hit and that "Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day," referring to a type of drone originally designed by Iran that is now used extensively by Russia.
Since launching a full-scale invasion of its neighbor in 2022, Russia has systematically hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leading to energy and heating shortages—prompting Ukraine to hit back at Russian oil refineries it says fund the war.
More recently, Trump's war in Iran has led to oil shortages and ensuing price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead of midterm elections early next month.
'Up to our people'
The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine's key western allies, including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission.
Several leaders called on Russia to uphold the deal.
But that support was in contrast to broad criticism of the US-Russia diesel deal earlier in the week, which has led to mounting tensions between Trump and Zelensky.
Zelensky said the diesel deal was a "weak decision," while several of Ukraine's European allies expressed outrage and pledged to increase pressure on Moscow.
Seven US senators—including four Republicans—released a statement Sunday blasting the diesel deal with Russia, saying it was illegal.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney added to the chorus on Sunday after a call with Zelensky, saying the diesel deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe."
Asked about the criticism on Saturday, Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" who would finally settle the war.
Zelensky pushed back, telling ABC News that "it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader."
He said that fuel prices were rising because of the US-Israeli war on Iran and the blocked Strait of Hormuz.
"Everybody understands it," he said.
Support for Zelensky
Germany's foreign minister said Sunday that Berlin continued to "fully support" Zelensky.
"Europe needs stability and that means that we are very clearly continuing to stay by the side of Ukraine and its government," Johann Wadephul said in Berlin.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed the Ukrainian leader "as he leads the fight for his people's freedom."
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also said his country "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now."
In Kyiv, several residents expressed concern about Trump's call for Zelensky to be replaced.
"I believe our president is the best, and Americans should think about their own president," said 40-year-old Olesia Goncharuk.
"We Ukrainians decide our own fate and our own freedom, and we are free people," she told AFP.

articles.title: Anduril bets on mass-produced missile interceptors
articles.body:
- Anduril unveiled Steelfin, a family of two-stage surface-to-air interceptors aimed at cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles, with flight tests planned next year.
- The company plans to build several thousand a year and says Steelfin will fit existing launchers including Patriot, Mk 41 and Typhon.
Anduril Industries has unveiled Steelfin, a family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles designed to shoot down cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles at a fraction of the cost of today’s interceptors, with flight tests set to begin next year.
The company announced Steelfin on Oct. 12, the first day of the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. Anduril says it plans to build on the order of several thousand Steelfin missiles a year in the short term. It did not give a unit price, name a customer or say which U.S. service is backing the program, saying only that it has been developing Steelfin for years while investing alongside multiple customers. The company has completed ballistic testing with representative air vehicles but has not yet flown a Steelfin missile.
The first stage is a solid rocket booster that can be swapped for different motors depending on how far and how fast the missile needs to fly, and how tightly it must pack into a launcher. The second stage is a common “terminal interceptor” that carries the airframe, electronics, software and flight controls shared across the family, with open interfaces so Anduril can drop in different seekers and mission systems without redesigning the missile.
Anduril says the approach lets it build versions for every layer of air and missile defense, from short-range point defense of a single site to upper-tier ballistic missile defense, while aiming for a fraction of the cost of current interceptors in each class. The company did not say what those benchmark costs are, but a single Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptor costs about $4 million, and the Missile Defense Agency is pursuing a separate low-cost interceptor effort with a target price below $750,000 per round.
Because the variants share parts, Anduril says they can run down the same production line with the same tooling and workers, letting it shift output to whichever version is in demand. The company also says the common interfaces let it buy commercial components and use multiple suppliers.
Steelfin is designed to fire from launchers the U.S. military already fields, including the M903A2 launcher used by the Patriot air defense system, the U.S. Navy’s Mk 41 Vertical Launch System aboard cruisers and destroyers, the U.S. Army’s Typhon mid-range missile launcher, and newer containerized launchers. Anduril says it will work with existing fire control systems such as the U.S. Navy’s Aegis and the U.S. Army’s Integrated Battle Command System, known as IBCS, rather than requiring a new command network.
The launch comes as U.S. air defense stocks have been drawn down by combat in the Middle East. This month alone, Raytheon received contracts worth up to $6.3 billion for SM-3 Block IB interceptors and up to $24.4 billion for SM-6 missiles to replenish U.S. Navy inventories. Anduril already makes smaller counter-drone interceptors such as Roadrunner and Anvil, but Steelfin is its first family aimed at cruise and ballistic missiles.

articles.title: EU adopts record sanctions listings targeting Russia’s military industry
articles.body:
EU foreign ministers have adopted nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex, the bloc's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas announced on Monday.
In a statement through US social media company X, Kallas described the move as the "single largest expansion" of the EU's sanctions list since Russia’s war in Ukraine began in February 2022.
"More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles. We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," she said.
Separately, the EU Council announced that it had decided to extend its sanctions framework targeting the proliferation and use of chemical weapons for five years, until October 30 2031.
The council also extended the validity of individual sanctions listings under the framework for one year, until October 30, 2027.
According to the statement, the restrictive measures currently apply to 31 individuals and six entities.
Those listed are subject to asset freezes, while EU citizens and companies are prohibited from making funds or economic resources available to them, directly or indirectly.
The individuals listed are also subject to travel bans to the EU.

articles.title: Israeli soldiers say ordered to drop heavy bombs on inhabited Gaza buildings without evacuation: Report
articles.body:
Four Israeli military intelligence soldiers acknowledged they received instructions to use “heavy bombs” against inhabited buildings in the Gaza Strip without evacuating residents first, in strikes that killed and injured hundreds of Palestinians, according to a media report on Monday.
The soldiers gave their accounts to the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, as Israel continues its genocide in Gaza, which began in October 2023.
The Israeli army has repeatedly claimed that it warns civilians in Gaza to evacuate before strikes, a practice Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have frequently boasted.
However, soldiers’ testimonies contradict these claims, as they revealed a complete change in open-fire regulations since the start of the war on Gaza, where approximately 2.4 million Palestinians live.
One intelligence soldier, identified only as A, who was tasked with tracking Hamas commanders in Gaza, said: “We knew almost nothing about Hamas and its military wing at the field level.
“In October 2023, we started almost from scratch to identify where their members and operatives were,” he said.
He added that the criteria for defining a target were quickly loosened, alongside “a sharp change in the concept of proportionality and the use of heavy weapons” and a significant easing of the policy governing the killing of civilians considered “collateral damage.”
Expanded targeting policy
Haaretz said the testimonies of the four soldiers portrayed “a fundamentally different concept of warfare, in which even relatively minor targets could be considered sufficient justification for attacks to harm civilians.”
The newspaper said the large number of civilians classified by the military as “collateral damage” was not simply the result of failures or mistaken identification, but stemmed from a policy of expanding the use of firepower “to the maximum extent.”
Haaretz said similar accounts had been presented during the three years of the war and that efforts to compensate for the intelligence failures of Oct. 7, 2023, “contributed to unprecedented tolerance for civilian casualties.”
The newspaper cited an Oct. 31, 2023 Israeli airstrike on a large residential complex in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza as one example. The stated target was Ibrahim Biari, a Hamas battalion commander in Jabalia.
“We knew Biari was underground, beneath large buildings, but we did not know beneath which building,” said a soldier identified only as D.
“So they chose buildings that were still inhabited and decided to destroy all the buildings above the tunnel where he was located. We did not carry out an evacuation because it was important to kill him without allowing him to escape,” he said.
Soldier A, who said he took part in the mission, said members of the targeting cell understood that the number of civilians likely to be harmed “was extremely high.”
“In the military intelligence estimates of potential collateral damage, there was talk of 250 to 300 people, so the decision was passed up for direct approval by the chief of staff,” he said.
“After the strike, as time passed, we understood that the number of dead was around 250,” he added, referring to Palestinian civilians.
“I remember being shocked when several densely populated buildings were flattened, killing hundreds, in order to kill a battalion commander who only a few weeks earlier would not even have been considered a target,” he said.
Responding to the Jabalia massacre, the Israeli army claimed that the strike had been “replanned several times to reduce harm to civilians,” saying the expected number of civilian casualties “was not in the hundreds.”
The army claimed that after the strike, “the damage was found to have exceeded its initial assessment.”
OPINION: Gaza’s displaced face a deadly choice: collapsing buildings or flooded tents
Civilian bloodshed
Nadav Weiman, executive director of Breaking the Silence, a left-wing Israeli organization, denounced the army’s conduct in Gaza.
“We cannot allow the killing of 300 civilians to assassinate a battalion commander,” he said. “Nor can we kill 20 civilians to kill every Hamas truck driver and then claim publicly that we did everything possible to prevent harm to innocent people.
“It is time for those who issued these orders to take responsibility instead of trying to get rid of the soldiers who courageously decided to tell the public the truth,” Weiman said.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Haaretz said another case described by the soldiers involved the Oct. 13, 2023 targeting of Hamas commander Ali Qadi.
According to the newspaper, an intelligence soldier in the Gaza Division had warned that Qadi “was behaving unusually,” but the division’s intelligence officer disregarded the warning.
“A few days after the war began, Qadi became a target and was subjected to heavy fire,” soldier A said.
“He was in the house with his family, and they decided to kill him. The army quickly announced that he had been killed, but in reality Qadi was the only person who survived the attack. Everyone who was killed had no connection to the target,” he said.
Without evacuation
Another soldier, identified as B, who served in a drone unit, said that after the war began, the division was authorized to operate under expanded parameters, meaning attacks expected to injure up to 20 noncombatants “did not require approval from a senior official outside the targeting cell.”
A third soldier, identified as C, who served in military intelligence, said that several months after the ground offensive began on Oct. 27, 2023, his unit was asked to prepare an entry zone into Gaza City for a maneuvering division.
He said several high-rise buildings in the area were considered a threat to Israeli troops and that an intelligence assessment estimated that about 25% of residents were still inside their homes.
“When we tried to ask how many residents remained and whether that was reasonable, we were told that those residents were targets for the forces on the ground. I could not understand or believe that we were talking about such numbers,” he said.
He added that the forces planning to enter the area could have waited considerably longer before approving the attack.
“So in the early stages we attacked without a full evacuation. Defending the soldiers was given priority, which is understandable, but the numbers (of civilian casualties) kept growing and became unreasonable,” he said.
The Israeli army has killed more than 74,300 Palestinians and injured over 175,400 others in a brutal war since October 2023 that has left the entire enclave in ruins.

Four Israeli military intelligence soldiers acknowledged they received instructions to use “heavy bombs” against inhabited buildings in the Gaza Strip without evacuating residents first, in strikes that killed and injured hundreds of Palestinians, according to a media report on Monday.
The soldiers gave their accounts to the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, as Israel continues its genocide in Gaza, which began in October 2023.
The Israeli army has repeatedly claimed that it warns civilians in Gaza to evacuate before strikes, a practice Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have frequently boasted.
However, soldiers' testimonies contradict these claims, as they revealed a complete change in open-fire regulations since the start of the war on Gaza, where approximately 2.4 million Palestinians live.
One intelligence soldier, identified only as A, who was tasked with tracking Hamas commanders in Gaza, said: “We knew almost nothing about Hamas and its military wing at the field level.
“In October 2023, we started almost from scratch to identify where their members and operatives were,” he said.
He added that the criteria for defining a target were quickly loosened, alongside “a sharp change in the concept of proportionality and the use of heavy weapons” and a significant easing of the policy governing the killing of civilians considered “collateral damage.”
Expanded targeting policy
Haaretz said the testimonies of the four soldiers portrayed “a fundamentally different concept of warfare, in which even relatively minor targets could be considered sufficient justification for attacks to harm civilians.”
The newspaper said the large number of civilians classified by the military as “collateral damage” was not simply the result of failures or mistaken identification, but stemmed from a policy of expanding the use of firepower “to the maximum extent.”
Haaretz said similar accounts had been presented during the three years of the war and that efforts to compensate for the intelligence failures of Oct. 7, 2023, “contributed to unprecedented tolerance for civilian casualties.”
The newspaper cited an Oct. 31, 2023 Israeli airstrike on a large residential complex in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza as one example. The stated target was Ibrahim Biari, a Hamas battalion commander in Jabalia.
“We knew Biari was underground, beneath large buildings, but we did not know beneath which building,” said a soldier identified only as D.
“So they chose buildings that were still inhabited and decided to destroy all the buildings above the tunnel where he was located. We did not carry out an evacuation because it was important to kill him without allowing him to escape,” he said.
Soldier A, who said he took part in the mission, said members of the targeting cell understood that the number of civilians likely to be harmed “was extremely high.”
“In the military intelligence estimates of potential collateral damage, there was talk of 250 to 300 people, so the decision was passed up for direct approval by the chief of staff,” he said.
“After the strike, as time passed, we understood that the number of dead was around 250,” he added, referring to Palestinian civilians.
“I remember being shocked when several densely populated buildings were flattened, killing hundreds, in order to kill a battalion commander who only a few weeks earlier would not even have been considered a target,” he said.
Responding to the Jabalia massacre, the Israeli army claimed that the strike had been “replanned several times to reduce harm to civilians,” saying the expected number of civilian casualties “was not in the hundreds.”
The army claimed that after the strike, “the damage was found to have exceeded its initial assessment.”
Civilian bloodshed
Nadav Weiman, executive director of Breaking the Silence, a left-wing Israeli organization, denounced the army’s conduct in Gaza.
“We cannot allow the killing of 300 civilians to assassinate a battalion commander,” he said. “Nor can we kill 20 civilians to kill every Hamas truck driver and then claim publicly that we did everything possible to prevent harm to innocent people.
“It is time for those who issued these orders to take responsibility instead of trying to get rid of the soldiers who courageously decided to tell the public the truth,” Weiman said.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Haaretz said another case described by the soldiers involved the Oct. 13, 2023 targeting of Hamas commander Ali Qadi.
According to the newspaper, an intelligence soldier in the Gaza Division had warned that Qadi “was behaving unusually,” but the division’s intelligence officer disregarded the warning.
“A few days after the war began, Qadi became a target and was subjected to heavy fire,” soldier A said.
“He was in the house with his family, and they decided to kill him. The army quickly announced that he had been killed, but in reality Qadi was the only person who survived the attack. Everyone who was killed had no connection to the target,” he said.
Without evacuation
Another soldier, identified as B, who served in a drone unit, said that after the war began, the division was authorized to operate under expanded parameters, meaning attacks expected to injure up to 20 noncombatants “did not require approval from a senior official outside the targeting cell.”
A third soldier, identified as C, who served in military intelligence, said that several months after the ground offensive began on Oct. 27, 2023, his unit was asked to prepare an entry zone into Gaza City for a maneuvering division.
He said several high-rise buildings in the area were considered a threat to Israeli troops and that an intelligence assessment estimated that about 25% of residents were still inside their homes.
“When we tried to ask how many residents remained and whether that was reasonable, we were told that those residents were targets for the forces on the ground. I could not understand or believe that we were talking about such numbers,” he said.
He added that the forces planning to enter the area could have waited considerably longer before approving the attack.
“So in the early stages we attacked without a full evacuation. Defending the soldiers was given priority, which is understandable, but the numbers (of civilian casualties) kept growing and became unreasonable,” he said.
The Israeli army has killed more than 74,300 Palestinians and injured over 175,400 others in a brutal war since October 2023 that has left the entire enclave in ruins.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine skipped strikes on Russian energy
articles.body:
- Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not strike Russian energy facilities overnight into Oct. 12 after Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
- He said Russia kept attacking Ukrainian gas and power infrastructure, and Moscow has not confirmed agreeing to the ceasefire.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not strike any energy facilities inside Russia overnight into Oct. 12, after President Donald Trump announced an immediate halt to attacks on energy targets, but that Russia kept hitting Ukraine’s gas and power infrastructure.
Zelenskyy made the comments in a live interview with Fox News on Monday. Trump said on Truth Social on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy facilities. Moscow has not confirmed accepting any such deal, and the exact scope of the proposal is still unclear.
“We didn’t attack any energy objects on the territory of Russia because President Trump said that there will be an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. And we didn’t attack, but Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, infrastructure and other things,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
He said Kyiv was ready to observe the ceasefire but doubted Moscow was, describing the overnight strikes as Vladimir Putin’s answer to Trump and saying Russia had signaled it knew nothing about an energy ceasefire.
Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, said Russian forces hit a power plant in Kyiv, cutting electricity and water, and then struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv after Trump’s announcement. Sienik said Russia had attacked electricity generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times over the past week. Russia has not commented on those claims.
A White House official told Axios that Trump’s proposal initially focused on stopping attacks on oil refineries, with a broader halt covering power plants and electrical grids possibly to follow. Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign against Russian refineries has been a point of friction with Washington, and Trump has argued the strikes push up fuel prices. Zelenskyy rejected a refinery-only arrangement, saying an energy ceasefire has to cover Ukraine’s power grid, and tied any pause on refinery strikes to Russia doing the same.
“If Russia will not attack our energy, we will not attack the energy,” said Zelenskyy.
He also disputed Trump’s view that Ukrainian strikes are behind higher diesel prices, pointing instead to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. On Friday, Trump announced a deal with Russia to release Russian diesel to the United States and global markets, which critics in Congress say gives Moscow more revenue for the war.
Zelenskyy also responded to Trump’s suggestion over the weekend that Ukraine needs a new president. He said he was ready to hold elections but that Ukraine would need at least 60 days of security for its infrastructure to prepare, given ongoing Russian drone and missile attacks. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected the idea of a 60-day pause on Monday, arguing that European countries would use it to rearm Ukraine.
“I don’t think he deserves a respite,” Lavrov said, according to the BBC.
Zelenskyy said he last spoke with Trump in person at the U.N. General Assembly in New York in late September. Russia has not said whether it will stop striking Ukrainian energy facilities.

articles.title: Deployment of 39,000 troops foiled enemy ground invasion plan

He said the enemy had expected that airstrikes and the assassination of commanders would pave the way for proxy forces and terrorist groups to enter Iran. However, the rapid and extensive deployment of army and Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) units along the borders thwarted the plan.
Jahanshahi said that following the 12-Day War in 2025, Iran’s armed forces reviewed battlefield experience, revised operational plans, reorganized combat formations and strengthened defensive positions.
He said combat-readiness exercises at military bases and the reinforcement of border units were among the measures taken to counter potential threats.
The commander said the Ground Forces were prepared to counter any act of aggression, citing their mobile assault brigades, rapid-response forces, special units and mechanized forces.
General Jahanshahi added that army personnel considered the defense of Iran’s territorial integrity their duty, stressing that the armed forces had assumed responsibility for protecting national interests and ensuring the country’s security following the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia faces new missile and drone fire after major attacks on airports
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia faces new missile and drone fire after major attacks on airports
RIYADH, Oct 12 - Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday and that Riyadh airport would remain shut for now, days after Saturday's deadly missile strike on a departure terminal that was claimed by Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.
Incoming drones and missiles were reported by the Saudi-led coalition backing government forces in Yemen, though there was no immediate news of whether they were intercepted.
The Houthis have been attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities since last week as part of a rapidly escalating conflict that has spilled over from the wider regional conflagration between the United States and Iran.
Those attacks have shut down parts of Saudi airspace, suspending operations at Riyadh airport, and largely emptying the skies over the capital even as the city hosts a major energy conference.
Saudi Arabia now faces a nightmare predicament, having re-entered Yemen's civil war to push the Houthis from the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait oil route and stop the group making further gains after its sudden advances in September.
With the Yemeni forces Riyadh supports having made some gains against the Houthis around Bab el-Mandeb but still on the back foot on other fronts, Yemeni military sources said, any pressure on the Houthis could take time to pay off.
Saudi Arabia's long-time regional rival Iran offered to mediate between its Houthi allies and the kingdom. "We have repeatedly expressed our readiness to help facilitate dialogue between the parties," foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday.
Meanwhile, despite intensified Saudi airstrikes against the group, including what Yemeni television said were hits on al-Jawf province on Monday, the Houthis show no sign of letting up their own barrage of attacks on Saudi infrastructure.
The group has repeatedly threatened to target airports and airspace, as well as Saudi oil installations that provide the engine for the kingdom's economy and its ambitious development plans.
UAE CALLS FOR JOINT GULF ACTION
Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at Monday's conference that the kingdom would stay focused on bringing in investment as part of its wider economic development goals.
"The development of our energy system and industrial capability continues," he said.
Saudi Arabia's neighbour the United Arab Emirates on Monday called for a revival of joint Gulf action on security and defence in response to the attacks. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said the targeting of Saudi Arabia undermined the security of all Gulf states and added that the neglect of collective Gulf security had "emboldened others" to overreach against regional states.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE had been partners in the Yemen conflict for years, but they backed different forces within the Yemeni military coalition supporting the government and fell out last winter.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi Arabia in strikes on the Houthis, but there has been no sign yet of any US action. REUTERS

articles.title: Iran launches drone strikes on Iranian Kurdish opposition camp in northern Iraq
articles.body:
Iran continued its drone attacks on Kurdish Iranian opposition groups on Monday. Iran has struck the Kurdistan Region of Northern Iraq, according to reports in local Kurdish media and a statement from the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (KDPI). The party said that “at 12:01, a drone struck the Azadi camp in Koya.” This occurred in the middle of the day, just after noon. Images online showed a drone flying through the sky.
Koya is located between Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Region, and Sulaymaniyah, on the border with Iran. Koya has long been an area where Kurdish Iranian dissident groups have camps and housing for their members who have fled the Islamic Republic over the last decades.
Rudaw media in the Kurdistan Region of Northern Iraq added that “two drones struck a camp belonging to the Iranian Kurdish opposition group, Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran, in Erbil province’s Koya district on Monday, causing material damage but no casualties, a senior party official and a security source told Rudaw English, as Kurdish political leaders gathered in Erbil for a regional forum.”
Iran continues to show that it will attack Kurdish groups.
American forces left Iraq on September 30. Many Kurdish leaders expressed concern that this could leave their region in northern Iraq vulnerable. They lack air defenses, and Baghdad has denied them the ones they need for protection. Iraq in general does not have proper air defenses, a result of years of misrule and Baghdad’s inability to acquire relevant defensive capabilities.
Iran carries out over 1,000 strikes in Kurdistan region
Iran has carried out more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks on the Kurdistan Region, many of them targeting Kurdish opposition groups. The Islamic regime’s goal is to threaten and intimidate these groups and terrorize the region. It doesn’t want the groups rising up in the Kurdish regions of western Iran.
Rudaw noted that the KDPI camp “had been evacuated before the attack and no one remained at the site.”
A security source also confirmed to Rudaw English a second drone attack on the same site,” KDPI said. “This is the 175th time the Islamic Republic has attacked the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan.”
Meanwhile, KDPI spokesperson Khalid Azizi told Rudaw that the group was not sending its forces into Iraq. KDPI appears to be messaging in order to reduce tensions.
An Iranian diplomat recently appeared to threaten the Kurdistan Region. The KRG government in Erbil has long sought to balance its relations with Iran while also having some of the Kurdish opposition groups present.
“We have discussed this with both the Iraqi government and the Kurdistan Regional Government [KRG]. We have decided and pledged that we will not turn Iraqi Kurdistan or Iraq into a rear front,” Khalid Azizi, the KDPI spokesperson, told Rudaw’s Hiwa Jamal on Monday.
Rudaw noted that “Azizi said the party saw no need to deploy armed units into Iranian Kurdistan, arguing that Kurdish opposition groups and their supporters inside Iran were already engaged in a civil struggle.”
Suicide drones utilized by IRGC
The Hana Human Rights group, which focuses on human rights violations in Iranian Kurdistan, described the drone attack as targeting the housing complex of families of the KDPI. “According to information received by the Hana Human Rights Organization, Iranian Islamic Republic suicide drones that had flown from Piranshahr toward the Kurdistan Region of Iraq targeted one of the camps housing the families of members of the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan in Koysinjaq [Koya].”
The new attack comes days after KDPI issued a statement on Friday responding to comments by Consul General of Iran Faramarz Asadi, who accused Kurdish opposition parties of forming an alliance under pressure from foreign powers. The KDPI defended the Alliance of Political Forces of Iranian Kurdistan, which was launched in February and brings together several Iranian Kurdish opposition groups.
The alliance was a “political decision aimed at cooperation and coordination to achieve the legitimate aspirations of the Kurdish nation in its own homeland. It is not evidence supporting the accusations Tehran has leveled against them,” the KDPI said.
Iran has called the Kurdish groups “terrorists.” Only hours after Asadi made his comments, two explosive-laden drones targeted a base belonging to the Khabat Organization of Iranian Kurdistan near Erbil.

articles.title: As long as US continues war, security not to return to Hormuz
articles.body:
He made the remarks in his weekly press briefing on Monday, emphasizing, "As long as the United States persists in its blockade and military aggression, security will not return to the strategic Strait of Hormuz."
He seized this opportunity to commemorate the name and memory of famous and outstanding Persian poet Hafez Shirazi, noting that Hafez holds a unique and special place among all poets, especially for Iranians and is considered an inseparable part of Iranian-Islamic culture and civilization.
In response to the recent speech by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Baghaei emphasized that the address should be viewed as part of America’s cognitive warfare against Iran.
Presenting a distorted picture of historical events to justify Washington’s warmongering is both dangerous and an affront to Greek culture and civilization, he emphasized.
"Mr. Rubio has inadvertently acknowledged important realities, including the fact that Iran has endured for millennia. The West as it exists today, in terms of meaning and thought, would not exist had Iranian and Muslim thinkers not served as translators and interpreters of Greek ideas during the dark ages of the Middle Ages. Iranian civilization has consistently established and sustained itself through acts of connection and creation," he underlined.
Addressing Rubio’s advisors with a sarcastic tone, Baghaei noted, “I urge them to present a copy of the * Divan of Hafez * to the US Secretary of State Rubio, so that he may become acquainted with the refinement of Iranian civilization and culture. The United States cannot portray itself as the representative of Western and Greek civilization.”
The Americans and those who drafted Rubio’s speech were aware of these contradictions but deliberately ignored them in order to justify aggression and violence, he said, adding, “Undoubtedly, European countries and those who consider themselves heirs to Western civilization have a duty to clarify their position on this matter.”
In his reaction to Trump’s recent remarks claiming that Iran has lost its leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, he emphasized the gap between American claims and the reality on the battlefield, stating, “What we are witnessing in the Strait of Hormuz today is not an act of leverage by Iran, but rather the result of a direct US attack on our country's territory.”
Noting that Iran has taken necessary measures in accordance with international law and in defense of its national sovereignty, the foreign ministry spokesman reiterated, “As long as the United States persists in its blockade and military aggression, security will not return to this strategic waterway."
Stating that the security of the Strait of Hormuz is of greater importance to Iran than to any other country, Baghaei added, "Through its acts of aggression, the United States has created trouble not only for the region but also for itself and the entire world. This reality must be kept alive in the eyes of global public opinion."
Elsewhere in his remarks, the spokesperson referred to Iran-Russia Cultural Week, describing it as one of the most magnificent joint cultural events between the two nations.
The cultural event was held in four Russian cities and was warmly received by the Russian public and officials as well.
In response to a question regarding Iran's stance on the recent agreement between Russia and the United States concerning diesel fuel, he said, "Each party makes decisions based on its own interests, and we, as the Islamic Republic of Iran, will act based on our own national interests."
Pointing to the contradiction in the American narrative, Baghaei added, “I find it interesting if the Strait of Hormuz issue had indeed been resolved, why was the American side compelled to turn to Russia to purchase oil?"
The foreign ministry spokesman then pointed to the recent telephone conversation between Iran’s Foreign Minister Araghchi and his Saudi counterpart bin Farhan, emphasizing, “It is natural for the media to make their own claims. Iran’s consultations with regional countries are ongoing, and we are deeply concerned about recent developments in the Arabian Peninsula.”
Iran once again declares its readiness to assist in any way with dialogue between the Yemeni and Saudi sides. Continued tension serves only the interests of the Zionist regime in the region, and Iran does not accept the continuation of war between two Islamic nations. The people of Yemen have the right to live a dignified life in an atmosphere free from pressure and tension, he continued.
In response to a question regarding the details of the US response to Iran’s seven-day plan and whether a reply has been conveyed to the mediators, Baghaei stated that exchange of messages through mediators is ongoing. What was raised on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly and is known as Iran’s seven-day plan reflected Iran’s legitimate and legal demands.
Lifting the naval blockade, halting the war on all fronts, releasing Iran's frozen assets, and everything else agreed upon in the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding will be raised as Iran's indisputable rights in any negotiation, he stipulated.
Regarding the recent meeting between the presidents of Iran and Russia and Vladimir Putin’s subsequent phone call with Donald Trump, the foreign ministry spokesperson stated that Iran’s consultations with Russia concerning the nuclear issue are nothing new. Russia played a positive and constructive role in reaching the JCPOA understanding. A relationship based on mutual trust is a valuable asset shared by the two countries, and Iran is committed to preserving and strengthening this bond.
Baghaei emphasized that Pakistan and Qatar continue to play a mediating role between Iran and the United States.
In another part of the press conference, Baghaei pointed to the double standards displayed by regional and European countries regarding the attacks on Yemen and Saudi Arabia, stating this is not the first time Iran has witnessed a dual approach by global powers toward international issues.
Regarding the detention of students in France following the student protest, he stated that Iran has unequivocally condemned this action and made its position clear. Iran also pursued the matter with the French Embassy in Tehran during a meeting convened by the country’s human rights division and conveyed to them its concerns regarding the gross violation of human rights in France.
The French government must address the detention of five to six thousand individuals, the use of violence against students, and the presence of police forces inside classrooms, Baghaei stated.

articles.title: Shin Bet's answer to 7 October failures is an 'Islam school'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Shin Bet's answer to 7 October intelligence failures is to 'study Islam', not Israeli occupation
Israel's domestic intelligence agency, Shin Bet, is planning to establish a school of Islamic studies following its failure to anticipate the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, focusing on religious ideology rather than the decades of Israeli occupation, dispossession and violence that shaped the emergence of Hamas and other Palestinian factions.
The initiative, reported by the Israeli news website Walla, raises questions about Israel's attempts to explain its intelligence failures by a lack of understanding of Islam, rather than examining the political realities that gave rise to Hamas and the institutional failures that allowed the attack to take place.
The project is being spearheaded by Shin Bet chief David Zini and will provide specialised education on Islam, its different schools of thought and Palestinian society to intelligence personnel working across various departments.
The school will operate alongside Shin Bet's existing Arabic-language training programme, which also provides instruction to some Israeli military personnel.
According to Walla, the project will involve academics, researchers, specialist institutions and current and former senior intelligence officials, with its curriculum tailored to the operational challenges facing the agency.
The initiative follows internal investigations into Israel's intelligence failures preceding 7 October, when Palestinian fighters breached the Gaza perimeter and attacked Israeli military positions and communities.
Despite possessing extensive intelligence about Hamas's preparations, Israeli security agencies failed to anticipate the scale and timing of the assault.
Walla reported that one conclusion drawn by Israel's intelligence establishment was that officials lacked sufficient understanding of Islam, Palestinian culture and Hamas's ideological foundations, particularly in Gaza.
Investigators reportedly identified shortcomings in their understanding of the movement's development following the release of Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar from Israeli prison in 2011, as well as the continuing influence of the organisation's founder, Sheikh Ahmed Yassin.
Sheikh Yassin was assassinated in an Israeli airstrike in 2004, while Sinwar was killed by Israeli forces in Gaza in October 2024.
A senior Israeli intelligence official told Walla: "We did not realise the extent to which Hamas hates Israel, how unwilling it is to accept any compromise, or how strong and prepared it was before 7 October, even though the warning signs were clearly visible."
However, framing Hamas primarily through its religious ideology risks reducing a movement rooted in the Palestinian experience of occupation to a question of Islamic beliefs.
Hamas was established in 1987 during the First Palestinian intifada uprising against Israeli occupation, nearly two decades after Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza in 1967.
Although the movement emerged from the Palestinian branch of the Muslim Brotherhood and draws on Islamist ideology, its formation and development were closely related to the Palestinian struggle against Israeli military rule, territorial dispossession and the denial of national self-determination.
Hamas has previously offered Israel a long-term truce if it withdraws from the entirety of the West Bank and Gaza, while signalling its acceptance of a Palestinian state only on those territories.
Its political and armed activities have arguably been shaped by continued occupation, repeated Israeli military offensives, the blockade of Gaza and the failure of successive political efforts to secure Palestinian statehood.
Treating Islam as the central explanation for Hamas's actions therefore risks confusing the movement's ideological identity with the political and historical conditions that produced it.
The focus on Islam also comes amid the Netanyahu government's growing cultivation of far-right political movements in Europe, including parties and figures associated with Islamophobia and hostility towards Muslim immigration.
Israeli officials, particularly Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli, have increasingly sought alliances with European nationalist parties around a shared opposition to alleged "radical Islam". The outreach has included France's National Rally, Spain's Vox and Austria's Freedom Party, as Israeli leaders increasingly portray the country as a defender of Western civilisation against an alleged Islamist threat.
Hamas's 7 October assault on Israel took place in a year when Israeli violence in the West Bank and East Jerusalem had already killed more Palestinians in any full year since the UN began recording fatalities in 2005.
Israeli military raids, particularly in Jenin and Nablus, had intensified, while illegal settlement expansion and settler attacks placed growing pressure on Palestinian communities.
In Gaza, Israel had launched another major military offensive in May 2023, carrying out hundreds of airstrikes. The escalation left 33 Palestinians dead, including at least 12 civilians, according to the UN, and damaged thousands of homes.
These developments came against the backdrop of Israel's blockade of Gaza, imposed in 2007, which had devastated the territory's economy and severely restricted the movement of its population.
Just a day before the 7 October attack, The New Arab reported that 2023 had already become the deadliest year for Palestinian children in the occupied West Bank, with Israeli forces killing 47 children since January, surpassing the 45 killed throughout 2022.
Tensions had also intensified at the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem, while the prospect of Saudi-Israeli normalisation threatened to further marginalise the Palestinian national question.
Israel's occupation overlooked in 7 October reckoning
Hamas named its operation "Al-Aqsa Flood", citing Israeli actions at the holy site, the blockade, Palestinian prisoners and the occupation among its stated grievances.
The focus on religion risks obscuring a more immediate explanation for Israel's failure to anticipate the attack, as its intelligence agencies had already possessed detailed warnings about Hamas's plans.
Israeli investigations into the 7 October attack have exposed failures that went far beyond a lack of cultural or religious understanding.
Israeli intelligence reportedly possessed detailed information about Hamas's plans, including a document outlining an assault remarkably similar to the one eventually carried out, but senior officials dismissed the scenario as unrealistic.
In September 2026, an investigation published by Haaretz revealed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had also reportedly received a direct warning from UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed around 10 days before the attack that Hamas was preparing a major offensive.
According to the report, Netanyahu reassured the Emirati leader that Israel was prepared for any scenario but failed to pass the warning to senior Israeli security officials. An Emirati source subsequently confirmed the reported conversation to The Times of Israel, although Netanyahu's office denied it had taken place, calling the allegations an "absolute lie".
Warnings from Israeli surveillance personnel stationed near Gaza were also reportedly ignored, raising questions about institutional complacency and the failure to act on intelligence already available, rather than simply a lack of understanding of Hamas's ideology.
Despite these revelations, three years after the attack, Israel has still not established an independent state commission of inquiry into the political, military and intelligence failures surrounding 7 October, amid opposition from Netanyahu and disputes over how such an investigation should be conducted.

articles.title: Czech intelligence chief says Russia could resort to riskier operations in NATO states
articles.body:
Czech intelligence chief says Russia could resort to riskier operations in NATO states
PRAGUE, Oct 12 - Russia could resort to riskier and more significant operations in NATO member states supporting Ukraine within months, the head of the Czech security service said on Monday, as Moscow seems to be adopting a tactic of "escalation for de-escalation".
• "This could involve sabotage attacks on the territory of a NATO member state against a facility connected to aid for Ukraine, a drone or missile attack on a weapons depot intended for Ukraine, or, in an extreme case, even a limited military action against one of the neighbouring member states of the Alliance," Michal Koudelka told a parliamentary security conference
• He said that last threat was not currently immediate as "Russia has all its forces concentrated in Ukraine"
• Koudelka, director general of the Czech Security Information Service, said his agency had no specific information on a direct threat to the Czech Republic but was monitoring operations aimed at the country and allies closely
• He said Russia's hybrid activities were aimed at weakening unity in the NATO military alliance
• President Vladimir Putin said this month Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully. Moscow has also repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations REUTERS

articles.title: Roundup: Yemen's Houthis claim new strike on Riyadh airport as Tehran offers to facilitate dialogue
articles.body:
SANAA/RIYADH, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Monday evening that it had launched a new ballistic missile strike on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, while Tehran reiterated its readiness to facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a statement that the group targeted the Riyadh airport with a ballistic missile, claiming the missile "accurately hit" the target.
He said the group also launched a drone attack on King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, southwestern Saudi Arabia, claiming a direct hit.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition said in a statement that its forces had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile fired toward Riyadh on Monday evening.
Explosions were heard in the Saudi capital around the time of the reported attack, and residents received alerts via mobile apps.
The Houthi group has intensified strikes on the Riyadh airport in recent days.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said Monday that a Pakistani resident was killed and 11 others injured in a strike targeting the airport Sunday afternoon.
The authority said it had extended the suspension of operations at the airport.
A Saturday Houthi strike on the airport killed 12 people and injured 309 others, according to the authority.
Also on Monday, the Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out 119 strikes on several Houthi-held areas over the past 24 hours.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported that at least nine people were killed and seven others injured in airstrikes on Al-Jawf, a province near the border with Saudi Arabia.
Yemeni military spokesperson Majid al-Nuzaili said in the day that government forces had carried out 1,879 attacks on Houthi military targets in recent hours, claiming that about 950 Houthi fighters had been "neutralized."
The escalation has sparked mounting regional and international concern.
At a weekly press conference on Monday, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran has "repeatedly expressed readiness to use our good offices to facilitate dialogue between the (warring) parties."
His remarks came a day after Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi, in a phone conversation with his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah Al Saud on Sunday, voiced Iran's readiness to provide "any kind of assistance" to help initiate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government. The renewed fighting marked a major escalation after a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities. ■

articles.title: Saudi Arabia says drones and missiles still targeting kingdom as Iran-backed Houthis step up attacks
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia said Monday it was dealing with more drones and missile strikes as a slew of countries warned against travel to the kingdom due to fatal attacks on Riyadh's airport by Iran-backed Houthi militants.
The Australian and New Zealand governments on Monday cautioned their citizens against traveling to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and other Saudi destinations, joining similar advisories from the U.K., U.S., Canada, France, Germany, Japan and others.
It came as the Saudi aviation authority extended the suspension of operations at the airport, which has been hit by numerous projectiles over the past week. The deadliest strike came on Saturday, when 12 people were killed and more than 300 were injured, according to officials. Another strike on Sunday killed one person and injured nearly a dozen.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which have raised questions over the robustness of Saudi Arabia's defense capabilities despite its huge military spending.
The fatalities come as the kingdom hosts major corporate conferences, including the World Petroleum Congress, the International Energy Forum Ministerial Meeting and the Future Investment Initiative.
Airlines canceled hundreds of flights scheduled for the coming days, and about 100 flights were forced to divert to other airports, according to Flightradar24. The Federal Aviation Administration warned U.S. carriers of potential risks of flying over and around Saudi Arabia.
Delta Air Lines is scheduled to debut a nonstop flight from Atlanta to Riyadh on Oct. 23, but a spokeswoman said the carrier hasn't made a decision yet on whether to postpone the new route.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that the U.S. "may" join Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against the Houthis.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi. said Sunday that he had told Saudi Minister of Foreign Affairs Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud by phone that Tehran was willing to take steps to start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, where the Houthis are based.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei meanwhile said Iran was still reviewing a U.S. response to its proposal for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and would reply through its intermediaries, Reuters reported.
— CNBC's Leslie Josephs contributed to this report.

articles.title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
- Published
Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".
There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
- What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? 
  - Published21 hours ago
Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.
He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities."
"I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.
Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday.
On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.
Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.
Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".
On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district.
Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured.
When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".
Asked about the ceasefire on Monday, Trump said they agreed "because I said you agree", adding that the war "has to get settled".
"That war is a disaster if you see the numbers," he said.
For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides.
Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".
Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.
In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.
Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.
The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.
However, there has been a mixed response among European officials.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."
Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman, BBC Verify

articles.title: Dozens killed in airstrike on gold mine in Sudan
articles.body:
At least 72 workers were killed by airstrikes on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border, a Sudanese rights group said on Sunday, after survivors described scenes of chaos in the mountainous region.
The Emergency Lawyers rights organization accused the Egyptian air force of carrying out the attack. Agence France-Presse could not independently confirm the account and Egypt has issued no official comment.
The attack on Saturday was the second this year on Jabal al-Uqaydat, after airstrikes, reportedly by Egypt, killed 23 workers in the informal gold mining site in June.
Photo: Reuters
The Egyptian army did not claim the strikes, but said at the time that it had conducted a “large-scale operation” against illegal gold mining within its borders.
The border between Sudan and Egypt is disputed, with both countries claiming the resource-rich Halayeb triangle. However, Cairo is a key ally of Sudan’s army, at war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The attack on Saturday “resulted in the deaths of 72 civilian miners, according to preliminary information, while efforts to document and verify the casualty toll are ongoing,” said the Emergency Lawyers, which documents atrocities in Sudan’s war.
Two survivors described their harrowing escape from the mine.
Miner Abdelaziz Youssef said a jet appeared overhead at about 8am on Saturday and “struck five times, many people were killed.”
“We ran up the mountain terrified of another strike,” he said.
Another survivor, Sharaf Ali, said there were thousands of people working at the remote site when it was hit.
“After the airstrike people scattered, some people came to al-Ansary market, others went in the other direction, that’s why no one knows how many exactly were killed,” he said from the gold market, just south of the Halayeb triangle.
Both survivors said they saw bodies on the ground as they fled, with many more feared trapped under the rubble, hours away from any urban center.
Since April 2023, the conflict has killed more than 200,000 people and created a deep humanitarian crisis that has pushed many into the dangerous gold mining industry, which fuels both sides’ war efforts.

articles.title: Iraqi fighter jets destroy Daesh terrorist group position in eastern province: report
articles.body:
Iraqi F-16 fighter jets carried out two air strikes that destroyed a position used by Daesh terrorist group in the eastern province of Diyala, security officials said on Sunday.
The strikes targeted the group in the Narin area, according to a statement by Iraq's Security Media Cell carried by the official Iraqi News Agency (INA).
The operation was based on intelligence provided by the Military Intelligence Directorate and coordinated with the military's aerial reconnaissance and surveillance center.
The Security Media Cell said the position was completely destroyed but gave no details on casualties. It said further information would be released later.
The strikes came less than two weeks after the US-led coalition's mission against Daesh terrorist group in Iraq officially ended on September 30, nearly 12 years after its launch.
Iraq declared victory over Daesh terrorist group in December 2017 after retaking all territory held by the group, although Iraqi forces have continued operations against its remaining remnants.

articles.title: Seventeen nations join NATO nuclear exercise in Italy
articles.body:
NATO’s annual nuclear deterrence exercise begins on Tuesday and is being hosted by Italy this year, with seventeen nations taking part, according to the alliance.
Steadfast Noon is described as a long-planned, routine training activity, part of the effort to maintain readiness and test the procedures that contribute to deterrence and defence. The overall scale is in line with previous iterations, and no live weapons are used at any point.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said: “NATO is a defensive Alliance. This exercise helps us ensure a safe, secure, effective, and credible capability to preserve peace, prevent coercion and deter aggression. It also sends a clear message of unity and resolve.”
The alliance adds that the exercise is not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country.
Flying is expected to run from Aviano in Pordenone province and Ghedi in Brescia province, along with other locations across the area of responsibility, over roughly ten days, according to Il Sole 24 Ore. Aviano hosts United States Air Force units, and Ghedi is an Italian Air Force base operating the F-35A.
Seventeen participating nations is an increase on the fourteen that took part last year and the thirteen the year before. France does not take part, having never joined NATO’s Nuclear Planning Group, and the United States contributes flight crews and maintenance personnel.
Last year’s edition was led by the Netherlands from Volkel, supported by Kleine Brogel in Belgium and RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk, and drew around seventy aircraft from fourteen allied nations across a mix of conventional and dual-capable types. Italy has hosted the exercise six times before, in 2010, 2013, 2014, 2018, 2021 and 2023.
The Italian Air Force has said that no live ammunition is to be used.

articles.title: Iran pledges stronger deterrence, asserts sovereignty over Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Iran pledges stronger deterrence, asserts sovereignty over Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN— Iranian military officials have reaffirmed the country’s determination to strengthen its defense capabilities, protect its maritime interests and oppose efforts to restore a US-dominated security order in West Asia, arguing that regional stability must be based on national sovereignty and cooperation among neighboring countries.
The statements by senior military figures and defense officials address several interconnected issues, including Iran’s military preparedness following recent hostilities, the strategic management of the Strait of Hormuz, the future of regional security arrangements and the growing controversy over Washington’s use of historical and civilizational rhetoric in its confrontation with Iran.
Military preparedness and deterrence
Iranian military officials say the country has drawn lessons from recent conflicts and strengthened its ability to respond to potential threats.
Rear Admiral Bemani, deputy commander of the Iranian Army’s Navy, said Iran had studied its adversaries’ weaknesses and developed new weapons and tactics considering recent military confrontations.
He said the Iranian Army’s Navy, working alongside Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy, had inflicted significant blows on US forces at certain stages of the fighting. According to Bemani, US forces are now operating farther from Iran’s maritime borders than in previous periods.
He warned that any renewed miscalculation would prompt a response from Iran’s Navy and could force hostile forces to move farther away from the country’s maritime borders.
Bemani also distinguished between the responsibilities of the armed forces and those of the government in addressing the US naval blockade. While the government handles its political and economic dimensions, he said, the military remains focused on resistance, defense preparedness and responding to threats.
Caretaker Defense Minister Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza has likewise emphasized the importance of strengthening Iran’s scientific, industrial and defense capabilities. He said national security requires the means to defend the country’s sovereignty and ensure that the armed forces are adequately equipped to protect Iran.
The emphasis on domestic capabilities reflects the Iranian military leadership’s stated position that deterrence depends not only on weapons and operational readiness but also on scientific advancement, industrial capacity and the ability to adapt to evolving military threats.
Strait of Hormuz: Strategic management and maritime sovereignty
The Strait of Hormuz remains another central element of Iran’s security calculations, given its geographical position and importance to global energy supplies.
Major General Yahya Rahim Safavi, head of the Lt. Gen. Qassem Soleimani Research Institute of Sacred Defense Sciences and Teachings, has identified the strategic management of the waterway as a key component of Iran’s approach to countering the US naval blockade.
Safavi said Iran’s geographical position and rights as a coastal state underpin its authority to safeguard its interests in the strait and surrounding waters. He stressed that exercising sovereignty should not automatically be interpreted as an intention to escalate tensions.
He also distinguished between closing the waterway and managing maritime traffic, arguing that these are fundamentally different approaches. In his assessment, the transport of military equipment that directly threatens Iran’s national security could make the management or restriction of maritime traffic a strategic necessity.
Safavi added that alternative pipelines do not eliminate the Strait of Hormuz’s importance to international energy markets.
According to the US Energy Information Administration, approximately 20 million barrels of oil and petroleum liquids passed through the strait daily in 2022, accounting for roughly one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption. The waterway is also a major route for liquefied natural gas shipments, making its security a matter of international economic significance.
Iranian officials maintain that maritime security cannot be separated from the wider political and military circumstances in the region. From their perspective, the management of the strait must take account of Iran’s sovereignty, the security threats it faces and the need to protect vital national interests.
Safavi has also presented Iran’s approach as part of a broader response to maritime pressure and sanctions, while arguing that regional security should be pursued through the participation of countries in the area.
Tehran rejects a US-led security order
Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi, spokesperson for Iran’s Armed Forces, has said Iran will not allow the regional order envisaged by the United States and Israel to be restored in West Asia.
Shekarchi called on neighboring countries to reconsider their reliance on an ineffective US security umbrella. He argued that recent conflicts had demonstrated the risks of depending on Washington for regional protection.
He accused the United States of fuel smuggling, maritime theft and psychological warfare surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, adding that political statements and media messaging could not change realities on the ground. He also questioned Washington’s ability to guarantee regional security and urged neighboring governments not to base their security calculations on the policies of US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
 
Shekarchi said Iran’s armed forces were more capable than before and remained prepared to defend the country against threats.
The statements reflect Tehran’s long-standing emphasis on regional participation in security arrangements. Iranian officials argue that countries sharing West Asia’s geographical and strategic environment should play the leading role in maintaining its stability rather than relying on military structures dominated by outside powers.
In this view, regional cooperation is not merely a diplomatic preference, but a security requirement shaped by geography, shared interests and the consequences of military confrontation.
Civilizational confrontation and Washington’s historical rhetoric
Alongside the military and strategic debate, Iranian officials have strongly criticized the use of historical and civilizational references in contemporary political disputes.
Caretaker Defense Minister Ebn al-Reza condemned remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Athens that invoked the ancient conflicts between Greece and Persia. He warned against turning historical and cultural differences into a basis for present-day political or military confrontation.
“Civilizational confrontation is playing with fire,” Ebn al-Reza said, cautioning that those who ignite such tensions may not be able to control their consequences.
He stressed that Iran possesses an ancient civilization and a distinct national identity that do not depend on external recognition. He also argued that the country must strengthen its scientific, industrial and defense capabilities to safeguard its independence.
Brigadier General Ali Balali, an adviser to the commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force, offered a broader ideological interpretation of the confrontation. He said the United States and Israel sought to exploit the wealth and resources of Eastern countries while preventing the emergence of a new Islamic civilization.
“Civilization belongs to the East, and they have no civilization of their own,” Balali said.
He urged neighboring Muslim countries to be aware of efforts by Washington and its allies to prevent the peoples of the East and the Muslim world from becoming more capable and prosperous. Balali also criticized the historical record of Western powers, citing the mass killing of Indigenous peoples in the Americas and violence against populations in Africa.
He maintained that Western powers would ultimately fail to prevent the emergence of a global order shaped by Islamic civilization.
The controversy has also drawn attention to Trump’s statements during the war against Iran. On April 1, he threatened to bombard Iran and said US forces would “bring them back to the stone ages,” while also threatening Iranian power plants and other infrastructure. On April 7, he warned that “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again” if Iran failed to meet his demands.
The remarks have become part of the wider dispute over the language used to describe the conflict and its potential consequences. Iranian officials have argued that such rhetoric cannot be separated from threats against the country’s infrastructure, population and sovereignty.
The exchange has also revived historical references on both sides. Iranian political figures have invoked episodes from the country’s past, including the capture of Roman Emperor Valerian by the Sasanian king Shapur I in 260 AD, in response to Washington’s references to ancient Greco-Persian wars.
For Iranian officials, the issue extends beyond competing interpretations of history. They frame it as a broader question of who has the authority to define civilization, determine the political future of other societies and shape the emerging international order.
Taken together, the statements by Iran’s defense and military officials present a unified message: the country intends to strengthen its deterrent capabilities, safeguard its sovereign interests in strategically important waters and resist external efforts to determine the future of West Asia. In their assessment, lasting regional stability requires respect for national sovereignty and a greater role for regional countries in shaping their own security arrangements, rather than renewed dependence on outside military powers.

articles.title: Houthis claim missile attack on Riyadh airport, drone strike on Saudi air base in Khamis Mushait

The Houthi group claimed Monday evening that it had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile and the Khamis Mushait air base in southern Saudi Arabia with a drone.
