articles.title: AEVEX shows off jet-powered Specter attack drone at AUSA
articles.body:
- AEVEX is displaying a full-size model of Specter, a turbojet-powered one-way attack drone developed with Divergent Technologies, at AUSA 2026.
- The company has not released Specter’s speed, range or payload, and has introduced a maritime unit following its BlackSea Technologies acquisition.
AEVEX is showing a full-size model of Specter, its new jet-powered one-way attack drone, at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington this week, along with a maritime drone line built from its recent purchase of BlackSea Technologies.
The California-based company announced Specter on Sept. 23 as a high-speed, turbojet-powered autonomous strike platform under development with Divergent Technologies, a Los Angeles company that builds structures through additive manufacturing. AEVEX says Specter will come in ground-launched and air-launched versions and has a swappable nose section that can carry explosive warheads, electronic warfare equipment or surveillance sensors without redesigning the airframe.
The drone uses AEVEX’s CompassX autonomy software, which the company says is built to keep working when GPS and communications are jammed. AEVEX has not released Specter’s speed, range, size, payload weight, price or flight test schedule, and has not named a customer.
Divergent’s role is to make the drone easier to build in large numbers. Its DAPS production system designs and prints complex structural parts digitally, which AEVEX says lets it change the design quickly and plan for high-rate production from the start of engineering. The model at AUSA is the first time the company has shown Specter at full size.
AEVEX is best known for the Phoenix Ghost loitering munition, which the United States sent to Ukraine starting in 2022, and for larger Group 3 drones such as Disruptor. The company went public on the New York Stock Exchange this year. It also buys rocket-assisted takeoff motors for its drones from X-Bow Systems, which has delivered hundreds of them under a $12 million contract.
The company used AUSA to introduce AEVEX Maritime Systems, a new unit formed after it acquired BlackSea Technologies, a Baltimore-area maker of uncrewed surface and underwater vessels that supplies the U.S. Navy and other U.S. forces. The acquisition was valued at about $650 million. AEVEX says its portfolio now covers air, surface and subsurface drones, aimed at an army expecting to fight with jammed navigation, cut communications and supply lines under attack.

articles.title: HMS Dragon went from dry dock to deployment in a week
articles.body:
A Type 45 destroyer sent from maintenance to the eastern Mediterranean in seven days has returned to Portsmouth after 214 days away, having shielded the British bases in Cyprus from drone and missile attack, according to the Royal Navy.
HMS Dragon was in dry dock when she was activated as part of the British response to the conflict in the Middle East, which had brought the sovereign base areas on Cyprus under attack. Working alongside Army and Royal Air Force capabilities, the destroyer formed part of the shield against air attack over the island.
General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of Naval Staff, said: “HMS Dragon’s seven-month deployment has shown the Royal Navy at its best.
“Deployed at short notice, her crew have protected our bases on the island of Cyprus, safeguarded shipping and worked closely with our allies across the Mediterranean and Middle East. They have operated in some of the world’s most dangerous waters with skill and professionalism. Every member of Dragon’s crew should return home proud. And to the families who supported them throughout, thank you for the sacrifices you have made.”
The ship was later sent east of Suez to provide air defence for a proposed international mission to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, sailing through the Bab el Mandeb Strait at the foot of the Red Sea, where Houthi forces in Yemen have been firing missiles and drones at shipping since 2023. Dragon also ran maritime security patrols in the Indian Ocean and spent a period attached to the French carrier strike group led by FS Charles de Gaulle.
Around 950 friends and family met the ship at Portsmouth Naval Base and along the harbour walls.
Vice Admiral Steve Moorhouse, the Fleet Commander, said: “The resilience, professionalism and fighting spirit of Dragon’s ship’s company throughout the last seven months have been outstanding. In an increasingly uncertain world, we need a warfighting ready Navy that can respond at pace wherever the nation requires. Dragon has shown exactly what that looks like. To the friends, families and loved ones who have supported the ship’s company throughout this challenging deployment, thank you, your contribution has underpinned Dragon’s success.”
Dragon is the third of six Type 45 destroyers, all based at Portsmouth, and the class is the fleet’s first line of defence against aircraft, missiles and drones.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia faces further Houthi attacks after calls for halt
articles.body:
A person inspects the damage at the site of a warehouse hit by Saudi-led airstrikes, in Sana'a, Yemen, Oct. 9 2026.EPA/YAHYA ARHAB
Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia strongly condemned on Oct. 11 “hostile” attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis against the Gulf kingdom, including the deadly strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
In a joint statement, the four countries condemned “in the strongest terms the ongoing hostile attacks perpetrated by the Houthi militia against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including the heinous attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh... which constitute a blatant violation of international law.”
The countries described the attacks as a “dangerous escalation” posing a direct threat to Saudi Arabia’s security and stability, as well as civilian safety.
They said the attacks “cannot be justified or accepted under any pretext.”
The four countries reaffirmed their solidarity with Saudi Arabia and support for all legitimate measures it takes to counter the attacks, deter threats and prevent their recurrence.
They also held the Houthis “fully accountable” for the consequences of the attacks and any repercussions threatening regional and international peace and security.
The countries called for an “immediate and unconditional” end to the attacks.
The death toll from the Oct. 10 Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh rose to 13 after an injured Indian national died Oct. 11. The attack also left 309 people injured, according to Saudi authorities.
Türkiye and Pakistan agreed on Oct. 5 to activate collective deterrence measures under a mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia and rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities to the kingdom.
The decision was announced after the three countries’ defense and foreign ministers held an emergency meeting in Riyadh. It marked the first time the alliance, known as the Mecca pact, has been invoked since it was signed Aug. 7.
The accord stipulates that an attack on any of the three countries will be treated as an attack on all three, echoing a central provision of NATO’s founding treaty.
The alliance emerged amid escalating regional tensions following the outbreak of war between the United States, Israel and Iran.

articles.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy accuses Russia of striking power plant after Trump's truce announcement
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Russia struck a power plant in Kharkiv immediately after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine supported the proposal but had yet to see evidence that Russia had agreed to it.
“This energy ceasefire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war,” he said, adding that Kiev was awaiting details of discussions between Washington and Moscow.
Trump said on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to immediately stop attacks on energy infrastructure, without providing details.
The Kremlin did not confirm an agreement on Monday.
Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said contacts were continuing and Moscow would announce any developments.
“We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same,” Zelenskyy said.
He also warned that Ukraine would respond if Russian attacks continued.
“If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure, and stop killing our people,” he said.
Zelenskyy urged Washington to ensure Moscow honoured the proposed truce.
“We need American pressure on Russia, not sanctions relief, not concessions, but real pressure, so that we can achieve at least what the American president posted about yesterday – an energy ceasefire,” he said.
Presidential elections, diesel deal
Asked about elections, Zelenskyy said holding a vote under current conditions was “completely impossible,” citing ongoing Russian attacks and the difficulty of ensuring that military personnel could participate.
Zelenskyy said he was ready to work with parliament to find a way to hold elections if the US secured a full ceasefire lasting at least 60 days.
His remarks followed Trump’s call Saturday for Ukraine to get a new president.
“If the American president has such a strong desire, and after all, he has made a deal with the Russians, he lifted sanctions on them, then he can influence the leader of the Kremlin to have a full ceasefire,” Zelenskyy said. “And if we have at least a 60-day full ceasefire, then I'll be ready to work on holding elections.”
He also criticised Washington’s reported decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, questioning the deal’s potential impact on global markets.
Zelenskyy said the reported volumes of 300,000 to 500,000 tonnes per month would have little effect on global supplies, which he put at about 120 million tonnes monthly.
“Let's propose a diesel deal with Ukraine,” he said.
Zelenskyy argued that Kiev could refrain from striking Russian oil infrastructure if Washington helped secure a halt to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid.
“We are influencing whether these ships are moving. We define whether the refineries are working,” he said.
Zelenskyy warned that continued disruption of maritime trade could cause food shortages in parts of Africa, Asia, and the Middle East that receive Ukrainian agricultural exports.
“In two to three months, everybody will be talking about a crisis in agriculture because there will be food shortages for countries on the African continent, for some countries in Asia, in the Middle East, because we are exporting millions of tonnes of food to those markets, and now the sea is being blocked, and the United States is not feeling that,” he said.

articles.title: British tanker completes fourteen missions in Saudi deployment
articles.body:
A Royal Air Force Voyager sent to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refuelling has already flown fourteen operational missions, alongside air defence also deployed by Britain, the Prime Minister told the House of Commons.
Andy Burnham set out the deployment in a statement on the United Nations General Assembly and the international meetings that followed it, describing the Middle East as one of the subjects he had discussed with President Trump in New York.
He said: “I confirmed Britain’s decision to send air defence and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air to air refuelling support. I can confirm today it has already completed 14 operational missions. This support is needed to protect civilians. I condemn the appalling attacks on the King Khalid International Airport. We will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.”
The deployment was agreed in late September in response to a Saudi request, with the Prime Minister acting on the advice of the Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, and the Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband. Mr Burnham said then that Britain was acting to secure the interests of this country and the wider region, and that pathways needed to be kept open. Saudi Arabia was reported to be running low on interceptor stocks as Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks, which began on 8 September, continued.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh came on 8 October, when a Houthi ballistic missile killed three people, among them a Saudia pilot, Captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, and wounded dozens more, several of them foreign nationals. A Saudia aircraft was damaged. Operations at the airport have since resumed.
Attacks on Abha and King Khalid airports in early October killed three civilians and injured thirty-six, according to the Saudi civil aviation authority, and strikes on Jazan and Najran airports wounded at least three. The coalition said on 18 September that it had intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at King Khalid, and an explosion was heard near the airport the following day with smoke rising from a fuel storage area.
Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to deploy forces under mutual defence arrangements signed with Saudi Arabia earlier this year, and a Pakistani foreign ministry spokesman has said his country now has a substantial number of forces and resources in Riyadh, acting in defence of Saudi territory without crossing into Houthi-held areas.
Voyager is the Royal Air Force’s only air-to-air refuelling aircraft and also carries the strategic air transport role, flying in two configurations, the KC Mk 2 with two underwing pods for fast jets and the KC Mk 3 with an additional centreline hose for larger aircraft.

articles.title: The U.S. allowed the export of Russian diesel to revive peace talks - Reuters
articles.body:
The U.S. allowed the export of Russian diesel to revive peace talks - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
Washington believes that diesel exports will soften Moscow’s position and restore dialogue. The U.S. told Kyiv that Putin is not yet ready for negotiations.
The United States allowed the export of Russian diesel fuel in order to bring Russia back to negotiations on ending the war. Washington believes this will soften the Kremlin’s position and help restore the trilateral dialogue after previous unsuccessful attempts. Reuters reports this, citing three unnamed people familiar with the course of the negotiations, UNN reports.
Details
According to the publication’s sources, at a brief meeting in Miami, U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner told the Ukrainian delegation that Russian dictator Vladimir Putin is currently not ready for negotiations on ending the war. At the same time, the announced agreement is intended to "help restore contacts."
A third source said that the United States told the Ukrainians that the agreement on diesel fuel could help "soften" Moscow’s position, as it "sends a signal that Trump is open to cooperation" with Russia
The publication also notes that U.S. representatives reminded them of the military and intelligence assistance provided to Kyiv, but did not threaten to halt it over a refusal to stop strikes on oil refineries.
Previously
In the opinion of U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian dictator Vladimir Putin is more interested in concluding a peace agreement than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

articles.title: Taiwan tracks 10 Chinese ships, 5 military aircraft
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked five Chinese military aircraft, six naval vessels, and four official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Monday and 6 a.m. on Tuesday.
Four of the five People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line and entered the country’s central and southwestern air defense identification zone, according to the MND.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems to monitor PLA activity.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese aircraft 72 times and ships 135 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: Taiwan’s nuclear restart faces an environmental review dispute
articles.body:
The Nuclear Safety Commission (NSC, 核安會) on Sept. 24 approved the re-operation plan that Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) filed in March for the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant in Pingtung County, after three rounds of review and 589 comments. Taipower now has to carry out the work in the plan and its own inspections on ageing, radiation and seismic resistance, then report back to the commission for review and on-site checks. Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) has named 2028 as the earliest restart. The NSC has given no date.
THE DEBATE
No challenge has been identified as to whether Ma-anshan needs an environmental impact assessment (EIA) under the Environmental Impact Assessment Act (環境影響評估法) before it runs again. The Ministry of Environment says it does not. Environmental groups say it does. If a suit came after a licence, a judge would rule on the procedure once the inspections ended.
Photo: Tien Yu-hwa, Taipei Times
Article 29 of the act’s implementing criteria requires an assessment to build a nuclear plant, add units or decommission one, and does not mention license renewal. The ministry last amended the criteria on Feb. 5; the nuclear item still lists those three cases.
Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭?明) in May last year asked: “Why does a restart or a life extension need no EIA, when decommissioning needs one?” Peng said the act would undergo review. But on March 22 he said current law requires no assessment for a life extension and that the NSC’s substantive review already resembles one. NSC Chairperson Chen Ming-chen (陳明真) said in December last year that the commission already assessed the environmental effects of radiation and would “take full responsibility.”
In written answers on Oct. 5, Lin Chien-Yen (林正原), a researcher at the Green Citizens’ Action Alliance (綠色公民行動聯盟), said Article 5 of the act lists the development of nuclear and other energy among activities that require an assessment, and that the criteria’s silence does not take license renewal out of the system. He cited Article 6 of the Nuclear Reactor Facilities Regulation Act (核子反應器設施管制法), under which an operator wishing to resume after its license expires must obtain a replacement license, valid for up to 20 years. Lin wrote that a renewal goes through a new application and a new review, and that the law in force on the day of the application should decide whether it meets the EIA requirements.
Photo: TT file photo
Anton Ming-Zhi Gao (高銘志), a professor at National Tsing Hua University’s Institute of Law for Science and Technology, cites Asia Cement Corp. The Taipei High Administrative Court in 2019 revoked the 20-year extension of the company’s mining rights at a mountain in Hualien County’s Sincheng Township (新城) after four Truku residents sued. The Supreme Administrative Court on Sept. 16, 2021 made the revocation final (Interpretation No. 894). The Ministry of Economic Affairs had granted the extension without the consultation and consent that Article 21 of the Indigenous Peoples Basic Act (原住民族基本法) requires. The court ruled under the Mining Act (礦業法). Gao reads it as treating an extension as a new administrative decision, subject to the law in force on the date of application, and he applies that reasoning to the EIA Act.
Huang Ching-ting (黃靖庭), deputy secretary-general of Citizen of the Earth, Taiwan (地球公民基金會), notes that judgment 894 does not say whether an extension creates a new right or continues an old one. It applies the law in force at the time of the extension — in that case Article 21. Huang treats a nuclear license renewal as the approval of a new period of generation.
“Even decommissioning must go through an EIA,” she wrote. “Going by the meaning of the law, would extension or restart, a more intensive development than decommissioning, not need one?”
Gao said a license renewal already includes an assessment of environmental effects, outside the procedure that the EIA Act sets, and a court that found the act applicable might not accept it as a substitute. He expects any suit after the NSC issues a license, at the High Administrative Court, and leaves open who would have standing, whether a court would suspend the license and what remedy it could order. The alliance did not say whether it planned a challenge. It wrote that it would follow the authorities’ decision on the EIA and the licensing procedure.
The Court of Justice of the European Union in July 2019 ruled in Inter-Environnement Wallonie (Case C-411/17) that Belgium’s 10-year extension of the Doel 1 and 2 reactors required a prior environmental assessment. The same judgment allowed a national court to maintain the extension where electricity supply faced a genuine threat. Theodoros G. Iliopoulos and Daan Bijnens of Hasselt University wrote in 2020 in the Maastricht Journal of European and Comparative Law that the court had added electricity shortage to the grounds for regularizing a project after the fact, and that the ruling moved the dispute into a second phase.
In the referendum on Aug. 23 last year, 4.34 million people voted to restart Ma-anshan and 1.51 million voted against. The yes votes did not reach a quarter of the 20.02 million eligible voters and the proposal failed.
Another referendum, to be held alongside the nine-in-one local elections on Nov. 28, asks whether the government should use nuclear power to revive the economy and abolish the “nuclear-free homeland” policy. Neither result binds the NSC.
EXPERTS should WEIGH IN
Meanwhile, the Green Citizens’ Action Alliance, Citizen of the Earth and 32 other groups on Sept. 29 said nobody should read the outcome as permission to restart and asked for geologists, seismologists and emergency-medicine specialists to participate in a safety review. Gao sat on a Taiwan People’s Party expert group on nuclear power that broadly backed a careful restart, and split with it over the EIA.
Gao said fuel supply and the US-Taiwan nuclear cooperation agreement barely come up in the legal debate over Ma-anshan. On small modular reactors (SMRs), he said the law assumes Taipower as operator and sets liabilities too heavy for a private company running one beside a data center or a chip fab. The National Atomic Research Institute (國家原子能科技研究院) estimated in April that Taiwan’s first SMR electricity would come in 2035 at the earliest.
In a 2022 study published in Energy Strategy Reviews, Gao, Yeh Tsung-Kuang (葉宗洸) and Chen Jong-Shun (陳中舜) found that the electricity mix the government announced on May 25, 2016, which removed nuclear power from last year’s targets in favor of 50 percent gas, 30 percent coal and 20 percent renewables, had not gone through a strategic environmental assessment.
Gao calls the NSC the body with the greatest legal capacity to halt the process. He sees no sign that it intends to and expects Ma-anshan to pass on safety, given its operating record. Article 16 of the NSC’s license-review rules, which the commission last amended on Oct. 8 last year, lists six documents a renewal application must include, from an integrated ageing assessment to a seismic safety evaluation. Item six lets the competent authority designate other documents, and Lin said the commission could use it to ask for environmental assessment reports. Gao considers a licence decision more likely next year than this year. The alliance estimates two to five years of work by Taipower before the commission’s next review.
Both instruments exist today. The environment ministry can amend Article 29 of the EIA criteria to state whether it covers license renewal, in the review Peng announced in May last year. The NSC can invoke item six of Article 16 before it rules. Either step fits inside the inspection years still ahead, would fix the legal basis of the license before anyone asks a judge and would give the groups opposed to the restart a procedure to take part in.
In Belgium the question went to court after the extension.
Romain Blachier works in renewable energy and teaches political science. He chairs the France-Formosa Association and is a columnist and associate fellow at the Fondation Jean-Jaures.

articles.title: X-Bow to build boosters for U.S. Army’s cheap cruise missile
articles.body:
- Leidos selected X-Bow Systems to develop and produce booster motors for the U.S. Army’s Low-Cost Containerized Munition, with full-rate production planned in 2027.
- Leidos’ agreement covers an initial 3,000 missiles; the value of X-Bow’s deal and the number of motors were not disclosed.
Leidos has picked X-Bow Systems, a New Mexico rocket motor maker, to develop and build the booster motors for the U.S. Army’s Low-Cost Containerized Munition, a ground-launched cruise missile the Pentagon wants to buy in large numbers.
X-Bow announced the selection on Oct. 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. Under the agreement, the company will design the motor, run qualification tests and static test fires, and then move to full-rate production in 2027. Neither company disclosed the value of the deal or how many motors X-Bow will build.
The booster is the solid rocket motor that pushes a missile out of its launch container and up to flying speed in the first seconds after launch. Solid rocket motors have become one of the main bottlenecks in U.S. missile production, with most of the work long concentrated among a handful of large suppliers.
“Modern conflict is decided by how many rounds you can put downrange, not how exquisite each one is,” said X-Bow founder and CEO Jason Hundley.
The Department of War launched the Low-Cost Containerized Munition program in May, signing framework agreements with Leidos, Anduril, CoAspire and Zone 5 Technologies as part of its “Arsenal of Freedom” effort to field precision weapons in volume. Leidos said its agreement covers an initial 3,000 missiles. The Pentagon has laid out plans to buy roughly 10,000 low-cost cruise missiles over three years across the program.
Leidos’ design builds on its AGM-190A Small Cruise Missile, known as Black Arrow, which was developed for launch from aircraft. The company says its containerized version is about twice the size of the AGM-190A, carries more fuel for longer range, and uses a modular airframe and open architecture so it can be upgraded quickly. It will be ground-launched at first, with possible ship- and air-launched versions later. Production is planned at Leidos facilities in Huntsville, Alabama, and McEwen, Tennessee.
X-Bow, based in Albuquerque, builds solid rocket motors using its own additive manufacturing process for the propellant. The company said the Leidos award is the sixth new propulsion program it has won in 2026, across the U.S. Navy, U.S. Army and the Missile Defense Agency, and that it recently completed its first major production contract with more than 2,100 rocket motors delivered. In July, the Missile Defense Agency awarded X-Bow about $11 million to develop a solid rocket motor for a low-cost interceptor, and the company has also worked on motors for the U.S. Navy’s Standard Missile family.

articles.title: North Korea fires ‘several ballistic missiles’
articles.body:
News coverage showing file footage of a North Korean missile launch is seen on a screen at Seoul Station in Seoul on October 12, 2026. (AFP Photo)
North Korea on Oct. 12 fired multiple ballistic missiles off its east coast, Seoul’s military said, after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along their heavily fortified border.
Since the blast that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), both countries have touted the test-firing of upgraded missile technology.
“Our military detected around 09:20 several ballistic missiles launched from the Pyongyang area towards the East Sea,” the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said on Oct. 12, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
“Our military has stepped up surveillance and vigilance against possible additional launches,” it added in its statement.
Japan’s Defense Ministry separately confirmed the launch of at least one suspected ballistic missile.
Some of the North Korean missiles detected flew more than 900 kilometers, the JCS said, while Seoul and longtime ally the United States were now conducting an analysis of their exact specifications.
South Korea’s National Security Office convened an emergency security meeting following the launch to review the country’s military readiness.
A joint Seoul-U.N. investigation last week concluded that North Korea had planted the landmines that exploded in the DMZ over a year ago, something Pyongyang has angrily denied.

articles.title: Russia says Europe bought $320 billion in hydrocarbons since 2022
articles.body:
Russia says Europe bought $320 billion in hydrocarbons since 2022
Russia said on Monday that European Union countries had bought $320.7 billion worth of its energy resources since 2022, despite sanctions over the war in Ukraine. The figure fuelled tensions as European officials criticised a US deal to import Russian diesel, while Stockholm called for the bloc to use frozen Russian assets to boost support for Kyiv.
Russia said on Monday that it had sold European countries more than $320 billion worth of hydrocarbons since 2022, despite sanctions imposed over the war in Ukraine.
"For the period from 2022 to today, this figure amounts to $320.7 billion. This is the volume of energy resource deliveries to European Union countries," Russian Deputy Prime Minister in charge of energy Alexander Novak said on television.
He said European countries purchased $21.3 billion worth of Russian hydrocarbons in the first nine months of 2026 alone.
"In other words, despite sanctions-related restrictions, we continue to supply energy resources in certain areas for which exemptions have been granted," he added.
Novak said Russian oil exports may reach their pre-war levels by the end of the year.
Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard pointed to the Russian figure as she arrived in Luxembourg on Monday for a meeting with her European Union counterparts.
She contrasted it with the 218.7 billion euros ($244 billion) in support that the EU had sent to Ukraine since the start of the war.

articles.title: Why do Iran’s oil ‘intermediaries’ owe the government billions?
articles.body:
Why do Iran’s oil ‘intermediaries’ owe the government billions?
Iran says intermediaries handling its oil sales owe it billions of dollars, but how did the debts accumulate?
As the United States maintains a naval blockade of Iran’s ports and imposes more sanctions on its oil exports, Tehran is confronting another problem: billions of dollars in revenue from previous oil sales that it says have gone missing.
A spokesperson for Iran’s judiciary said in September that a network of oil intermediaries known as “trustees” owed the Iranian government between 10 billion euros ($11bn) and 11 billion euros ($12bn). That figure was equivalent to half of the total oil revenue projected in Iran’s government budget for the current fiscal year.
US officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, have tied Iran’s struggles to access oil revenues as evidence that its economic pressure campaign is having an effect. In August, Bessent said that “Iran’s shadow banking system was buckling” under pressure from the US campaign against the country, which has been ramped up as Washington seeks a way to force Tehran to capitulate in the war between the two countries, launched by the US and Israel in late February.
So who are the oil intermediaries, why does Iran depend on them, and what has happened to the billions of dollars they owe? Let’s take a closer look.
Who are Iran’s oil intermediaries?
The debt, and the crisis it has created for the Iranian government, both stem from an oil-sales arrangement Tehran adopted in 2012 in response to US sanctions targeting Iranian oil exports.
American and European sanctions targeting Iranian oil sales and revenue collection began in 2012. The stated rationale behind both sets of measures was that revenue from oil sales helped finance Iran’s nuclear programme and that restricting Iranian oil exports could prevent the programme from advancing.
In response, the Iranian government devised a way to circumvent international sanctions on its oil sales. Unable to sell oil through the Oil Ministry and receive the proceeds through the Central Bank, it began selling oil to domestic buyers or using it to settle outstanding obligations to institutions and organisations owed money by the state.
This arrangement gave rise to a network of oil intermediaries often referred to in Iran as the “trustee network”. Rather than selling all its oil through official government channels, the state entrusted crude oil to institutions, individuals and companies to sell on its behalf. The proceeds were supposed to be transferred to the government’s treasury, with the sellers or recipient institutions subsequently recovering their agreed costs and outstanding claims. Some institutions sold the oil themselves, while others contracted private trading companies to handle the sales.
The Oil Industry Pension Fund, established for retired Oil Ministry employees familiar with the oil-sales process, was among the first institutions to receive crude oil for sale. Other recipients included Khatam al-Anbiya Construction Base, a major hub for large-scale infrastructure projects. Even the municipal police received payments owed to them by the government in the form of crude oil.
Effect of the nuclear deal
Even in those early experiments, discrepancies emerged between the revenue expected from oil sales and the amounts sellers actually deposited into the government’s treasury. These discrepancies eventually gave rise to some of Iran’s largest economic corruption cases.
The accounting discrepancies and the government’s inability to recover money from private sellers entrusted with Iranian oil persisted until 2016, when the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) nuclear deal was signed and when sanctions on Iranian oil sales were lifted. The government was subsequently able to regain control over oil sales.
Individuals who had sold Iranian oil but failed to return the proceeds were imprisoned. With the ability to sell oil again through legal and transparent channels, the government was able, for a time, to manage its oil revenues and spending with greater control.
How did money from oil sales go unreturned?
After US President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from the JCPOA in 2018 during his first presidential term, the Iranian government once again had to rely on private oil traders to sell its oil. But the problems associated with selling oil through intermediaries rather than official state channels, including delays in returning revenues, accounting discrepancies, debts owed by oil sellers to the government, and the occasional seizure of Iranian oil shipments at sea, once again constrained the government’s ability to manage its oil revenues.
Moreover, the US expanded its sanctions beyond Iranian government institutions and interests, adding bank accounts involved in transactions with the Iranian government, currency-exchange offices, companies, and individuals to its sanctions lists. As a result, the time between individuals participating in Iran’s oil-trading network and being sanctioned themselves, along with their assets and companies, and having their accounts blocked or frozen grew progressively shorter.
This contributed to an accumulation of debts owed by sanctioned oil traders – no longer able to access their accounts – to the government. It also left Iran with little choice but to expand its private oil-sales network. That meant increasing the number of people involved in trading Iranian oil, reducing the volume of oil allocated to each individual or company and, ultimately, increasing the risk that the proceeds would not be returned.
Iranian officials have also accused trustees of exploiting the sanctions workarounds to enrich themselves.
The billions of dollars owed by private oil sellers to the Iranian government are a combination of outstanding payments, disputed financial obligations and allegations of corruption. Iran’s judiciary chief recently addressed the issue, warning that oil sellers who refuse to return the proceeds from oil sales will face legal action. But such warnings do not change the sanctions environment or remove the obstacles that prevent some oil sellers from returning the money.

articles.title: A Chinese Auto Giant Sponsors Portugal's National Football Team. Its Trucks Are Used by Russia to Attack Ukraine.
articles.body:
As part of its “Vast Ocean Plan” for global expansion, one of China’s largest automotive companies recently announced its sponsorship of Portugal’s national football team.
“Europe stands as a strategic priority,” Changan Automobile said in a press release in May, adding that its partnership with the Portuguese Football Federation offered a new opportunity for “brand engagement across the region.”
In an earlier phase of a global push by the state-owned company, Changan moved into Russia. Later, as international car makers left following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Changan started exporting more vehicles to fill the gap in the market, according to the industry analysis group inovev.
Reporters found that some of those vehicles have been used in Russia's war against Ukraine, as launchpads for models of drones known to have attacked both military targets and civilians.
Changan Automobile did not respond to requests for comment.
The Portugal Football Federation said the contract with Changan was signed after being reviewed for “the tight Federation compliance rules.”
Trucks at War
In March, a unit of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces published a video on Telegram showing strikes on Changan Hunter pickups fitted with launch pads for Russian drones, including the Geran model.
According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a U.S. think tank, Russia acquired the original design for the Geran from Iran and has innovated it over the past few years. Today, the Geran is one of the main weapons deployed by Russia, targeting both Ukrainian military and civilians.
In July, a Changan Hunter appeared in a video published by Russian propagandist Vladimir Solovyov. The video shows Russian soldiers in camouflage and masks assembling several drones, including a Geran, and arming it with an explosive device. The video then shows a drone being launched from a speeding Hunter pickup.

Iran denies any role in British air base incident
Iran has denied any involvement in an alleged plot targeting a British airbase used by US bombers to launch strikes against Tehran, challenging accusations by the UK government and demanding evidence to substantiate its claims.
Iran's ambassador to Britain, Ali Mousavi, rejected the allegations during a meeting with British Middle East minister Stephen Doughty at the Foreign Office on Monday, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.
Mousavi insisted that Tehran had no role in the suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford on 27 September and urged British authorities to refrain from making accusations that he said lacked evidence.
He called on London to provide any documents or evidence supporting its allegations, warning against what he described as "hasty positions and unsubstantiated accusations".
The ambassador also reiterated Iran's willingness to cooperate with British authorities in establishing the facts surrounding the incident.
Mousavi stressed Iran's commitment to international law, respect for national sovereignty and non-interference in other countries' internal affairs.
He added that Tehran's condemnation of military attacks launched against Iran from British bases did not imply any involvement in the Fairford incident.
The denial came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of likely directing the suspected plot and announced further sanctions against Tehran.
Addressing Parliament on Monday, Burnham said British authorities assessed that the operation was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran and "almost certainly" directed by the IRGC.
"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)," Burnham told lawmakers.
US bombers have used RAF Fairford to carry out strikes against Iran. Last week, US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted the withdrawal of the aircraft from the base.
US officials told Reuters that the suspected plot involved plans to launch a drone attack.
Five British men were arrested near RAF Fairford in the early hours of 27 September on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offences.
Police detained the men near the base in three vans but later released them without charge on police bail under stringent conditions.
Police said petrol had been discovered in the vehicles, but no viable explosives were found.
Two other men, including a British-Iranian national, were also arrested and later released.
British counterterrorism police are continuing their investigation, including examining whether a foreign state was involved.
Burnham warned that Britain would take further action against what he described as Iranian-linked criminal networks.
"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," he said.
"We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm."
Britain has previously accused Tehran of involvement in plots on British soil, allegations Iran has repeatedly rejected.
In July, London used new powers aimed at countering state-sponsored activity to ban support for the IRGC and a linked group accused of involvement in attacks targeting locations associated with Jewish and Israeli communities, as well as Persian-language media.
Iran has dismissed allegations linking it to the Fairford incident as "unfounded and malicious speculations", insisting that British authorities must produce evidence rather than level accusations against Tehran.

articles.title: Saudi coalition tackling drones, missiles headed toward kingdom
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said Monday it was dealing with drones and missiles heading toward Saudi Arabia, as hostilities with the Iran-aligned Yemeni group persist.
State-backed broadcaster Al Ekhbariya reported that the military coalition was responding to a missile and drone threat but did not specify where the projectiles were headed.
"The coalition is currently dealing with a threat involving drones and cruise missiles targeting the kingdom," the broadcaster said.
The latest report of attacks comes amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis, with airports and other civilian and energy facilities targeted in recent days.
On Sunday afternoon, an unidentified projectile struck King Khalid International Airport's Terminal 4 in Riyadh, killing a Pakistani resident and injuring 11 others, according to Saudi authorities.
The Saudi-led coalition also said it intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile near the airport.
A day earlier, on Saturday, a Houthi attack struck a passenger terminal at the airport, killing 13 people and injuring 309 others, according to Saudi authorities.
The Saudi-led coalition accused the Houthis of carrying out Saturday's attack and described the strike as a "full-fledged war crime."

articles.title: Faslane submarine base in Scotland to get ballistic shelters
articles.body:
Three contracts worth a combined £2.55 million have gone to the Northern Ireland construction firm Henry Brothers for infrastructure work at His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde, awarded by Babcock International Group, according to the News Letter.
The work covers upgrading security fencing around a key support building at Faslane, supplying and installing specialist ballistic security shelters across the base, and refurbishing an existing Pressure Test Building. Work begins immediately.
Nick McKeown, regional director for Scotland at Henry Brothers, said in comments reported by the paper: “Being appointed to deliver these new projects at HMNB Clyde reflects the trust Babcock places in Henry Brothers and our capability in delivering complex, secure and highly specialised infrastructure.
“Our workforce has extensive experience across the defence sector, and we remain committed to ensuring the Royal Navy’s operational facilities are robust, resilient and fit for purpose. These new appointments strengthen our partnership with Babcock and underline our shared focus on delivering high-quality, dependable facilities for the submarine fleet.”
The three projects form part of Babcock’s investment in infrastructure at the base, which supports the Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines that carry the deterrent and the Astute class attack boats. Ballistic shelters are protective structures intended to shield personnel from blast and fragmentation.
The Ministry of Defence has described the work at Clyde as a multi-decade programme, and told Parliament this month that the purchase of the former Finnart Oil Terminal on Loch Long supports the longer-term transformation of the Clyde estate, with mine hunting equipment and autonomous systems relocating there from 2028.

articles.title: EU approves Lebanon mission despite 'US objections'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lebanon's Aoun hails EU security mission amid 'US objections'
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed the EU's decision on Monday to establish a new three-year security support mission in Lebanon, amid reported US objections to the bloc's plans for a greater security role in the country.
The mission, approved by the Council of the European Union, aims to strengthen the Lebanese army and Internal Security Forces as the country prepares for the withdrawal of UN peacekeepers from its southern border with Israel.
The decision, announced on Monday, establishes the European Union Support Mission in Lebanon (EUSM Lebanon) for an initial three-year period, with the aim of supporting the country's stability, sovereignty and state institutions.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the mission would provide advice and assistance to Lebanon's security institutions to strengthen their control over the country's territory, border security and internal security.
"Europe is investing in Lebanon's future," Kallas said, describing the mission as a significant upgrade in security relations aimed at helping Lebanese state institutions restore full sovereignty and build lasting stability.
The mission will include civilian and military components operating under a unified political mandate, providing training and advice on border surveillance, intelligence gathering, reconnaissance, counter-smuggling operations, maritime security and cybercrime.
The military component will focus on strengthening the Lebanese army's capabilities in land border monitoring and control, maritime security and operational coordination.
The civilian component will provide specialised training and advice to the Internal Security Forces, including on cybercrime and counter-smuggling, while helping develop sustainable training structures.
It will also support security management at Lebanese ports, including the Port of Beirut.
The mission will contribute to the implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which calls for the deployment of Lebanese government forces in southern Lebanon and the withdrawal of armed groups from the area.
It will also complement existing EU assistance through the European Peace Facility and coordinate with EU member states, the United Nations and other international partners supporting Lebanon's security sector.
The decision formally establishes the mission, although its deployment remains subject to further operational planning and a separate decision by the EU Council.
The announcement follows a visit to Beirut on 8 October by Kallas, who outlined plans for a European mission to strengthen Lebanon's security institutions.
Kallas stressed that the initiative was not intended to replace the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), whose current mandate is scheduled to end on 31 December, with a phased withdrawal expected over the following year.
US objections to European security role
However, the Lebanese news website Al-Modon reported on Monday that Washington had expressed objections in principle to the proposed European mission, citing sources familiar with discussions over Lebanon's future security arrangements.
According to the report, the US opposes establishing another international military arrangement resembling UNIFIL, preferring existing coordination mechanisms and a greater security role for the Lebanese army.
The reported disagreement reflects competing approaches to the international presence in Lebanon, with European governments seeking to maintain a role in supporting the country's security institutions as UNIFIL prepares to leave.
The reported American objections have not been independently confirmed, and there has been no indication that Washington has formally opposed Monday's EU Council decision.
Al-Modon also reported that discussions were underway over a separate monitoring committee potentially involving Italy, Switzerland and Jordan, although its composition and responsibilities had yet to be finalised.
The proposed committee would address questions surrounding the verification of security commitments, including the deployment of Lebanese forces, the withdrawal of Israeli troops and the monitoring of violations.
Israel has also opposed the deployment of a new international force to replace UNIFIL, favouring direct security coordination with the Lebanese army through US-backed mechanisms, according to Al-Modon.
The future of southern Lebanon's security arrangements remains contentious as Israeli forces continue to occupy positions inside Lebanese territory and carry out military operations despite agreements intended to secure their withdrawal.
Lebanese officials have repeatedly called for an international presence capable of monitoring violations and supporting the army's deployment across the south.
UNIFIL, established in 1978, has played a central role in monitoring the border area, documenting violations and coordinating with Lebanese forces.
Its departure raises questions about who will independently monitor the situation along the Blue Line, particularly as disputes persist over Israeli military activity, Hezbollah's weapons and the implementation of existing security agreements.
While the newly approved European mission is intended to strengthen Lebanon's security institutions, it will not assume UNIFIL's peacekeeping responsibilities, leaving the future of international monitoring in southern Lebanon unresolved.

articles.title: Kremlin says Trump wants Zelenskyy replaced over lack of will to end war
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday that US President Donald Trump’s call for new leadership in Ukraine reflected what he described as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s lack of political will to end the war.
In an interview with RIA Novosti, Peskov said Zelenskyy must take responsibility and make “difficult decisions” to resolve the Russia-Ukraine war.
"Trump said he believes the time has come for a new president. Why? Because the president of Ukraine must make very consequential and very difficult decisions to stop this war,” he said.
“Either Zelenskyy assumes that responsibility and demonstrates that political will, or he does not," Peskov added, saying Zelenskyy currently lacks the will to do so.
Peskov’s statement came after Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to "get a new president,” accusing Zelenskyy of missing multiple opportunities to end the war.
Trump also criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, warning that attacks on refineries could worsen global fuel shortages and affect American farmers and ranchers.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he was ready to hold presidential elections in Ukraine if Russia agreed to a complete 60-day ceasefire, adding that Kyiv is also ready to take steps toward de-escalation, including a mutual ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
The same day, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure, without providing details.
Zelenskyy later posted on the US social media platform X that Trump’s announcement of a ceasefire on energy infrastructure was “good news” but Russian attacks continued, including on a power plant in Kharkiv.

articles.title: Taiwan Defense Minister Koo condemns China's live-fire drills in 5 sea areas
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) on Monday condemned China's planned live-fire drills in five maritime areas, saying the exercises create insecurity and that the military would closely monitor the situation.
China’s Maritime Safety Administration announced live-fire exercises in the Bohai Sea from Monday to Friday, the northern Yellow Sea on Monday, the South China Sea daily from Monday to Friday, and the southern Yellow Sea from Friday to Saturday, per CTS News. Military training is also scheduled in the East China Sea Tuesday to Thursday, with specific time windows varying by day.
Speaking before a Legislative Yuan meeting, Koo said the defense ministry had a comprehensive understanding of the situation in the Taiwan Strait, per Rti. The initial assessment was that they involved artillery units firing exercises along China’s coastal areas and posed a relatively low threat to waters surrounding Taiwan.
Koo said the ministry would continue to monitor Chinese military training. He condemned what he called the PLA’s “repeated exercises and military activities” across the Indo-Pacific, saying they warranted close attention.
The drills come as Japan's Self-Defense Forces and the US military prepare to hold their biennial Keen Sword exercise from Oct. 19-29. The Japan Times reports that the US military plans to deploy anti-ship missiles to Japan's Yonaguni Island, near Taiwan.
Asked about the reported deployment, Koo said US military deployments were based on local threat assessments and necessary operational requirements, per TaiSounds. He declined to comment on specific arrangements.
Koo also declined to comment on how other democracies might intervene in a conflict in the Taiwan Strait. He stressed that Taiwan's priority was to strengthen its defense capabilities and ensure national security.

articles.title: Trump insists Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire is in place, drone strike kills woman in Kyiv
articles.body:
Trump insisted an energy ceasefire was in place between Russia and Ukraine despite reported Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites. A Russian drone hit a Kyiv apartment block, killing one woman and injuring at least five.
US President Donald Trump has continued insisting on Monday that an energy ceasefire is indeed in place between Ukraine and Russia, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that Moscow struck his country’s energy sites.
“Well, they agreed,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for Ohio.
“Because I said, ‘You agree.’ That's why they agreed. " Because I said they agree,” he added.
When pressed about the attacks by Russia, Trump said, “Well, I'd have to look at it and see, because there's been violations on both sides."
Drone strike killed one, injured five in Kyiv
Meanwhile, a 25-story residential building in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district was hit by a Russian drone on Monday night, which killed one woman and injured at least five other people, the city's military administration said.
Earlier in the day, falling debris from Russian attacks sparked a fire in a private residential building in the same area, and at least two people were injured in daytime strikes.
The latest attacks came as President Zelenskyy said Monday that while Ukraine is willing to halt attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure, Moscow has continued to strike his country's energy sites.
Trump’s brief social media post Sunday offered few details but said the energy ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!” On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov wouldn’t say whether Russia had agreed to such a ceasefire, saying only: "Contacts are ongoing."

articles.title: Le Pen projected to win French presidential election – poll
articles.body:
Le Pen projected to win French presidential election – poll
French right-wing politician Marine Le Pen has emerged as the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race and would defeat both left-wing and centrist rivals in hypothetical runoffs, according to a new poll.
Published on Monday, the Toluna Harris Interactive survey for French broadcasters M6 and RTL puts Le Pen, the longtime face of the National Rally (RN), at 67% against Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, and 56% against former centrist Prime Minister Edouard Philippe.
Le Pen also leads all five first-round scenarios tested, with 35% to 37% support. Melenchon comes second with 18% to 19%, while Philippe polls between 13% and 17%.
The survey also suggests growing confidence in Le Pen’s leadership. Some 51% of respondents believe she would make a good president, up six percentage points from the previous poll, compared with 47% for RN president Jordan Bardella.
Le Pen reached the presidential runoff in both 2017 and 2022 but lost to Emmanuel Macron on each occasion. The incumbent is barred from seeking a third consecutive term. Macron’s approaching departure comes as France faces mounting fiscal pressures.
In July, the Paris Court of Appeals reduced Le Pen’s five-year ban on holding elected office following her conviction for misusing EU funds, clearing the way for her to contest the 2027 election.
Her party has also strengthened its parliamentary position. In September, RN and its ally, the Union of the Right for the Republic (UDR), secured enough Senate seats to form a parliamentary group for the first time.
Macron’s centrist camp has lacked a parliamentary majority since 2022, leaving successive governments struggling to pass budgets. France’s public debt reached €3.6 trillion (over $4 trillion), or 119% of GDP, as of the end of June, while the proposed 2027 budget faces opposition in the fragmented parliament.
Both Le Pen and Melenchon have criticized NATO and Western policy toward Ukraine. Le Pen has advocated withdrawing France from NATO’s integrated military command, lifting sanctions on Russia, and pursuing a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine conflict. Melenchon has called for France to leave NATO altogether.
RN has repeatedly opposed open-ended military funding for Kiev and warned against steps that could bring France into direct confrontation with Russia. Le Pen has called for the normalization of relations with Moscow.
The prospect of a Le Pen presidency has reportedly alarmed Ukraine’s Western backers. The Telegraph reported in August that officials feared her election could undermine French-led efforts to coordinate military and financial aid for Kiev, as well as plans to deploy Western troops to Ukraine following a ceasefire.
The Toluna Harris Interactive survey was conducted online from October 5 to 8 among 2,004 registered voters.

articles.title: Turkey intelligence confirms PKK evacuated 4 northern Iraq bases
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey intelligence confirms PKK evacuated four northern Iraq bases
Turkey's intelligence services said on Monday PKK militants had withdrawn from four key bases in northern Iraq, confirming a move announced by the Kurdish group last week.
The decision comes two months after Turkey voted through a bill offering limited amnesty for PKK militants in a major step in the peace process seeking to end decades of deadly violence.
"The PKK evacuated the Hebat, Yajk, Sabri and Sason hideouts in Baze, in the Metina region of northern Iraq, on October 8," security sources said in a statement carried by state news agency Anadolu.
It was widely understood to be from the National Intelligence Organisation (MIT).
On Thursday, the PKK said it had withdrawn all its armed forces "both within and outside Turkey that could be considered near the border...a few days ago".
That included a withdrawal "from four war tunnels and positions in Metina, west of Zap", a strategic border area that in the past was frequently targeted by the Turkish military.
Ankara has repeatedly said that all disarmament moves by the PKK must be verified by Turkish intelligence, which is a key part of the law passed in August.
Such verification must ensure an end to all military activities and the handover of weapons and ammunition stockpiles before the legislation's legal measures can be implemented.
In May last year, the PKK announced it was disbanding following a historic call by their jailed leader Abdullah Öcalan.
Two months later, its militants took part in a historic disarmament ceremony in northern Iraq where they began symbolically destroying their weapons.
The Turkish statement said the evacuation would allow the process to move forward, ultimately allowing former militants to return home.
"Following the cessation of PKK activities in all areas, social reconciliation will be achieved with organisation members who will return to Turkey in the later stages of the process, benefiting from the law," it said.
"The goal is to ensure the integration of PKK members into society through integrated programmes in many areas such as education and the economy."
'Concrete measures'
Cihan Aydin, co-chair of the Human Rights Association, welcomed the PKK's withdrawal, telling AFP on Thursday it was "a very important indicator" of the group's determination to see an end to the conflict.
He said the move should be met with a "positive" response from the Turkish state, notably through democratisation reforms.
"Concrete goodwill measures will strengthen confidence in the process and make it more resilient," Aydin said.
Earlier this month, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan reiterated the government's determination to achieve a "terror-free Turkey".
But on Thursday, the PKK accused Ankara of failing to pursue the process with sufficient sincerity and speed, despite the militants fulfilling their own commitments.
As part of the initiative, Turkey has established four sub-committees to oversee practical aspects of the PKK's decision to dissolve itself, including one focused on disarmament that Öcalan will join.
Senior Erdogan adviser Mehmet Ucum said Öcalan will join the disarmament sub-committee, while stressing this would not mean he would be released.
The 77-year-old has played a key role in advancing efforts to end the conflict from his cell on İmralı Island near Istanbul, where he has spent the past 27 years serving life in solitary confinement, with the PKK leadership repeatedly demanding he be freed as part of the process.
The new law does not specify what will happen to him.

articles.title: Germany faces 'shadow war' that goes beyond Cold War threats, minister warns
articles.body:
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt warned on Monday that Germany faced a "shadow war" more far-reaching than the Cold War, and said the threat underscored the need to strengthen the country's BfV domestic intelligence agency.
"The shadow war we are witnessing today has an objective that extends far beyond anything seen during the Cold War," Dobrindt said at a BfV press conference in Berlin.
Officials from many Western countries have warned for months that Russia is mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
"Its clear aim is to destabilize us – to destabilize us fundamentally," Dobrindt said, without directly naming Russia.
His comments echo warnings by Germany's head of foreign intelligence, the BND, this month that Germany was at risk of entering a violent conflict with Moscow.
The security service of Germany's neighbor, the Czech Republic, said on Monday that Russia could resort to riskier and more significant operations in NATO member states supporting Ukraine within months.
Alleged Russian drone attack drives calls to expand German intelligence powers
Calls to expand Germany's intelligence powers have gained urgency since a failed attack involving an explosives-laden drone at a German airport in August, which authorities blamed on Russia.
The head of BfV said on Monday that Russia employed virtually every tool in its hybrid operations, ranging from disinformation campaigns, information manipulation and sabotage to assassination plots prepared in Germany.
"This is a fact we must deal with," said BfV President Sinan Selen.
Asked about the Leipzig drone incident, which the Kremlin has dismissed as fabricated, Selen said that he expected more actions of a similar nature.
The government's reform bill, which would give intelligence services broader powers, including the ability to take active defensive measures, is currently being examined by parliamentary committees after a first reading in September.
Germany seeks to strengthen intelligence capabilities amid growing threats
"Germany cannot be a second- or third-rate player when it comes to developing services and capabilities; we must remain at the forefront, given the challenges we face," Dobrindt said.
Created after World War Two, when memories of Nazi rule were still fresh, the German services have traditionally been more constrained than those of allies such as France, Britain, or the US.

articles.title: Putin would halt strikes on election day if Ukraine holds vote: Kremlin
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin is ready to halt strikes on Ukraine on voting day if Kyiv “genuinely wants to hold election,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday.
Peskov’s remarks came a day after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to hold a vote if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.
Speaking at a briefing, Peskov claimed Ukraine needed a 60-day truce not to organize the ballot, “but to regroup, heal their wounds, and continue the war.”
“In reality, Kyiv has no desire to hold elections; that is perfectly obvious,” he said.
He also said that Russia seeks long-term peace in Ukraine and is prepared to do whatever is necessary to achieve it.
“The Kremlin—and President Putin, as well as officials at other levels—have repeatedly stated: we do not want a truce; we want long-term peace, and we are ready to do everything possible to achieve it,” Peskov said.
Asked about the energy truce between Russia and Ukraine announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday, Peskov said contacts were ongoing.
“I have just spoken on this topic. As soon as we have something to tell you, we will let you know,” he said.
Peskov also accused European countries of obstructing a peace settlement in the Russia-Ukraine war, describing US efforts as “much more appealing.”
"Europeans clearly do not belong to the 'party of peace' seeking a peaceful settlement in Ukraine. Europe is more of a "party of war,'" he said.

articles.title: Merz opposes Trump's diesel deal with Putin and assures Zelensky of Germany's support
articles.body:
Merz opposes Trump's diesel deal with Putin and assures Zelensky of Germany's support
According to Ukrinform, the statement was reported by the German television channel n-tv.
Merz said that Europe could not agree to such a decision and that Russia would only engage in serious negotiations under pressure.
The chancellor stressed that pressure on Russia should not be eased but increased.
Commenting on Trump's initiative to halt strikes on energy infrastructure, Merz pointed out that Russia had continued attacking Ukraine's civilian energy supply infrastructure following the announcement.
Against the backdrop of Trump's statements about the need for a change of president in Ukraine, the German chancellor also emphasised that Zelensky could count on Germany's support in this situation.
Merz added that Germany would continue working towards a just and lasting peace that safeguarded both Ukraine's freedom and Europe's security.

According to Trump, a further 500,000 tonnes would be delivered in November, followed by another one million tonnes. Russia subsequently pledged to release an additional three million tonnes of diesel fuel onto the market.
President Volodymyr Zelensky stressed that "gifts to Putin will not bring peace."
Trump also stated that it was time for Ukraine to elect a new president after announcing the agreement with Russia on diesel fuel supplies. articles.title: Sudan’s Burhan orders inquiry after reported killing of 72 miners near Egyptian border
articles.body:
Adel Abdelrheem, Rania Abushamala
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan on Monday ordered a fact-finding investigation into the reported killing of miners near the Egyptian border on Saturday.
The council said in a statement that the committee would include representatives of the Public Prosecution and relevant judicial and security bodies.
It will investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident and submit a report on its findings. No deadline was announced.
“Protecting the lives of Sudanese citizens and safeguarding their safety and dignity is a fundamental responsibility of the state,” Burhan said.
He stressed “the need to deal with the incident seriously, ensuring that the facts are uncovered and borders are protected and respected.”
“The leaderships of the two brotherly countries are in contact to establish the circumstances of the incident and make the facts public,” he added.
On Sunday, the independent Emergency Lawyers group said the death toll from an airstrike in the North al-Wadi area inside Sudanese territory had risen to 72 miners. It said Egyptian aircraft were suspected of carrying out the attack.
The announcement came hours after the independent Sudan Doctors Network reported that 13 miners had been killed and 28 injured in aerial bombardment near the Egyptian border.
There was no immediate comment from Cairo on the report.
Sudan’s artisanal mining sector employs more than 2 million people, often in harsh conditions, and accounts for around 80% of the country’s gold production.
The government permits artisanal mining while seeking to regulate the sector, which provides employment for large numbers of Sudanese.
Sudan relies on gold as a major source of foreign currency after losing three-quarters of its oil revenues following South Sudan’s secession in July 2011.
The country has been engulfed in war between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

articles.body:
