After Holborn and St Pancras: Can the Greens still influence UK politics?
Zack Polanski’s defeat in Holborn and St Pancras last week denied the Greens a parliamentary breakthrough in Keir Starmer’s former constituency. Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali held the seat with 45.2% against Polanski’s 32.8% on a turnout of 38.8%.
The comfortable Labour hold gives Prime Minister Andy Burnham breathing space in his effort to revive Labour’s popularity, which plummeted under Starmer and saw many left-wing voters defect to the Greens.
Although the Green leader didn’t win a seat, the substantial support for the party leaves Burnham with a challenge on his left that he cannot afford to ignore.
The result points more to a consolidation of opposition on Labour’s left rather than a fresh wave of defections, since the Greens’ share was only about 3.5 points higher than the combined Green and independent pro-Palestinian vote for Andrew Feinstein in the 2024.
“If this election had taken place a few months ago, when Keir Starmer was Prime Minister and the Greens still at their peak, the result would likely have looked very different,” Luke Tryl, UK Director of More in Common, told The New Arab.
He added that the result signals Burnham is consolidating left voters behind the party again.
Labour responds to the challenge
Burnham has made Labour a tougher proposition for challengers on its progressive flank. YouGov’s pre-election survey of 4–5 October put Labour on 27%, up three points from the previous week, and the Greens on an unchanged 11%.
YouGov also reported in September that 39% of 2024 Green voters would consider Labour, up from 24% in May, which supports the picture of a Labour recovery.
During the campaign, Reuters reported that a number of former Green supporters were receptive to Burnham’s tougher rhetoric towards Israel and closer European ties.
“Burnham may have hurt them pretty badly, but he hasn't put them completely out of the running,” Tim Bale, Professor of Politics at Queen Mary University, told The New Arab.
“There are still a lot of university-educated younger voters and ethnic minority voters who remain deeply suspicious of a Labour government they think has done nothing for them and is insufficiently critical of Trump and the Israeli government.”
For the Greens, Labour’s shift creates a dilemma, as it gives credibility to their claim that voting Green forces Labour to listen, but it may also remove some voters’ incentive to switch party in the first place.
Even Polanski noted this at the party conference, where he told delegates: “Vote Green and watch Labour move.”
Electoral pressure can raise the cost of ignoring progressive voters even before a party wins enough seats to bargain over legislation.
Still, that influence needs to be shown. Green pressure is one plausible factor in Labour’s repositioning, alongside public campaigning, internal party demands, Burnham’s own instincts, and the UK’s response to Israel’s atrocities in Palestine.
“The result backs up what has been seen in the national opinion polls: Labour's support has risen and the Greens' popularity has dipped,” Mitya Pearson, associate professor at the University of Warwick, told The New Arab.
“This does not mean that the Labour Party can now ignore the Greens; clearly there is a group of voters on the left who are willing to defect away from Labour if they don't feel listened to,” she added.
“However, Labour have arrested a lot of the Greens' previous momentum by changing leader.”
Palestine and the limits of Labour policy
The Labour government’s settlement measures in September illustrate both the shift and its limits.
On 8 September, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced plans to ban imports from illegal settlements, act against those facilitating settlement expansion and refuse export licence applications that materially contribute to Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.
He said the legislative package would be in place within six to nine months, alongside immediate sanctions against extremist settlers.
At Labour’s conference on 28 September, Miliband addressed those campaigning for Palestinian rights, saying “you were right”, describing a “reset” in Labour’s approach and referring to “ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank”.
That marked quite a notable shift in British government rhetoric.
Still, this represents a limited change rather than a comprehensive overhaul of London’s foreign policy.
Indeed, Miliband opposed the wider Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) campaign, defended trade with Israel within the Green Line, and reaffirmed Labour’s commitment to a two-state solution, even as settlement expansion continues to undermine its viability, and Israeli officials reject Palestinian statehood.
This is where the Greens’ position remains distinct from Labour’s in attracting pro-Palestine voters. The party demands a full two-way arms embargo, broader sanctions, and an end to military and intelligence cooperation, and reiterated that position following Miliband’s address.
Still, while Labour gained electoral credit for this rhetorical shift, that boost may not last if the policies towards Israel are delayed or narrowly applied, and the Greens can remain poised to scrutinise that gap.
The Greens’ ability to sustain that pressure may now be complicated by their own divisions over the conference motion declaring “Zionism is Racism”. Passed on 4 October by 1,022 to 813, it commits the party to an explicitly anti-Zionist position and a single democratic state across historic Palestine.
Polanski missed the vote while campaigning and has since said he would have opposed it. The chair of Jewish Greens, meanwhile, has called for his resignation, while four of the party’s five MPs publicly opposed the motion.
Combined with criticism from Jewish organisations and the European Green Party’s distancing, the split risks fracturing the broader progressive coalition the Greens need if they are to keep pressuring Labour.
The move would appeal to many pro-Palestine voters. But along with showing divisions within the party, British political analysts suggest the motion had made Polanski and the Greens more polarising across the broader electorate.
It would still be premature to link the motion as the cause of the Holborn defeat. YouGov had already documented weakening Green support before the conference vote, and its effect in this constituency requires evidence from voters rather than assumptions based on timing.
Building influence beyond this election
Repairing internal divisions is only part of the Greens’ task. To rebuild momentum, they also need a domestic programme that gives voters a clear reason to choose them over a recovering Labour Party.
Polanski’s proposed three-year cap on rent increases, set at the lowest of inflation, wage growth or 2%, offers one concrete dividing line. Its credibility will depend on addressing housing supply, enforcement and how tenants benefit in practice.
As More in Common’s Luke Tryl noted, the battle for the left has shifted: unless Polanski can rebuild momentum, Labour now holds the upper hand.
For the Greens, the picture looks promising in some areas. Hannah Spencer’s February victory in Gorton and Denton, with 40.7%, demonstrated that concentrated Green support can win under first-past-the-post.
Targeted campaigns and strong local government remain a more realistic route to influence than hoping to replace Labour nationwide.
Green MPs will have limited formal influence in this parliament given Labour’s majority, said Mitya Pearson, although they could still challenge inner-city Labour seats.
Combined with Labour’s need to unite progressive voters, “this pressure will likely continue to influence the policy decisions the Labour government makes”.
Burnham’s task is to turn renewed expectations into delivery. If Labour follows through on housing, living standards, and Palestinian rights, it may retain voters who previously considered the Greens.
If its promises disappoint, an opening could return, but only if the Greens’ organisation and policy credibility enable them to exploit it.
For now, Polanski’s defeat checks the Greens’ advance and hands Burnham breathing space, even though the vote share suggests the Greens remain competitive in some Labour-held urban seats.
For Palestinians and their supporters, the real test is not the by-election result but whether Labour turns its new language on settlements, arms, and Gaza into concrete action.
If Labour fails to deliver, an opening could re-emerge, but the Greens will need the organisation, unity, and credibility to exploit it.
Jonathan Fenton-Harvey is a journalist and researcher who focuses on conflict, geopolitics, and humanitarian issues in the Middle East and North Africa.

articles.title: China warns against escalation, urges dialogue after Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport
articles.body:
Saadet Gokce
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
China on Monday warned against further escalating regional tensions and urged dialogue and negotiations after at least 14 people were killed in recent attacks on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh, according to state media.
Beijing is "seriously concerned about the significant casualties caused by the attack and the escalation of the conflict," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing, state-run Global Times reported.
China "consistently opposes attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure," she said, urging against actions that could further escalate regional tensions, resolve differences and disputes through dialogue and negotiations, and work toward achieving peace and stability in the region at an early date.
On Sunday afternoon, an unidentified projectile struck the airport's Terminal 4, killing a Pakistani resident and injuring 11 others, according to Saudi authorities. The Saudi-led coalition also said it intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile near the airport.
A day earlier, on Saturday, a Houthi attack struck a passenger terminal at the airport, killing 13 people and injuring 309 others, according to Saudi authorities.
The Saudi-led coalition accused the Houthis of carrying out Saturday’s attack and described the strike as a "full-fledged war crime."
The attacks come amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, with airports and other civilian and energy facilities targeted in recent days.

articles.title: How Trump’s Policies Are Testing Farmers’ Loyalty Ahead of Midterms
articles.body:
Rising diesel and fertilizer costs, coupled with President Donald Trump’s shifting tariff policies, have made it harder for Oklahoma farmer Brent Rendel to plan future crops. Over the past few months, he says, the political mood among fellow farmers—traditionally some of the President’s most reliable supporters—has begun to shift.
“From my discussions with other farmers, there is a higher level of dissatisfaction with what's going on with the [Trump] Administration,” says Rendel. “You didn't used to really see that, but now we're seeing it and hearing it.”
That dissatisfaction could pose a political problem for Trump and Republicans ahead of the pivotal midterm elections. Trump won 69% of the rural vote in 2024, but an AP-KFF poll, conducted in August, found that 57% of rural voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the economy. Among rural Republican voters, around one-quarter (27%) disapproved of his handling of the economy—and that group was "substantially less likely" than those who approved to say they were certain to vote in November.
Three-quarters of rural voters described the cost of living in their communities as “fair” or “poor.” A Reuters/Ipsos poll, conducted in June, had already put Trump's approval rating among rural Americans dropped at a new low of 50%, with just 31% approving of his handling of economic issues.
The findings come as Democrats poll competitively in some traditionally Republican states such as Texas, Iowa, and Kansas. Democratic leaders are also addressing farmers' economic frustrations in their policy proposals. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, ranking member of the Senate Agriculture Committee, last month unveiled a bill intended to lay the groundwork for “America’s first-ever fertilizer reserve.” American farmers are “getting crushed from all sides by this Administration,” Schumer said as he introduced the Strategic Fertilizer Reserve Act with endorsements from the National Farmers Union and New York Farm Bureau.
Farmers and agricultural experts interviewed by TIME described four overlapping pressures: Trump’s expansion of low-tariff beef imports, rising fertilizer and diesel costs stemming from a global energy crisis triggered by the Iran war, and tariffs that have increased some production costs while provoking retaliation against American exports.
The impact has been felt by consumers, who have seen a steady climb in grocery prices. In one September AP-NORC poll, 64% of Americans said Trump has “gone too far” on imposing new tariffs on other countries. Trump’s latest tariff row with Canada has prompted further economic concern, particularly in rural states such as Montana, which listed Canada as its largest export market in 2025.
In response, White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told TIME that Trump “has repeatedly affirmed his support for America’s great farmers and ranchers.”
She added: “While the President has been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, the Administration continues to implement the proven Trump agenda of tax cuts, deregulation, and energy abundance to keep America on a solid economic trajectory.”
Trump campaigned on promises to keep the U.S. out of foreign wars and focus on prosperity at home.
The farmers who spoke to TIME say the economic consequences of his policies are now reaching their day-to-day operations.
Beef imports
The average price of ground beef in the U.S. has risen sharply since the end of 2020. It climbed from $5.58 per pound in August 2024 to $6.92 in August 2026, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Shrinking cattle herd sizes, drought and strong demand have all contributed to the increases. At the start of this year, the U.S. cattle inventory hit a 75-year low.
The price surge has created a political challenge for Trump.
“A major part of [Trump’s] campaign to households around the U.S. two years ago, was the fact that they could keep inflation low,” says Joe Glauber, a research fellow at the International Food Policy Research Institute, noting that many rural Americans and farmers are concerned that this hasn’t materialized.
Trump’s 90-day scheme to suspend tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of imported foreign beef to ease the strain on grocery bills went into effect on Sept. 1. The stated intention was for the imported beef to be sold at 25% lower than market price.
But the American Farm Bureau Federation (AFBF), an agriculture lobbying group, has urged Trump to reverse course, citing its own analysis that found the increased imports have not lowered prices for consumers. The AFBF tracked daily prices of 80% lean ground beef at 41 grocery stores in 22 states, starting the day after the proclamation went into effect. In 30 of those 41 stores, ground beef prices cost relatively the same on Sep. 23 as they did on Sep. 2.
Incumbent Texas Commissioner for Agriculture Sid Miller, an eighth-generation farmer and rancher, says farmers have felt the effects of the fallout of the beef import scheme.
“I haven't talked to one rancher that's not upset about it,” says Miller. “Just the packers and the processors are reaping the benefits, not the consumer or the cattle rancher. Calves that are going to market now are bringing $300-500 a head less.”
Derrell Peel, a professor of agricultural economics at Oklahoma State University who specializes in livestock and cattle markets, says ground beef has become the “poster child for higher food prices,” making it a focus of the political debate.
“Cattle producers increasingly feel that Trump is willing to throw them under the bus to try to get lower beef prices before the election,” Peel tells TIME. “None of the political actions have had any significant impact on beef prices and there is no quick solution to high beef prices.”
In Florida, Kansas, Kentucky, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Texas—10 major beef-producing states—Trump has seen a decline in approval rating, according to Civiqs polling data collected between Aug. 21-Sep. 21.
“For Republicans, as a rule, our strongest voting bloc is the rural areas of the United States,” says Miller.
“I think we're going to lose some statewide races in Texas because of multiple things,” he adds, listing tariffs, diesel fuel costs, and fertilizer prices as other key concerns. “It's like death from 1000 cuts.”
Recent ICE raids targeting meatpacking plants across Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas are also causing concern and placing further strain on the U.S. beef supply chain.
“ICE [recently] raided workers from packing plants in Kansas, shutting the packing plants down,” says Miller. “That lowers prices for the cattlemen because the cattle back up, they can't get processed, and it raises prices for the consumer, because there's less beef on the market.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Sept. 25 disputed the nature of the raids and said “ICE is not conducting worksite operations in Kansas.” Industry groups said worker absences nevertheless forced some plants to close temporarily.
Fertilizer
Steve Sheffels, a wheat farmer who serves as president of the Montana Grain Growers Association, says that around 40% of his expenses go towards buying fertilizer. He says that outlook could become “dire” if prices continue to rise.
Rising fertilizer costs, combined with extreme weather in Montana over the past year, has led Sheffels to conclude that “we are not able to produce our crops and make money doing it.”
Sheffels highlights a specific example of how his costs have risen since the onset of the Iran war.
“We just got done seeding this fall, and the cost of starter fertilizer, which has a lot of potassium in it, was just under $1,000 a ton,” he says. “Last year, it was $600 a ton.”
The rise of fertilizer costs is a major concern as crops such as corn and wheat heavily rely on nitrogen fertilizer. Natural gas is key in the production of nitrogen-based fertilizers, including urea and anhydrous ammonia. Exports of liquified natural gas from Gulf countries have been severely disrupted by the war and shipping disruptions have continued.
The shipping of natural gas exports via the Strait of Hormuz “remained effectively suspended” through August, according to data published last month, while other fertilizer product exports “remained sporadic and subdued” across the month.
In April, 94% of farmers responding to a Farmer & Rancher Policy Sentiment survey said the Iran war had impacted their business by raising fertilizer costs, energy costs, or both. While the survey came amid a sharp spike in fertilizer prices across April to June, concerns remain.
The price of anhydrous ammonia was up 9.3% as of late September compared to late February, before the onset of the war. The price of urea is up 7.9% for the same period, according to data from analytics company DTN.
Diesel fuel
In the U.S., the price of diesel hit record highs last month, sitting at a national average of over $6.52 per gallon on Sept. 22, according to the American Automobile Association.
Trump signed an Executive Order last week to waive the off-road requirement for a specific type of tax-free diesel fuel primarily used by the agriculture industry. Temporarily allowing highway use of red-dyed diesel “will put money directly back in the pockets of American farmers, truckers, and workers,” the White House said. While it may help lessen the costs associated with the transportation of harvested goods, Rendel says it “won’t be the solution for our farm economy woes.”
Days later, the President also announced that Russia had agreed to supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the American and global marketplace.
Prior to these efforts, Trump floated the possibility of a diesel export ban. But he ruled out the idea on Oct. 2 as the G7 group of nations committed to a co-ordinated release of 100 million barrels of diesel alongside other reserves through the International Energy Agency (IEA), in an effort to stabilise world energy markets.
In the meantime, farmers continue to grapple with increased prices.
“Diesel directly affects farm production costs for field operations, planting, harvesting, and for shipping both inputs and outputs,” says Peel. “The impact [when prices are increased] is very immediate.”
In the August AP/KFF poll, 67% of rural voters said they were “very or somewhat” worried about gasoline or other transportation costs.
Rendel is already feeling the impact. Last month, he explains, he had diesel delivered to his farm that cost him over $5 a gallon.
“I know in a lot of the world, that's probably not ridiculous, but for farm diesel, which is subjected to a lower tax rate in the U.S., that is ridiculous,” he says. “Anytime it goes over $4, it gets painful, and now we're already over five.”
“Fuel is a real strong pain point for everyone. As long as the war is going on, there's really not going to be any significant relief available,” he adds.
Crop farmers in particular rely on heavy, diesel-fueled machinery to sow and harvest.
“If fertilizer prices rise, which they have risen over the past year or so, you can really look at your soil fertility and make decisions that can save you some money. When seed prices go up, you can shop around and maybe find less expensive seed or reduce your seeding rates,” Rendel says. “But fuel's not that way. My combine, when I'm harvesting soybeans, uses about 200 gallons of fuel per day, and that doesn't change.”
Diesel is also essential for transporting goods once they are harvested. “I’ve got to deliver the grain to the buyer. The fuel is a very inflexible expense,” Rendel says, citing a lack of alternatives.
Sheffels is feeling the impact of transport costs as a result of diesel fuel prices, too. “We're having to pay more to get our grain moved around in the short term,” he says. “In the long term, it's going to have a huge [financial] impact because of the distances.”
The renewed trade war with Canada has added to concerns for farmers in the U.S., after negotiations between the two countries collapsed in August. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods took effect last month, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matching the levies imposed by the Trump Administration. Canada's counter tariffs apply to products covering $27.6 billion in imports from the U.S., focusing on sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, among other products.
“The U.S. and Canadian economies are highly integrated,” says Peel. “There are no winners in trade wars in general and especially in this one with so many components that will be impacted.”
Overall, tariffs on key production inputs have imposed roughly $2.6 billion in additional costs on crop farmers from February 2025 through July 2026, according to data from the Association of Equipment Manufacturers.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House in late September, Beijing agreed to drop tariffs on various U.S. agricultural products. However, soybeans were excluded from the list, and will remain subjected to 10% tariffs, offering little relief to farmers like Rendel.
Soybeans remained the top U.S. agricultural export to China in 2025, even as shipments fell by roughly three-quarters between 2024 and 2025 amid Trump’s implementation of wide ranging tariffs on Beijing.
For farmers already facing higher diesel and fertilizer costs, shrinking export markets create pressure at both ends of the supply chain. “You're hitting people at both levels, at the input level, and then look at the prices they get for their commodity if they're not able to export it,” says Glauber, from the International Food Policy Research Institute.
Sheffels says the repeated policy shifts are disruptive for farmers across America.
“The level of uncertainty that we've had to live with is completely unacceptable,” he says. “It's impossible to make investment decisions when you don't know what the rules are going to be five minutes from now, let alone in six months.”
With the midterms fast approaching, the question for Republicans is whether that frustration will change how some farmers vote—or whether they vote at all.

articles.title: IDF investigates last two interceptors launched in 48 hours against aerial targets in Lebanon
articles.body:
The IDF launched an interceptor toward a suspicious aerial target detected near Israeli troops operating in southern Lebanon, the military announced on Monday. No alerts were activated, in accordance with military policy.
The incident marks the second time in two days that Israeli forces in Lebanon have faced an unidentified aerial threat, with the defense establishment still unable to explain either incident.
During Sunday night's suspected aerial infiltration from Lebanon, the object was initially detected deep inside Lebanese territory, some distance from the Israeli border. It was flying at low altitude and high speed near the northern Israeli community of Arab al-Aramshe when it was detected by Israel Air Force radar. The information was subsequently relayed to the Galilee Division's surveillance operations center.
IDF surveillance soldiers identified the suspicious object and captured it on camera, but it disappeared shortly afterward, reportedly after crossing into Israeli territory. The military has yet to determine what the object was or what happened to it.
A military source in the IDF's Northern Command said officials had considered the possibility from the outset that the object was not a hostile aircraft.
"There were officials who, from the very first stage, claimed that it was a group of balloons tied together that had been carried by the wind," he said.
Overnight search operations utilized to determine circumstances of incident
Search operations continued overnight, with additional forces deployed at first light to locate the object or recover evidence that could help determine what happened.
Meanwhile, officials in the IDF's Intelligence Directorate used intelligence capabilities to verify the circumstances of the incident.
As of Monday, no new information had emerged to identify the object, and the military had provided no additional details about the separate aerial threat detected earlier that morning.
The two incidents have left the IDF without clear answers about the nature of the unidentified aerial threats facing its forces in southern Lebanon.

articles.title: Senior MP: Countries backing militant groups should await Iran's response
articles.body:
Senior MP: Countries backing militant groups should await Iran's response
TEHRAN – Chairman of the Iranian Parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission Ebrahim Azizi has warned regional countries providing resources to counter-revolutionary groups that Tehran possesses documented evidence of their support and will confront them decisively.
Speaking about security conditions in southeastern Iran, Azizi pointed to Sistan and Baluchestan province's 1,300-kilometer border with Pakistan and Afghanistan and its security implications, saying the counter-revolution's operations room has moved toward hybrid warfare with the support of certain regional states and currents aligned with the enemies of the Iranian nation.
"This is not an intelligence analysis, this is an intelligence document," Azizi said. He added that in recent meetings with relevant officials it became completely clear and evident that groups long based in those two neighboring countries have carried out actions with the backing and support of certain states.
Azizi said the Quds Headquarters of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Ground Force, the Islamic Republic Army and the Law Enforcement Command have implemented firm and serious measures. He expressed confidence that with combined actions underway in border security and border closure, as well as development and domestic defense, remaining concerns in the region will be resolved.
The Americans should know, and certain regional countries should know, that the countries which have provided heavy resources to counter-revolutionary groups in this province and supported them should know that all intelligence documents exist, he said. Just as the Islamic Republic defeated the United States and its allies in the combined war, it will also confront these proxies and groups seeking to assert themselves in line with American actions.
Azizi said some regional countries feeling defeated have joined this trend out of alignment with the Americans, stressing that the Islamic Republic is vigilant, awake, monitoring, prepared and powerful. He praised the readiness of the Quds Headquarters observed during his recent visit.
He emphasized that the Islamic Republic has for years brought all its capacities to serve border residents, particularly in the southeast in Sistan and Baluchestan and South Khorasan. Claims of discrimination and injustice in the province stem either from lack of knowledge or ill intent, he said.
Iran's armed forces, security forces, Intelligence Ministry, police and all pillars of the Islamic system will not allow insecurity to continue, Azizi said, condemning recent blind, brutal and inhumane acts, including the martyrdom of a female officer of the province's police social affairs deputy who was serving the people. He said such crimes show that counter-revolutionary groups neither know the people of Sistan and Baluchestan nor correctly understand the authority of the Islamic Republic.
Azizi said border closure is a serious priority, urging the government to urgently complete full border blockage with approved funds, accelerate smart border technologies, and dismantle insecurity chains to pave the way for development and prosperity of border areas.

articles.title: Britain calls in industry for fleet of drone submarines
articles.body:
The Royal Navy has opened preliminary market engagement for the Type 93 extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicle and the AUKUS Signature Payload Programme, inviting companies to register interest before any requirement is set, according to a notice published on Find a Tender at ten past twelve on Monday.
“The Royal Navy seeks to improve its understanding of the market and wider ecosystem for Extra-Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) platforms, associated payloads, and enabling functions,” it says. “This activity supports the development of the Type 93 capability and the Royal Navy’s commitments under the AUKUS Pillar II Signature Project.”
Registrations are sought from “XLUUV platform providers, payload providers, relevant technology and software suppliers including Autonomy, AI and Mission Management Systems, integrators, through-life support providers, and other relevant suppliers.” Those who come forward may be invited to collaborative workshops, one to one meetings, industry days and written requests for information, and small and medium-sized enterprises are flagged as particularly suitable.
“The Royal Navy is initially considering platforms approximately 2 metres in diameter and 12 metres in length, however organisations offering platforms of other dimensions are also encouraged to register,” the notice says, adding that it “should not be considered as a commitment from the Royal Navy to progress with any future procurement activities.”
XV Excalibur, the uncrewed submarine Britain already operates, is twelve metres long, two metres across and displaces nineteen tonnes. It was unveiled at Devonport in May last year, as this publication reported at the time, having been built by MSubs of Plymouth under the three-year Project Cetus, for which the Ministry of Defence awarded a £15.4 million contract in December 2022. It joined the Fleet Experimentation Squadron as a demonstrator with no operational role.
The Royal Navy controlled Excalibur in home waters from an operating centre in Australia during Talisman Sabre in July 2025, the first British and Australian demonstration of XLUUV interoperability under AUKUS Pillar II. It carried out the first underwater operation of a quantum optical atomic clock that November and transferred to Royal Navy ownership in December. In June the Submarine Delivery Agency awarded MSubs a further £6.7 million for trials and evaluation running to May 2028, work intended to move the programme towards functional payloads.
On 13 September, Excalibur fired an American Mark 48 exercise torpedo at the British Underwater Test and Evaluation Centre in Scotland. Britain and the United States described it as the first time either country had launched a heavyweight torpedo from an uncrewed vessel, carried out under Project Broadsword and Trial Iron, both part of AUKUS Pillar II.
The Type 93 designation first appeared in February last year, in Project CABOT documents setting out a persistent wide area anti-submarine search capability built around the Type 92 Sloop, an uncrewed surface vessel, and the Type 93 Chariot, described then as a drone submarine. Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, confirmed in July that the Defence Investment Plan had announced Type 92 uncrewed underwater sensing platforms and Type 93 extra-large uncrewed underwater vessels as part of the Atlantic Bastion programme, adding that the number of platforms to be procured and their construction schedules had not yet been determined.
He has also told Parliament that the Hybrid Navy will take at least £1.5 billion over four years, and that by 2030 the aim is to have the first large autonomous vessels in service, among them a prototype uncrewed missile platform and extra-large uncrewed underwater vessels carrying payloads developed through AUKUS.
The notice states that the programme “directly aligns with the Strategic Defence Review (SDR), Defence Investment Plan (DIP) and AUKUS Pillar II priorities, supporting the transition to a Hybrid Navy through the integration of autonomous and uncrewed maritime capabilities.”

articles.title: Hungarian Ad Agency Got Millions From Firm Owned by Orban’s Billionaire Friend
articles.body:
Just a few years after launching in 2020, Megafon Digital Incubator Center had become one of Hungary’s most influential political advertising agencies, mainly running social media campaigns in support of the ruling party and its leader, Viktor Orbán.
But Megafon appears to have lost its sense of purpose since Orbán was swept from power in national elections this past April. Four months after that stunning loss, its website was taken offline.
Now, internal documents from a firm called V-Híd Zrt reveal the source of much of Megafon’s income. Around $12 million in donations came from that company, which is owned by Lőrinc Mészáros, Orbán’s childhood friend.
Mészáros became fabulously wealthy during Orbán’s 16 years in power, building a business empire spanning sectors from construction to banking and energy. Mészáros’ companies won seven percent of all public procurement contracts — together worth about $2 billion — between 2018 and 2020 alone, according to Transparency International.
József Péter Martin, executive director of Transparency International’s Hungarian chapter, said the relationship between Megafon and Mészáros illustrates how Orbán and his Fidesz party relied on affluent elites and friendly media — and how those allies benefited in turn.
“It’s a vicious cycle,” Martin told OCCRP’s member center, Direkt36.
“Mészáros’s company wins the public procurement contract and gets rich as a result. He uses that money to fund a private company that works to keep Fidesz in power by spreading propaganda,” he said.
Research groups like the Rule of Law Lab at New York University have documented in detail how Orbán and Fidesz co-opted the media to maintain power.
Public broadcasters became government mouthpieces, while there was a “consolidation of private outlets under allied ownership,” the Rule of Law Lab said in a report early this year. Eventually, the report noted, Mészáros “became Hungary’s largest media owner.”
Mészáros did not own Megafon, but his company’s money was key to its operations, according to the documents obtained by Direkt36. They show that payments from V-Híd amounted to one third of Megafon’s total revenue from 2022 to 2024. The funding grew year-by-year, accounting for more than half of Megafon’s entire income in 2024.
The payments from V-Híd were referenced in the documents as “donations.”
Neither V-Híd nor Megafon responded to requests for comment. Mészáros did not respond to requests for comment.
Communications included among the documents show a cordial relationship between the two companies. In one February 2023 exchange, Megafon’s founder, István Kovács, wrote to V-Híd to express gratitude for the donations his company had received — and to say the company was open to more funding.
“On behalf of the entire Megafon team, I would like to once again thank you for your previous support,” Kovács wrote in an email.
A week later, a V-Híd executive issued an internal order: “Please transfer the 500 million to Megafon now!”
That amount — worth about $1.4 million at the time — was sent by V-Híd the same day, according to a transfer receipt included in the documents. In July 2023, V-Híd made another transfer of about $1 million.
Funds from V-Híd helped Megafon pump out a steady stream of pro-Fidesz messages on social media. These included videos posted before the 2024 municipal elections accusing the opposition of trying to drag Hungary into war by supporting Ukraine in its fight against Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
Megafon kept campaigning in the run-up to the vote this year, organizing an event featuring Orbán, and posting pro-Fidesz messages on social media.
But the advertising agency’s fortunes were about to change.
After winning elections in April, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar pledged to stop state advertising being funneled into pro-Fidesz media — including almost 500 outlets that had been consolidated as part of the Central European Press and Media Foundation (KESMA).
Some outlets reportedly stopped publishing and others downsized, including Mediaworks, which was owned by Mészáros and folded into KESMA. Mediaworks announced in mid-June that it would undertake a restructuring process that would involve “changes in staff numbers.”
Megafon appears to have suffered a similar fate. A document from a company that provides Hungarian business intelligence and commercial registry data shows that the Megafon had 72 employees in April. By August, the company was down to three staff members, and its website was taken offline.

articles.title: Which airlines have cancelled Saudi flights amid Houthi attacks?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Which airlines have cancelled Saudi flights amid Houthi attacks?
Major international airlines have suspended flights to Saudi Arabia following escalating Houthi attacks and threats against airports across the kingdom, leaving passengers facing cancellations, delays and diversions.
The disruption follows a series of attacks on Riyadh's main airport over the weekend that killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300, forcing authorities to temporarily close King Khalid International Airport.
The Houthis have warned that Saudi airports remain potential targets, raising concerns about further disruption to international air travel.
Some airlines have suspended services until mid-October, while others have extended cancellations until the end of the month.
Here's what to know about the flight cancellations, affected airports and travel warnings.
Which airlines have suspended flights to Saudi Arabia?
Several major international airlines have suspended flights to Riyadh, while others have cancelled selected services to Jeddah and Dammam.
According to Reuters, Lufthansa Group has suspended flights to Riyadh until 16 October, while Air France-KLM has halted services to the Saudi capital until the end of the month.
Other airlines have announced the following cancellations:
- Flydubai: All flights to and from Riyadh cancelled through 14 October.
- Air India: Riyadh services suspended until 15 October.
- Air India Express: Riyadh flights suspended until 14 October.
- SriLankan Airlines: Riyadh services suspended until 18 October.
- Etihad Airways: Selected flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam cancelled between 11 and 13 October.
- Emirates: Flights between Dubai and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam affected by cancellations on Monday, 12 October.
- Air Arabia: Cancellations and schedule changes affecting Saudi routes.
- Qatar Airways and Kuwait Airways: Riyadh flights cancelled.
- Gulf Air: Flight cancelled to and from Riyadh until 17 October.
- Delta Air Lines: Delayed the inaugural flight that was set to launch between Atlanta and Riyadh on 23 October until March 2027, citing "evolving developments in the region".
The cancellations do not amount to a complete suspension of international flights to Saudi Arabia, with several airports continuing to operate despite significant disruption.
Are Saudi Arabia's airports still open?
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been the worst affected following the weekend's deadly attacks.
Saudi authorities extended a notice to air missions (NOTAM) closing the airport until midnight local time on Saturday, 17 October.
Flight-tracking platform Flightradar24 ranked Riyadh's airport as the world's most disrupted airport on Monday.
Elsewhere, airports remain operational but are experiencing delays and cancellations.
Jeddah: King Abdulaziz International Airport remains open, although flights have faced significant disruption. Flightradar24 ranked it the world's second-most disrupted airport on Monday, after Riyadh.
Dammam: King Fahd International Airport is continuing operations despite delays. It has also received flights diverted from Riyadh.
Medina: Air traffic was continuing around Prince Mohammad bin Abdulaziz International Airport on Monday, according to live flight-tracking data.
Despite the disruption, aircraft are continuing to use Saudi airspace, according to flight-tracking data collected on Monday.
Why are Saudi airports being targeted?
The flight cancellations follow an escalation in attacks by Yemen's Houthis against Saudi Arabia, including the deadly strikes on Riyadh's airport over the weekend.
On Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree renewed the group's warning against using Saudi airports, describing them as "potential targets and sites for operations by our forces".
He urged airlines, airport employees and passengers to take the warning seriously.
The Houthis have, however, said that the holy cities of Mecca and Medina are exempt from their threats.
The warnings have raised concerns about the safety of civilian aviation and the possibility of further disruption if attacks continue.

Which countries have issued travel warnings for Saudi Arabia?
Several countries have updated their travel advice amid the escalating attacks, warning citizens about security risks and disruption to flights.
Australia and New Zealand issued warnings on Monday urging travellers to avoid Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and reconsider travel through other Saudi airports.
The warnings follow similar advisories from the UK, US, Canada, Japan and South Korea.
The UK's Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office advises against all but essential travel to several parts of Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh, Aseer, Najran and Jizan provinces.
On Sunday, it added Jeddah and Dammam to the areas covered by that advice.
British authorities also advise against all travel within 10 kilometres of the border with Yemen.
Meanwhile, the US Embassy in Riyadh has advised American citizens to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia as a whole, citing threats linked to the Houthis and continuing security concerns surrounding the US-Israeli war with Iran.

articles.title: UN official: Environmental protection must be integral to post-war recovery
articles.body:
UN official: Environmental protection must be integral to post-war recovery
TEHRAN – UN Resident Coordinator in Iran Christine Weigand has stressed the far-reaching and long-term environmental consequences of war, saying environmental protection must be incorporated into both emergency response measures and long-term recovery plans, as protecting the environment ultimately means safeguarding human health, livelihoods and the future.
Weigand made the remarks in Tehran on Sunday at a conference on the environmental consequences of war and human rights.
Referring to the loss of human lives, the displacement of families and the destruction of homes and infrastructure, she said the environment and valuable ecosystems were also among the victims of war, warning that the damage inflicted on them could persist for generations.
Conflicts and environmental degradation, she noted, reinforce one another, deepening human suffering, undermining livelihoods and food security, and making reconstruction and the achievement of sustainable development more difficult.
Weigand also referred to the United Nations’ designation of November 6 as the International Day for Preventing the Exploitation of the Environment in War and Armed Conflict in 2001. She noted that contaminated water resources, damaged agricultural land and degraded ecosystems have consequences that extend far beyond the immediate destruction caused by war, undermining communities’ ability to rebuild their lives.
Citing examples of environmental damage in the conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine, the UN official addressed the consequences of attacks on oil facilities and water infrastructure in Iran. She said attacks on oil facilities had released smoke containing hazardous substances into Tehran’s atmosphere, while damage to a desalination facility on Qeshm Island had reportedly disrupted water supplies to more than 25 villages.
Weigand also warned of the possibility of oil pollution reaching the mangrove forests on Qeshm Island, emphasizing that such contamination could threaten sensitive coastal ecosystems along the Persian Gulf.
Recalling her own experience of air pollution in Tehran following the attacks on oil facilities, she said that, for millions of people, the issue was not merely an environmental concern but one that directly affected the air they breathed every day.
The UN Resident Coordinator cautioned that the disappearance of visible smoke does not necessarily mean the danger has passed. Burning oil can release hazardous compounds, she explained, and the resulting pollution can contaminate soil and water, affect agricultural produce and threaten human health. These consequences may persist long after a conflict ends, with children and future generations particularly vulnerable.
Emphasizing that investment in environmental protection is an investment in people and their future, Weigand said healthy ecosystems sustain community livelihoods, provide clean water and safe food, and strengthen societies’ resilience to crises. Conversely, the degradation of these systems increases vulnerability and makes recovery more difficult.
She identified evidence-based assessments, stronger national environmental management capacities, cooperation among different sectors and national and international institutions, and investment in climate change adaptation as essential measures for protecting and restoring the environment in conflict-affected countries.
Weigand also highlighted the longstanding cooperation between the UN Country Team in Iran and national partners in areas including climate resilience, sustainable water resource management, biodiversity conservation and pollution reduction. She reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to continuing this cooperation and its readiness to support national efforts to address emerging environmental needs.
Concluding her remarks, the UN official stressed that commitment to protecting and restoring nature must remain unwavering in the face of global environmental challenges.
“Our shared responsibility is to protect what remains, restore what has been damaged, and invest in building a more sustainable and peaceful future for all,” she said.

articles.title: Uncrewed truck with anti-drone laser shown at AUSA
articles.body:
- Harbinger’s uncrewed Praesidia hybrid truck is powering an AeroVironment LOCUST X3 30-kW counter-drone laser at American Rheinmetall’s AUSA 2026 booth.
- The companies have not said whether the laser-armed configuration is tied to any U.S. Army contract or test.
An uncrewed hybrid truck built by California’s Harbinger is powering a 30-kilowatt AeroVironment counter-drone laser at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington this week, shown at American Rheinmetall’s booth.
Harbinger CEO John Henry Harris said in a LinkedIn post on Oct. 12 that the company’s Praesidia vehicle is supplying power to an AeroVironment LOCUST X3 laser weapon mounted on the truck, with autonomy software from Forterra.
The display is at Rheinmetall’s booth, No. 2285. Harris pitched the combination as cheap, mass-producible equipment with “unlimited magazine depth,” a reference to the fact that a laser keeps firing as long as it has electrical power rather than running out of missiles or rounds. He did not say whether the system has been tested together in the field, whether any U.S. Army unit plans to use it, or what it would cost.
The Praesidia is a militarized version of the plug-in hybrid chassis Harbinger builds for commercial delivery trucks. It has no cab, is driven by wire so autonomy kits can control steering, braking and acceleration, and combines a large battery pack with a gasoline engine that acts as a generator. Harbinger says the vehicle can travel more than 800 km (500 miles) on a full tank and full battery, or about 170 km (105 miles) on electric power alone, and can export up to 350 kW of power to equipment it carries. That power is what a laser weapon needs: a high-energy laser draws electricity continuously while firing, and the vehicle carrying it has to supply it.
AeroVironment’s LOCUST laser family came from BlueHalo, which AeroVironment acquired in 2025. The U.S. Army has tested earlier LOCUST lasers mounted on Joint Light Tactical Vehicles as part of its effort to shoot down small drones without spending missiles. AeroVironment has not published detailed specifications for the X3 version beyond the 30 kW power level Harris cited.
The truck at AUSA comes from a program already under contract. In August, the U.S. Army gave American Rheinmetall an 18-month deal to build autonomous supply vehicles under Project Sustainment, using Harbinger’s chassis, Forterra’s autonomy software and Primordial Labs’ Anura control interface. Those vehicles are meant to haul supplies to company-sized units without a driver. Harbinger has also said it is configuring the Praesidia for battlefield communications, troop transport, perimeter security and counter-drone missions, and the CIA-backed venture firm In-Q-Tel invested in the company in June.

articles.title: Iran says reviewing US proposals for talks as indirect messages continue
articles.body:
Iran said Monday that it is reviewing US proposals for negotiations as Tehran and Washington continue to exchange messages through mediators, Anadolu reports.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told his weekly press conference that Pakistan and Qatar continue to play a mediating role between Iran and the US.
“The exchange of messages between Iran and the US through mediators continues,” Baqaei said.
“We are reviewing the Americans’ proposals for negotiations. Iran’s preconditions must be observed for any negotiations,” he added.
Baqaei said Russia also continues to play a “constructive” role regarding Iran’s nuclear file, pointing to Moscow’s involvement in the 2015 nuclear agreement.
He said Iranian and Russian relations are based on mutual trust and that Tehran welcomes supportive efforts by friendly countries, but stressed that, “technically and precisely,” mediation between Iran and the US remains in the hands of countries such as Pakistan and Qatar.

Strait of Hormuz
Turning to the Strait of Hormuz, Baqaei said developments there were a direct consequence of US and Israeli attacks on Iran and rejected suggestions that Tehran’s actions were intended to create negotiating leverage.
“What we have seen in the Strait of Hormuz since Feb. 28 was the direct result of the US and the Israeli regime’s attack on Iran,” he said.
“With the current US approach, security will not return,” he added.
Baqaei rejected US assertions that Iran had lost its leverage, saying such claims did not correspond with realities on the ground.
“They can say Iran has lost its leverage, but we are doing our work,” he said, arguing that energy markets were not responding to Washington’s assertions.
Baqaei also expressed “deep concern” over continuing tensions on the Arab Peninsula and said Tehran was ready to facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.
“We do not want war and hostilities to continue between two Islamic countries,” he said.
The spokesman said Iran’s consultations with regional countries were continuing and that Tehran had repeatedly offered to help facilitate dialogue and a peaceful settlement.
